CVE-2025-41450.exploitation_status: Known exploited: CISA added it to KEV on 25 Nov 2026 (deadline 9 Dec). No attacker named. Public exploit code reported since 13 Oct 2026. Its use in the October 2026 French supermarket attacks is unconfirmed.
CVE-2025-41450.how_exploited: An authentication bypass in the web management interface of Danfoss AK-SM 800A (AK-SM 8xxA) refrigeration and building system managers. Claroty Team82 found a hidden alternative login path, probably meant for vendor support, that accepts a 'code of the day' the device derives from its current date instead of the administrator password. Anyone who reconstructs the algorithm from the firmware can produce a valid code for any day, which gives a fully authenticated administrative session. That session also opens the way to post-login flaws such as the alarm-email command injection CVE-2025-41451, which can lead to remote code execution.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the AK-SM 800A web management interface over the network. Claroty cites a Censys count of 2,765 internet-exposed AK-SM 800A devices.
Firmware older than R4.2 (SM800A-4.2.4).
No valid account is needed. CISA rates attack complexity as high, and Claroty describes no user interaction.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers find internet-exposed AK-SM 800A web interfaces, either directly or through cellular modems and contractor remote-access paths.
Initial access: the attacker logs in through the hidden date-based login path and gets a full administrative session without the administrator password.
Execution: with that session the attacker can change settings directly, or chain CVE-2025-41451 (command injection in alarm-email settings) to run commands on the device.

Persistence: Midnight Blue notes that the controllers lack secure boot, so code planted after compromise can persist. CERT-FR says a factory reset removes persistence but leaves the device open to reinfection.

Impact seen in related attacks: in the October 2026 campaign against French and other European supermarkets, attackers forced refrigeration into defrost and destroyed stock. Which flaw gave them access has not been confirmed.
who_is_exposed: Operators of Danfoss AK-SM 800A (AK-SM 8xxA) system managers on firmware older than R4.2. These are common in supermarkets, cold stores and commercial buildings worldwide.
Highest risk: units whose web interface is reachable from the internet, including through cellular modems or public IP addresses used for contractor remote service.
Refrigeration service contractors who manage fleets of these controllers remotely.
Older AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 models that are end-of-life and cannot be patched also need to be removed from the internet. Danfoss tied most of the units hit in France to such models.
detect: Version check: read the firmware version on each controller. Anything older than R4.2 is vulnerable to this flaw, and anything older than R4.3.1 is also vulnerable to CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452.
Exposure check: confirm whether each controller's web interface can be reached from the internet, including through cellular modems and contractor links.
Controller audit log: look for administrative logins with no matching activity from a known technician, logins at unusual times or from unknown addresses, and new or changed user accounts.
Configuration review: compare setpoints, defrost schedules, alarm and alarm-email settings and remote-access settings against a known-good baseline, as CERT-FR and the national CERTs advise.
Physical signals: unexplained defrost cycles, rising cabinet temperatures or silenced alarms. Use independent temperature sensors, because a compromised controller's readings cannot be trusted.

Network and OT monitoring: look for connections from internet addresses not on your contractor allow-list. OT vulnerability scanners have plugins for this CVE. No indicators of compromise were published in the sources read.

steps: List every Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC controller, record its model and firmware, and record whether it can be reached from the internet.
Take the management interface off the internet now, including access through cellular modems. Check your insurance and service contract before cutting the contractor's data link, as CERT-FR advises.
Preserve evidence before changing exposed units: export logs and configuration, as CISA's forensic triage requirements describe.
Upgrade the firmware: R4.2 (SM800A-4.2.4) fixes this flaw, and R4.3.1 (SM800A-4.3.1) or later also fixes CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Follow Danfoss's AK-SM 800A software upgrade process.
Turn on Strict security/session mode and change all passwords, including default ones, as CERT-FR advises.
Restore remote access only through a VPN or a brokered remote-access service. Allow-listing contractor IP addresses on a firewall is acceptable only as a short-term measure.
Replace end-of-life models that cannot be patched, or keep them fully isolated.
fixed_versions: AK-SM 8xxA release R4.3.1 (SM800A-4.3.1) for CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452
workarounds: Minimise network exposure, keep the controller off the internet and behind firewalls, and use VPNs for remote access (CISA ICSA-25-140-03 recommended practices).
Remove internet exposure, restore access only by secure VPN or a protected network, and set the security level to Strict (CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-ALE-012).
verify: Confirm in the web interface that each unit reports R4.2 or later, and preferably R4.3.1 or later.
From an external network, including the cellular path, confirm that the controller's interface is no longer reachable.
Confirm that Strict mode is on and that only known accounts exist.
Rescan with an OT vulnerability scanner and confirm the finding is gone.
if_compromised: Cut the controller off from the internet. Keep refrigeration under local or manual control and check product temperatures with independent sensors.
Preserve the controller's logs and configuration exports before changing anything.

Restart the device, or factory reset it if a restart does not clear the compromise. Then update the firmware and reconfigure it from a verified baseline. CERT-FR warns that a reset alone leaves the device open to reinfection.
Change all credentials on the device and any reused elsewhere, such as contractor remote-access and alarm-email accounts, and check connected equipment.
Report to Danfoss and your national CERT. US federal agencies must report to CISA under BOD 26-04.

CVE-2025-41450.caveats: Danfoss advisory DSA-2025-03-01 returned 403 and was not read, so this rests on CISA, CERT-FR and Claroty. Who exploited it, and when, is not public. The link to the October 2026 supermarket attacks is unconfirmed. Claroty also cites R4.3.1 as the fix, while CISA gives R4.2. Midnight Blue reports six more unpatched flaws (no CVEs yet) up to firmware 5.3.2, so patching alone does not make an exposed unit safe.

CVE-2025-42884.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per CISA, which added it to KEV on 20 Nov 2026 and marks exploitation active; no attackers, victims or start date named, no public exploit code reported. Fixed by SAP Note 3660969 (11 Nov 2025).
CVE-2025-42884.how_exploited: JNDI injection in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal, recorded by SAP under CWE-943 (improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic) and rated 6.5. SAP says an unauthenticated attacker can inject JNDI environment properties or supply the address used in a JNDI lookup, so the portal's Java server queries a naming provider the attacker chose. SAP rates the result as disclosure or modification of information about the server, with no impact on availability. Onapsis, whose research lab found it, gives the same description.
preconditions: SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal with EP-BASIS 7.50 or EP-RUNTIME 7.50 without SAP Security Note 3660969 applied.
Network access to the portal's web interface; no login and no user interaction are needed (CVSS vector AV:N/PR:N/UI:N).
For an attacker-chosen naming provider to be reached, the portal server must be able to make outbound connections to it.
attack_path: Initial access: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted input to the Enterprise Portal's web interface.
Execution: the portal uses that input in a JNDI lookup, connecting to a naming provider the attacker chose instead of the intended one.
Impact per SAP: the attacker can read or change information about the server; no source read describes follow-on activity by real attackers.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal 7.50 (EP-BASIS and EP-RUNTIME 7.50) without the November 2025 note, on-premises or in a self-managed cloud.
Portals published to the internet for employees, partners or suppliers are most at risk; internal-only portals can still be reached from a compromised internal host.
Other SAP NetWeaver products are not listed as affected in the CVE record.
detect: Check every Enterprise Portal system for SAP Security Note 3660969 with the SAP Note Assistant or your SAP security monitoring tool.
Review the portal's HTTP access logs and the Java server's default trace and application logs for unauthenticated requests that carry naming-service addresses or unusual parameters.
Watch for outbound connections from SAP Java application servers to unknown hosts on directory or naming-service ports, which these servers normally do not make.
Neither SAP's public record nor Onapsis's patch-day summary publishes indicators or detection rules; SAP security monitoring products may include checks for the note.

steps: Apply SAP Security Note 3660969 (November 2025 Patch Day) to every SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal 7.50 system, following the note's instructions.
Until patched, restrict access to the portal from the internet to known users, for example through a reverse proxy or VPN.
Block outbound connections from SAP Java servers to the internet except to destinations they need, which limits lookups to attacker-controlled providers.
Because CISA reports active exploitation, review logs on portals that were exposed and unpatched for signs of abuse.
fixed_versions: SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal EP-BASIS 7.50 and EP-RUNTIME 7.50 with SAP Security Note 3660969 applied
verify: Confirm in the SAP Note Assistant (or system patch status) that note 3660969 is fully implemented on every portal system, including test and disaster-recovery copies.
Rerun your SAP vulnerability scanner or security monitoring check for CVE-2025-42884.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected portal from the internet and preserve HTTP, security audit and Java server logs.
Check for changed server configuration and naming entries, and compare against a known-good baseline.
Rotate service account passwords and connection secrets stored on the portal server.
Check connected SAP back-end systems for unusual logins from the portal's service users.
Report the incident to your national CERT (CISA in the United States) and open a case with SAP.

CVE-2025-42884.caveats: SAP Note 3660969 needs an SAP login and was not read; the description comes from SAP's CVE record, its 2025 bulletin (summarised copy) and Onapsis. SAP gives no public workaround. Only CISA reports exploitation, without detail, so attackers and any chaining with other flaws are unknown. CWE-943 in CISA's name is SAP's mapping; the flaw is a JNDI injection.

CVE-2025-61624.exploitation_status: Known exploited: Fortinet's advisory FG-IR-26-122 marks it exploited and CISA added it to KEV on 16 Oct 2026 (due 19 Oct). Unit 42 (14 Oct 2026) saw cluster CL-STA-0954, also tracked as UNC5820, use it to get root on FortiGate firewalls.
CVE-2025-61624.how_exploited: A path traversal flaw in the command line interface of FortiOS, FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager. An attacker who already holds an administrator account gives crafted names to existing CLI commands, and the device writes or deletes files outside the intended folder. Unit 42 reports the weak spot was an object name in the automation script feature: the attackers wrote script content to arbitrary places on the file system, which then ran with root privileges. That turns an administrator login, which normally has no shell, into full root control of the appliance's operating system, enough to plant a memory-resident implant.
preconditions: The attacker is authenticated with an administrator profile that has at least read-write permissions (Fortinet and CISA); Unit 42 saw it used from an administrative account, including super_admin.
The attacker can reach the device's management interface (CLI over SSH, console or the management channel).

An affected release: FortiOS 7.6.0 to 7.6.4, 7.4.0 to 7.4.9 and all 7.2, 7.0 and 6.4; FortiProxy 7.6.0 to 7.6.4, 7.4.0 to 7.4.11 and all 7.2 and 7.0; FortiPAM 1.0 to 1.7.0; FortiSwitchManager 7.2.0 to 7.2.7 and 7.0.0 to 7.0.6.
attack_path: Credential theft first: in the Unit 42 case the attackers exploited FortiManager flaw CVE-2024-47575 in September 2024 and stole a configuration archive with credentials and certificates for over 500 managed firewalls.
Access: they decrypted stolen administrator and VPN credentials, opened SSL VPN sessions into management segments and logged in to firewalls as administrators.
Privilege escalation: this flaw let them write script content as root on selected firewalls, escaping the restricted administrator shell.
Persistence: they dropped the PEERSTITCH loader, which injects code into the logging and IPsec VPN daemons, leaves no file on disk, opens no ports and lets tagged VPN sessions skip security checks.

Command and control and evasion: a rogue certificate-management component served as a control channel, the attackers impersonated the FortiManager using stolen trust material, removed artifacts and disrupted logging.
who_is_exposed: FortiGate firewalls (FortiOS), FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager on the affected releases, on-premises or virtual.
Highest risk: fleets managed centrally by a FortiManager or a managed service provider, where one breach exposes every device's administrator credentials.
Devices whose management interface is reachable from the internet or from broad internal networks raise the risk, since only an administrator login is needed.
FortiOS 7.2, 7.0 and 6.4 and FortiProxy 7.2 and 7.0 get no fix in those branches; they must move to a fixed release.
detect: Version check: compare each device's firmware with the fixed releases in Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-122.
Configuration history: audit configuration revisions for automation script objects whose names contain path traversal sequences (Unit 42 recommendation).
Logins: review administrator logins and SSL VPN sessions for unknown sources, logins with credentials that should be unused, and activity under the FortiGateCloud account name.
Management channel: review sessions on the FortiGate to FortiManager port for connections from anything other than your real FortiManager.

Implant hunting needs specialist work: memory maps of the logging and IPsec daemons for unexpected executable regions, cross-process memory writes, and crash logs showing segmentation faults in the logging, VPN or syslog services.
Indicators and a YARA rule for PEERSTITCH are published in the Unit 42 report; Fortinet lists virtual patch signature FG-VD-59270.0day.

steps: Upgrade each affected device to a fixed release, using Fortinet's upgrade path tool; move devices on branches with no fix (FortiOS 7.2, 7.0, 6.4; FortiProxy 7.2, 7.0; FortiPAM 1.6 and older) to a supported fixed branch.
Patch any FortiManager against CVE-2024-47575 and treat it as a possible source of stolen credentials.
Restrict management interfaces (SSH, HTTPS administration, management channel) to a dedicated management network or trusted hosts, never the internet.

Rotate every administrator and VPN credential, certificate and pre-shared key held in device or FortiManager configurations if there is any doubt they were exposed; Unit 42 notes stolen trust material stays valid until rotated.
Review the administrator account list and remove accounts that are not needed; enforce multi-factor authentication for administrators and VPN users.
fixed_versions: FortiOS 7.6.5 or later; FortiOS 7.4.10 or later; FortiOS 7.2, 7.0, 6.4: migrate to a fixed release
FortiProxy 7.6.5 or later; FortiProxy 7.4.12 or later; FortiProxy 7.2, 7.0: migrate to a fixed release
FortiPAM 1.7.1 or later; FortiPAM 1.6 to 1.0: migrate to a fixed release; FortiPAM 1.8 not affected
FortiSwitchManager 7.2.8 or later; FortiSwitchManager 7.0.7 or later
workarounds: Fortinet gives no configuration workaround. It lists a virtual patch, FG-VD-59270.0day, in FMWP database update 25.120, as a stopgap until upgrade.
verify: Confirm each device reports a fixed firmware version and that no device remains on an unfixed branch.
Confirm administrator access is only possible from the management network and that rotated credentials and certificates are in use everywhere, including FortiManager.
Re-audit the configuration for unexpected automation script objects after the upgrade.
if_compromised: Isolate the device's management access and preserve logs, configuration history and, where possible, a memory capture before rebooting, since the implant lives only in memory.
Engage incident response; Unit 42 notes patching alone will not evict attackers who hold stolen trust material.
Reinstall clean firmware from Fortinet, restore a configuration reviewed for rogue objects, and reissue all certificates, keys and passwords the device or its manager held.
Check downstream networks the firewall protects for sessions from attacker-controlled VPN accounts, and report to your national CERT (CISA for US agencies).

CVE-2025-61624.caveats: Fortinet rates it medium (CVSS 6.0; NVD 6.5) because an administrator login is required; it was found internally and published 14 Apr 2026. Unit 42's case is one telecom managed service provider and does not attribute it to a named state; the report does not date exactly when this flaw was used. Unit 42 report read; Fortinet advisory read in full.

CVE-2026-0322.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Palo Alto Networks reported very limited exploitation against the management interface when it published on 14 Oct 2026; CISA added it to KEV the same day (due 17 Oct). No attacker has been named.
CVE-2026-0322.how_exploited: A code injection flaw (CWE-94) in the PAN-OS management interface. An attacker who already holds valid administrator credentials and can reach the management interface over the network sends input that the interface fails to neutralise, so it is run as code with root privileges on the firewall or Panorama. Root on the device gives full control: the attacker can change configuration, read stored secrets and keep a foothold on a device that sits at the network edge.
preconditions: Network access to the PAN-OS management interface (web interface on the management port, or a data-plane interface with a management profile).
Valid credentials: the vendor rates privileges required as high, so a logged-in administrator account is needed.
An affected PAN-OS release (10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1 or 12.2 before the fixed hotfixes, or any unsupported release). No special configuration is needed.
attack_path: Credential access: the attacker obtains or reuses valid administrator credentials; the sources read do not say how this was done in the observed attacks.
Initial access: the attacker logs in to an exposed management interface.
Execution: the injection flaw runs attacker-supplied code as root on the device.
Persistence and control: experts quoted by CSO warn a rooted device can be quietly reconfigured to stay under the attacker's control; no post-exploitation activity has been published.
who_is_exposed: PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama (virtual and M-Series) on affected PAN-OS releases.
Highest risk: devices whose management interface is reachable from the internet or from untrusted networks.
Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected (vendor).
detect: Version check: compare each firewall and Panorama PAN-OS release and hotfix with the fixed versions below.
Exposure check: find every path to the management interface from outside trusted admin networks, including management profiles on data-plane interfaces.
Administrator logs: review login history for unusual source addresses, times or accounts, and compare against the three source addresses the vendor advisory lists for exploit attempts.
Configuration audit: look for unexpected configuration changes, new administrators or changed authentication settings on Panorama and every managed firewall.
Threat Prevention: Threat IDs 510046 and 510047 (content 9159-10287 and later) detect known attack patterns on inbound management traffic, but only with SSL decryption and not all variants.

steps: Inventory every PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama device and its PAN-OS release and hotfix.
Restrict management interface access to trusted internal addresses now, ideally a dedicated jump host only.
Upgrade to the fixed hotfix for your maintenance line (list below); move unsupported releases to a supported fixed release.
Where the subscription allows, enable Threat IDs 510046 and 510047 with decryption of inbound management traffic as a supporting control.
Review and reset administrator credentials, and enforce strong authentication for management logins.
US federal agencies: follow BOD 26-04 and CISA's forensics triage requirements named in the KEV entry.
workarounds: The vendor says there is no workaround; it advises restricting management access to trusted internal addresses and using a jump box as the only permitted management host, which lowers but does not remove the risk.
verify: Confirm each device reports a fixed PAN-OS release and hotfix after the upgrade, including Panorama and HA peers.
Confirm from outside the trusted network that the management interface cannot be reached.
Confirm the Threat Prevention content version is 9159-10287 or later if relying on the signatures.
if_compromised: Preserve evidence before changing anything: export logs, configuration and a tech support file from the device and Panorama.
Isolate management access and treat the device as fully controlled by the attacker (root).
Rotate every administrator credential and every secret stored on the device (VPN, LDAP, RADIUS, API keys, certificates).
Engage Palo Alto Networks support about rebuilding or restoring the device to a known-good state, then reapply a reviewed configuration.
Check internal networks reachable from the device for follow-on activity and report to your national CERT (US federal agencies to CISA).

CVE-2026-0322.caveats: Only the vendor advisory describes the flaw in detail; no researcher technical write-up was found, and the vendor found it internally. The sources do not say how attackers got the credentials, who they are, or what they did after access. CVSS differs between sources (vendor 8.6 on CVSS 4.0). The tech support file and rebuild advice are standard response practice, not steps from the advisory.

CVE-2026-101786.exploitation_status: Public exploit reported: Depthfirst's Zheng Yu published one on 18 Nov 2026 against MySQL 26.7.0. No exploitation in the wild reported (CISA ADP: none). Disclosed by Oracle on 20 Oct 2026.
CVE-2026-101786.how_exploited: Memory corruption in the MySQL Server optimizer (Oracle: Server: Optimizer component). Depthfirst describes an out-of-bounds write in a windowed bitwise aggregate: the buffer is sized when a prepared statement is prepared, for a parameter whose type is not yet known, but the value supplied at run time can be longer, and the length check existed only in debug builds. A logged-in user who runs such a prepared statement can overwrite server memory and, per Depthfirst, reliably run commands as the mysql service account, taking over the server.
preconditions: MySQL Server or MySQL Cluster 26.7.0 or 26.7.1 (the versions Oracle lists for this CVE).

An authenticated database account. Oracle rates the privileges required as high, but Depthfirst reached code execution with an account holding only the global right to create temporary tables and no read access to application tables.
Network access to the MySQL port, or an application path that lets a user run arbitrary SQL with prepared statements.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker logs in with a database account that can create temporary tables (an application, reporting or tenant account).
Execution: a prepared statement using a bound parameter in a windowed bitwise aggregate writes past the end of a buffer in the server process (Depthfirst).
Impact: the memory corruption is turned into command execution as the mysql operating-system account, which can read every database on the instance, its files and stored credentials.
No follow-on activity has been reported because no attacks have been seen.
who_is_exposed: Self-managed MySQL Server and MySQL Cluster on the 26.7 innovation line, 26.7.0 and 26.7.1, including the official container image Depthfirst tested.
Instances where accounts hold the global right to create temporary tables, which is common for application and reporting users.
Managed MySQL services offering 26.7 until the provider updates; check the provider's notice.
detect: Check the version of every MySQL Server and MySQL Cluster instance; 26.7.0 and 26.7.1 are affected.

Review which accounts hold the global right to create temporary tables, and look in the general or audit log for those accounts running prepared statements with window functions when they normally do not.
Watch the MySQL error log for server crashes and automatic restarts, which can accompany failed attempts at memory corruption.
Look for shells or other unexpected child processes started by the mysql service account, and for new files written by it outside the data directory.
Neither Oracle nor Depthfirst has published indicators or detection rules for this flaw.

steps: Identify every MySQL Server and MySQL Cluster instance on 26.7.0 or 26.7.1.

Upgrade to the fixed release that Oracle's October 2026 MySQL advisory points to in the MySQL release documentation; the advisory itself does not name it, so confirm the release in Oracle's notes before deploying.
Remove the global right to create temporary tables from accounts that do not need it (Depthfirst's advice), and grant it per schema only where required.
Review all database accounts, remove unused ones and rotate widely shared application credentials.
Keep the MySQL port off the internet; allow connections only from the application hosts that need them.
workarounds: Oracle gives no workaround. Restricting the right to create temporary tables is the researcher's advice and reduces exposure only for the route Depthfirst demonstrated.
verify: Query the server version on each instance after upgrading and confirm it is no longer 26.7.0 or 26.7.1 and matches the release Oracle names as fixed.
Re-list the grants of application and reporting accounts and confirm the global temporary-table right is gone where it is not needed.
if_compromised: Isolate the database host and preserve the MySQL error, general and audit logs and the operating-system logs before changes.
Rotate every MySQL account password and any secrets readable by the mysql operating-system account (replication users, backup credentials, key files).
Rebuild the host or container from a clean image on a fixed release and restore data from a backup taken before the suspected compromise.
Review systems the database host could reach, and report the incident to your national CERT or incident-response provider.

CVE-2026-101786.caveats: Oracle's advisory gives a component, versions and a 7.2 score but no technical detail and no fixed release; the MySQL 26.7 release notes read on 20 Nov list only 26.7.0 and 26.7.1, so the fixed release could not be confirmed. Oracle rates the privileges required as high, while the researcher reports needing only the temporary-table right. The Hacker News reports the chain was not independently reproduced.

CVE-2026-102764.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild as a zero-day since 29 Aug 2026; Mandiant attributes it to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor (per Rapid7 and CISA). CISA added it to KEV on 16 Oct 2026. Rapid7 reports a public Metasploit module.
CVE-2026-102764.how_exploited: Authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290): internal Remote Support components do not properly check where incoming messages come from. An unauthenticated remote attacker, with no user interaction, can make the appliance carry out file operations, which Rapid7 showed leads to an uploaded file running code as the site user. Mandiant saw attackers use this to plant a web shell, escalate to root and go after the credential vault.
preconditions: Self-hosted BeyondTrust Remote Support 26.2.3 or earlier without the BT26-05-RS patch; SaaS instances were patched by 9 Oct 2026.
The appliance is reachable over the network, typically from the internet; no credentials or user interaction are needed.
Privileged Remote Access shares the affected code; BeyondTrust has not found a way to exploit it there but advises patching.
attack_path: Initial access: spoofed internal messages make the appliance write attacker files without login.
Execution and persistence: Mandiant saw a web shell (SAWFLY) and a tunnelling tool (BARECLAW) deployed, then escalation to root.
Credential access: attackers tried to extract credentials from the Remote Support vault.
Defence evasion: logs were deleted; CISA adds lateral movement to reached networks as observed attacker goals.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running self-hosted Remote Support appliances (physical or virtual B Series) on 26.2.3 or earlier without BT26-05-RS.
Appliances older than 24.3.1, which cannot take the patch until upgraded.
Every system and account the appliance brokers sessions or stores credentials for, since vault theft reaches them.
SaaS customers are patched but should still review credentials and configuration (Rapid7).
detect: Confirm in the appliance interface whether BT26-05-RS is installed.
Hunt for unrecognised administrative or privileged sessions, especially from residential broadband or commercial VPN addresses (CISA, Rapid7).
Look for unknown script files in web directories, shells spawned by web service accounts, and unauthorised changes to accounts, permissions, Jump Items, Teams or session policies.
Look for gaps in log forwarding; Mandiant names evidence in access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL logs and publishes hashes and YARA rules (link, do not copy).
Ask BeyondTrust for its hunting package and for host-level inspection, which customers cannot do themselves; no indicator hits does not prove a clean appliance.

steps: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05 to every self-hosted appliance; manually if automatic updates are off.
Upgrade appliances older than 24.3.1 to a supported version first, then patch.
Limit external exposure to the services users and customers need and restrict admin interfaces to trusted networks (CISA).
Forward appliance syslog and session events to a SIEM and collect WAF, proxy and firewall logs for the exposure window.
Investigate for prior compromise even after patching; patching does not remove persistence.
Patch self-hosted Privileged Remote Access too, confirming the correct patch with BeyondTrust Support.
fixed_versions: BT26-05-RS patch for Remote Support 24.3.1 through 26.2.3
Remote Support 26.2.4 or later (per secondary sources)
workarounds: CISA: restrict external exposure and admin interfaces to trusted networks; this reduces risk but does not replace the patch.
verify: Confirm in the appliance interface that BT26-05-RS is installed or the version is fixed.
Confirm events are reaching the SIEM and that no new unknown admin sessions or accounts appear.
if_compromised: Isolate the appliance and preserve a VM snapshot or forensic image before changes or reboots.
Rebuild from a known-good, fully patched state; do not rely on patching a compromised appliance.
Rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, revoke all active support sessions, and review new MFA registrations on privileged accounts.
Review admin changes and downstream sessions for lateral movement; involve BeyondTrust Support and report to CISA or your national CERT.

CVE-2026-102764.caveats: BeyondTrust's own advisory BT26-05 refused automated reading (403), so this analysis rests on CISA's alert, HKCERT and Rapid7's account of the vendor and Mandiant findings. Sources differ on the patch date (8, 9 or 15 Oct). The 26.2.4 fixed version comes from secondary sources only.

CVE-2026-102895.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: the GPUStack advisory says exploitation was seen against version 2.1.1 (reported by Javier Sixto, ulex.fr). CISA added it to KEV on 9 Nov 2026. No actor named; reports disagree on public exploit code.
CVE-2026-102895.how_exploited: Improper authentication through spoofed origin (CWE-290, CWE-346). Before 2.2.0, GPUStack treated any request it believed came from the local machine as the built-in administrator, unless the localhost-authentication setting was on, and it is off by default. A same-host reverse proxy makes every remote request look local, and a client-controlled forwarding header can do the same. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the API gets full admin control and, per the advisory, can use admin features to run code on GPU worker hosts.
preconditions: The GPUStack server API is reachable by the attacker over the network; no credentials are needed.
GPUStack is older than 2.2.0 and the localhost-authentication setting is at its default (off).
The server sits behind a reverse proxy on the same host, or accepts a client-supplied forwarding header that makes requests appear local.
attack_path: Initial access: requests reach the API and are treated as coming from the local machine, so they run as the built-in administrator without logging in.
Persistence: the attacker can create long-lived administrator API keys or users, which keep working after the spoofing path is closed.
Credential access: worker credentials and cloud-provider secrets held by GPUStack can be read.
Execution: per the Cloud Security Alliance note, attackers registered a malicious inference backend that runs code on GPU workers and opened reverse shells on them.
Impact: changes to users, models, workers and configuration; CSA says cryptomining or cloud pivoting is plausible but not confirmed for this campaign.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted GPUStack servers before 2.2.0 whose API is reachable from the internet or untrusted networks.
Deployments behind a reverse proxy on the same host, which makes all remote traffic appear local.
Deployments reachable only by VPN or an authenticating gateway are less exposed, but an internal foothold or a request-forgery flaw nearby could still reach the API (CSA).
detect: Check the GPUStack version on every server; anything before 2.2.0 is vulnerable.
Search proxy access logs and GPUStack server logs for successful API calls that carried no authentication, and for registrations of new inference backends (CSA).
In the GPUStack console, review all administrator accounts and API keys, especially broad-scope keys, and compare registered inference backends with change records.
On worker hosts, look for shells or unexpected child processes started by inference backend processes and unexpected outbound connections.
In connected cloud accounts, look for resources or API activity nobody created. No indicators of compromise have been published.

steps: Upgrade to GPUStack 2.2.0 or later; CSA advises 2.2.2, which also fixes the separate CVE-2026-102894 SAML bypass. Recreate the containers so the new image is actually running.
Until upgraded, turn on the localhost-authentication setting so loopback requests must authenticate.
Make sure the reverse proxy or gateway cannot make external traffic appear local, and strip client-supplied forwarding headers at the edge.
Keep the API off untrusted networks, behind a VPN or edge authentication.
Because the flaw was exploited, check every instance that was reachable while vulnerable for compromise; patching does not remove attacker-created keys, users or backends.
fixed_versions: GPUStack 2.2.0 and later (2.2.2 also fixes CVE-2026-102894)
workarounds: Enable the localhost-authentication setting so loopback requests must authenticate (GPUStack advisory).
Ensure the proxy or gateway cannot make external traffic look local and strip client-supplied forwarding headers at the edge (GPUStack advisory).
Keep the API off untrusted networks, behind a VPN or edge authentication (GPUStack advisory).
verify: The running server reports version 2.2.0 or later after the containers were recreated.
Requests through the proxy without credentials are refused, and the localhost-authentication setting shows as enabled rather than blank.
if_compromised: Revoke API keys and remove administrator accounts you did not create; remove unexpected inference backends.
Isolate and rebuild worker hosts that show unexpected shells or processes.
Rotate all worker tokens and cloud-provider credentials GPUStack held, and audit cloud accounts for resources nobody created.
Preserve proxy and server logs, establish the window of exposure, and report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-102895.caveats: No victim count, first-exploitation date or indicators of compromise are public. Sources disagree on whether the forwarding-header route works in every mode or only with the embedded gateway, and on whether public exploit code exists. Post-exploitation detail about malicious backends and reverse shells comes from the CSA research note, which partly relies on secondary reports.

CVE-2026-103406.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: in CISA KEV since 25 Nov 2026 (due 28 Nov). Juniper says its SIRT received at least one report of malicious exploitation (24 Nov 2026). Attacker not named; no public exploit code reported.
CVE-2026-103406.how_exploited: An OS command injection (CWE-78) in the AutomatedProvisioner component of Juniper Session Smart Conductor, which handles Salt key management for the routers it manages. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the Conductor's Salt minion connection service presents a crafted minion ID; the Conductor uses that ID unsafely when handling keys and runs attacker-chosen commands as root. That gives full control of the Conductor, which centrally manages and configures the Session Smart Router fleet.
preconditions: Network access to the Conductor service that Session Smart Routers (Salt minions) connect to; no credentials or user interaction.
Session Smart Conductor before 7.0.5, 7.1.0 to 7.1.6, or 7.2.0 to 7.2.2.
Juniper's CVE record names the Conductor as affected; CISA's catalog entry names both the Conductor and the Router.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: finding Conductors whose router-facing management service is reachable, often over the internet so branch routers can connect.
Initial access and execution: posing as a router during Salt key management with a crafted minion ID, which runs commands as root on the Conductor.
Likely next steps (not yet reported): persistence on the Conductor, theft of configuration and credentials, and pushing malicious configuration to managed routers, since the Conductor controls them.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Juniper Session Smart Conductor on affected releases, on-premises or in the cloud.
Highest risk: Conductors that accept router connections from the internet, which is common in SD-WAN deployments with remote branch sites.
All Session Smart Routers managed by an affected Conductor, which are at risk if the Conductor is taken over.
detect: Version check: compare each Conductor's release with 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3.
List which networks and hosts can reach the Conductor's Salt minion connection service, and look for connections from addresses that are not your routers.
Conductor key management and Salt logs: key requests or minion registrations with unusual or malformed minion IDs, or from unknown assets.
Host behaviour: unexpected root processes, shells or downloads started by Conductor services, and new cron jobs, accounts or SSH keys.
Configuration audit: router configuration changes pushed from the Conductor that nobody on your team made.
No indicators or detection rules were published in the sources read.

steps: Upgrade Session Smart Conductor to 7.0.5, 7.1.7, 7.2.3 or a later release; update Session Smart Routers to fixed releases too, since the same bulletin fixes other critical router flaws.
Until upgraded, restrict access to Conductor and router management interfaces to known router and administrator addresses.
Check Conductors for signs of compromise; US federal agencies must follow CISA's forensic triage requirements under BOD 26-04.
After upgrading, review router configurations pushed by the Conductor.
verify: Each Conductor reports release 7.0.5, 7.1.7, 7.2.3 or later.
Managed routers reconnect and check in normally after the upgrade, and only known routers hold accepted keys.
if_compromised: Isolate the Conductor from untrusted networks without cutting off evidence; preserve logs and a disk image.
Rebuild the Conductor from a clean, fixed release rather than cleaning in place, and restore only reviewed configuration.
Rotate all secrets on the Conductor: administrator passwords, router keys and certificates, and credentials for integrations.
Audit every managed router for unauthorised configuration or software and reset trust between routers and the Conductor.
Report to Juniper (HPE) SIRT and your national CERT; US federal agencies report to CISA.

CVE-2026-103406.caveats: Juniper bulletin JSA112183 could not be read (the support portal rendered no content); this relies on CISA, the Juniper-published CVE record and news. Juniper lists no workarounds; access restriction is secondary guidance. The exact service and port are not stated. CISA names the Router too; the CVE record lists only the Conductor. Scale and attacker are unknown.

CVE-2026-104935.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild as a zero-day from early October 2026 by an actor Volexity tracks as UTA0576 (Ivanti: limited customers). CISA added it to KEV on 13 Oct 2026, the day of disclosure.
CVE-2026-104935.how_exploited: Authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) combined with a code execution flaw, both tracked under this CVE. Per Volexity, a public login-related endpoint hands requests to a protected internal handler using a routing value the client supplies, and the appliance checks access against one value but routes by another, so authentication is skipped. A file upload handler then stores a file before validating it, and the attacker races to run it before it is deleted, giving unauthenticated command execution. UTA0576 chained this with a separate privilege escalation (CVE-2026-111357) to reach root.
preconditions: The Connect Secure web interface is reachable by the attacker, normally from the internet; no credentials or user interaction are needed.
The appliance runs an affected release: 25.1.1.1 or earlier, 25.1.2.2 or earlier, or 22.8R2.4 or earlier (22.7 and older are not affected per the vendor, as reported by Rapid7 and NVD).
Root-level control in the observed attacks also needed CVE-2026-111357, fixed later on 29 Oct 2026; CISA's revised alert also lists CVE-2026-118527 as chainable.
attack_path: Initial access: crafted requests to the public login endpoint reach an internal handler without authentication.
Execution: an uploaded script is run in the short window before the appliance deletes it; commands ran in memory and no web shell or backdoor was left (Volexity).
Privilege escalation: a privileged background service was made to run attacker code as root through altered configuration and a temporary in-memory library change.

Credential access: credentials stored on the appliance, including directory service accounts, were taken, then used to query Active Directory for LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys and password attributes; Kerberoasting, password spraying and LDAP traffic capture followed.
Collection and reconnaissance: configuration and authentication logs were gathered and DNS reconnaissance run, apparently preparing for lateral movement.
Defence evasion: exploitation entries were removed from debug and Linux audit logs, scripts deleted and in-memory changes reverted, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool did not detect the compromise.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances (hardware, virtual or cloud instances) on the 22.8 or 25.1 lines below the fixed builds.
Appliances that were fully patched before 13 Oct 2026 were still vulnerable; Volexity's victim ran 22.8R2.4.
Active Directory environments whose service accounts are stored on the appliance, since the actor used them to pull privileged secrets.
detect: Check the Connect Secure version on every appliance against the fixed builds listed by Ivanti.

Review web and access logs for requests to the login endpoint that carry a routing header pointing at an internal handler, especially where requested path and routing target differ, and for unusual request volumes to it (Volexity).
Do not rely on the Integrity Checker Tool or on missing log entries: CISA and Volexity say compromise needs network and memory forensics; core dumps and memory images recovered most of the activity.
Look in the appliance's temporary directories for leftover artifacts and for unexpected packet-capture or sniffing processes.

In Active Directory and on the network, hunt for queries for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, Kerberoasting, password spraying and lateral movement that originate from the VPN appliance or its service accounts.
Compare against the indicators Volexity published in its public threat-intelligence GitHub repository (linked from its 13 Oct 2026 blog post).

steps: Update every Connect Secure appliance at once, outside normal patch cycles, to the latest release per Ivanti's advisory; CISA urges immediate update to the latest version.
Also apply the later fixes for CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 (added to KEV 30 Oct 2026), since CISA's revised alert lists 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 among affected versions for the chain.
For hardware and virtual appliances moving to 25.x, follow Ivanti's 25.x Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide; 22.8 reaches end of life on 31 Jan 2027.
Carry out network and memory forensics on any appliance that was exposed before patching, and hunt for compromise even after the update.
Reduce the reach of directory service accounts stored on the appliance to the minimum the VPN needs.
fixed_versions: 25.1.1.2 for the 25.1.1 line (later releases recommended because of the follow-on CVEs)
22.8R2.5 for the 22.8 line (later releases recommended because of the follow-on CVEs)
verify: Confirm the running version on each appliance (and each cluster node) is the latest Ivanti release, not only the first October fix.
Re-scan externally exposed appliances with your vulnerability scanner after the update.
Confirm forensic review found no signs of exploitation from before the update; a clean Integrity Checker result alone is not enough.
if_compromised: Isolate the appliance and capture memory and core dumps before rebooting or resetting, since the attacker worked in memory and tampered with logs.
Back up the configuration, factory reset the appliance (rebuild cloud or virtual instances), upgrade to the latest version, then restore the configuration (CISA).
Reset passwords for all domain, administrator and local accounts tied to the appliance; revoke and reissue certificates; reset API keys and licence server credentials (CISA).
Rotate LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys that could be read through the appliance's service account and review Active Directory for misuse (Volexity).
Follow Ivanti's recovery steps for Connect Secure 22.8 and 25.x and report the incident (US federal agencies under BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements).

CVE-2026-104935.caveats: Ivanti's own advisory page did not load for an automated reader; fixed builds come from Rapid7's reading of it and NVD, and CISA's later revision lists 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 as still affected by the chain, so install the latest release. Volexity details one intrusion; how widely the flaw was used is not known. No reliable vendor indicators of compromise exist.

CVE-2026-105133.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild since 7 Oct 2026 (Huntress: five organisations by 8 Oct), chained with CVE-2026-105134 to drop web shells and cryptominers; public exploit reported. CISA added it to KEV on 14 Oct 2026.
CVE-2026-105133.how_exploited: Improper authentication (CWE-287) in the AhsayCBS backup management console's API. The system password check can be bypassed by manipulating a value the client supplies, so a remote attacker gets past the console's authentication without credentials. On its own this gives access to protected API functions; in the observed attacks it was the entry point for CVE-2026-105134, a command injection in the replication receiver API, which runs commands as SYSTEM on the backup server.
preconditions: The AhsayCBS management web interface is reachable by the attacker, usually from the internet; no credentials or user interaction are needed.
AhsayCBS is older than 9.15.2.70 (v7, v8 and v9 lines) or older than 10.3.4.45 (v10 line); the earlier patches 9.15.2.59 and 10.3.4.0 did not fully fix it.
Code execution in the observed attacks also required CVE-2026-105134 on the same server.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker bypasses console authentication, then abuses the replication receiver feature to run commands as SYSTEM (Huntress).
Execution and staging: reconnaissance commands, then scripts and binaries downloaded from cloud object storage.
Persistence: JSP web shells hidden in the application's web directory, some keyed or self-deleting, a fake Edge update service and SYSTEM scheduled tasks, a registry Run key for a Python implant.
Defence evasion: Defender exclusions added, a miner disguised as an Edge process and hidden when Task Manager opened, a vulnerable driver loaded for kernel access.
Impact and follow-on: XMRig cryptomining, a command-and-control implant, tunnelling and remote access tools; on one linked Veeam server, activity consistent with stored credential theft.
who_is_exposed: Backup service providers and organisations that host AhsayCBS (on-premises or on cloud virtual machines) with the management console reachable from the internet.
Every AhsayCBS line: v7, v8, v9 below 9.15.2.70 and v10 below 10.3.4.45, including servers that installed the incomplete 9.15.2.59 or 10.3.4.0 patches.
Other backup systems on the same network, whose stored credentials attackers went after.
detect: Check the AhsayCBS version on every server; anything below 9.15.2.70 or 10.3.4.45 is vulnerable.
Alert on the AhsayCBS service process spawning command shells or other unexpected child processes outside normal startup and maintenance; web shell commands appear as its direct children (Huntress).
Look for new JSP files in the AhsayCBS web directories, unknown folders at the drive root or in Program Files, and replication receivers nobody configured.
Review scheduled tasks, services and Defender exclusions nobody added, Edge-named binaries with mismatched original file names, and Python running from the SYSTEM profile.
Watch for non-browser processes using DNS over HTTPS and for downloads of a vulnerable hardware-access driver.
Use the four Sigma rules Huntress published in its public threat-intel GitHub repository and the indicators listed in its blog posts.

steps: Apply the Ahsay hotfix at once (10.3.4.45 for v10, 9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9; partner portal login needed), then reboot the server as Ahsay instructs.
Restrict the management interface to trusted IP addresses or put it behind a VPN (Huntress).
Treat any server exposed before the hotfix as possibly compromised and hunt for the signs listed under detection; patching does not remove planted files.
Rotate credentials stored in AhsayCBS and in other backup software on the network if any sign of compromise is found.
verify: Confirm the console reports 10.3.4.45 or 9.15.2.70 or later and that the server was rebooted after the hotfix.
Confirm the management interface is no longer reachable from untrusted networks.
Re-scan the server with your vulnerability scanner after the hotfix.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve logs, disk and memory images before removing anything.
Rebuild the host from a trusted backup taken before the intrusion, because attackers may have hidden secondary backdoors (Huntress).
Rotate every credential stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and other backup software such as Veeam.
Check other backup and infrastructure servers for the same web shells, services and implants, and report the incident; US federal agencies follow BOD 26-04.

CVE-2026-105133.caveats: Ahsay's announcement gives fixed builds but no technical detail or exploitation statement; the technique comes from NVD, CISA and Huntress. Severity ratings differ between sources (medium alone, critical when chained). Earlier reporting said 10.3.4.0 was fixed; Huntress and Ahsay later said it was not.

CVE-2026-105134.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild since 7 Oct 2026 (Huntress; Bitdefender MDR saw three incidents), chained with CVE-2026-105133. CISA added it to KEV on 14 Oct 2026. No actor named. A public exploit was noted at NVD publication.
CVE-2026-105134.how_exploited: OS command injection (CWE-77/78) in the Replication Receiver component of the AhsayCBS backup server. An attacker manipulates one parameter in a network request to the replication receiver API so that attacker-supplied text is run as an operating system command, as SYSTEM on Windows. In observed attacks it was chained with CVE-2026-105133, an authentication bypass in the admin API's system-password check: the bypass reaches the protected component, the injection runs commands, and attackers then configured a malicious replication receiver and dropped a web shell into the web application.
preconditions: The AhsayCBS management web service is reachable from the attacker's network, typically the internet.
AhsayCBS v7, v8, v9 or v10 below the hotfix builds 9.15.2.70 or 10.3.4.45; servers on the earlier patches 9.15.2.59 and 10.3.4.0 remain vulnerable.
No credentials or user interaction: the chained authentication bypass removes the login, and NVD scores the injection as needing no privileges on its own (Bitdefender).
attack_path: Initial access: authentication bypass (CVE-2026-105133) followed by command injection in the Replication Receiver, giving code execution as SYSTEM.
Persistence: JSP web shells written into the directory served by the CBS web application; commands run through them appear as children of the AhsayCBS service (Huntress).
Execution: PowerShell scripts and tools staged from attacker-controlled cloud storage; a renamed service wrapper used to install a service disguised as the Edge updater.
Impact: an XMRig miner disguised as Microsoft Edge, hidden by a script that stops it while Task Manager is open, and a vulnerable hardware driver loaded for kernel access (Huntress).
Follow-on: credential reconnaissance, a user elevated to SYSTEM, and OpenSSH installed for remote access independent of the web service (Bitdefender).
who_is_exposed: Managed service providers and organisations running self-hosted AhsayCBS v7 to v10 servers whose web console is reachable from the internet.
Servers that took only the first patches (9.15.2.59 or 10.3.4.0), which the vendor later said did not fully fix the flaws.
Downstream customers whose backups, storage credentials and recovery copies are held on an affected server.
detect: Check the exact four-part build in the license section of the web console and compare it with 9.15.2.70 and 10.3.4.45.
Endpoint telemetry: the AhsayCBS service process starting command shells, PowerShell, certutil or curl outside normal maintenance (Huntress).
Look for new script files in the web application directory, new or changed replication receivers, and services named like the Edge updater.
Look for Edge-named binaries not signed by Microsoft, a driver file written to a temporary folder, new OpenSSH installs and accounts whose privileges changed after 4 Oct 2026.
Use Huntress's four Sigma rules for this campaign (in its threat-intel repository) and the indicator table in Bitdefender's advisory; both warn that file names and hashes vary.

steps: Inventory every AhsayCBS server, including those run for you by a service provider.
Restrict the management web service to trusted administrative networks or VPN at once.
Apply the 12 Oct 2026 hotfix from the Ahsay partner portal: 10.3.4.45 for v10, 9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9. Reboot the server afterwards.
Do not treat 10.3.4.0 or 9.15.2.59 as fixed; Ahsay said they did not fully address the flaws.
Assess every server that was reachable while vulnerable for compromise from 4 Oct 2026 onwards; patching does not remove web shells, services or OpenSSH backdoors.
fixed_versions: AhsayCBS v7, v8 and v9: hotfix 9.15.2.70
workarounds: Ahsay lists no workaround. Bitdefender and Huntress recommend restricting the management interface to trusted IP addresses or VPN until the hotfix is applied.
verify: The license section of the web console shows 10.3.4.45 or 9.15.2.70 or later after the reboot.
From an outside network, confirm the management service is no longer reachable unless intended.
if_compromised: Treat the host as fully compromised at SYSTEM level; isolate it and preserve web, application and endpoint logs.
Rebuild from a trusted backup rather than cleaning in place, since attackers hid secondary backdoors (Huntress).
Remove web shells, staged scripts, rogue services, scheduled tasks, replication receivers and OpenSSH configurations if rebuild is delayed.
Rotate AhsayCBS administrator accounts, backup storage destination credentials, service accounts and domain credentials used or cached on the host.
Keep monitoring for weeks, since dormant access can persist, and report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-105134.caveats: Ahsay's announcement does not describe the flaws and its hotfixes sit behind a partner login. Huntress at first reported 10.3.4 as unaffected and later revised that. Huntress saw cryptomining; Bitdefender's incidents showed no mining, encryption or exfiltration. Severity scores come from VulDB; NVD has not scored the flaws. No actor is named and victim counts are unknown.

CVE-2026-106931.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: EG Secure Solutions and JPCERT/CC (JVN#88474777) confirmed abuse when publishing on 14 Oct 2026; CISA added it to KEV on 20 Oct (due 23 Oct). No attacker, victims or scale named.
CVE-2026-106931.how_exploited: An OS command injection flaw (CWE-78) in the statistics feature of SiteGuard Server Edition, a host-based web application firewall for Apache httpd, Nginx and IIS. Input handled by the statistics processing reaches an operating system command without proper neutralisation, so an attacker can make it run commands of their choosing. The commands run with root or SYSTEM privileges, giving full control of the web server. The vendor has not published how the input reaches the feature.
preconditions: The statistics feature is enabled, which is the default.
SiteGuard Server Edition 2.20 or later, before 8.00 Update 5 (Apache, Nginx, IIS) or before 7.00 Update 6 (FreeBSD Apache and Nginx).
JVN's CVSS vectors rate it as needing local access with low privileges and no user interaction; how that access is obtained in the attacks seen is not stated.
attack_path: Access: the attacker reaches the statistics processing with low privileges, per JVN's scoring.
Execution and privilege escalation: crafted input is passed into an operating system command, which runs as root or SYSTEM.
Defence evasion: the vendor warns that updating may erase traces of an attack, which indicates evidence lives on the host.
Follow-on: the sources read do not describe what attackers did after gaining control.
who_is_exposed: Web servers running SiteGuard Server Edition for Apache httpd, Nginx or IIS, version 2.20 and later before 8.00 Update 5, with statistics enabled.
FreeBSD servers running SiteGuard Server Edition for Apache httpd or Nginx before 7.00 Update 6.
Not affected: IIS editions 3.10 through 4.00 Update 4. End-of-support versions are affected and have a vendor patch.
Mostly Japanese hosting providers and organisations; the vendor says SiteGuard protects over 1.5 million websites (BleepingComputer).
detect: Version check: confirm the SiteGuard Server Edition version and update level, and whether the statistics feature is enabled, in the web management screen.
Download and keep the diagnostic information from the web management screen before patching; the vendor and JPCERT/CC give no other indicators.
Host monitoring: child processes started by the SiteGuard statistics processing, or unexpected processes running as root or SYSTEM on the web server.
File integrity and accounts: new or changed files, scheduled tasks and accounts on the server that no administrator made.

steps: Find every server running SiteGuard Server Edition and record version, platform and whether statistics is enabled.
Before changing anything, download the diagnostic information from the web management screen and store it securely, as updating may erase attack traces.
Update to 8.00 Update 5 (Apache, Nginx, IIS) or 7.00 Update 6 (FreeBSD Apache and Nginx).
If upgrading is not possible, apply the vendor's patch that replaces the statistics processing files (also available for end-of-support versions).
Contact the vendor support desk or JPCERT/CC with questions; US federal agencies follow CISA's BOD 26-04 guidance.
fixed_versions: SiteGuard Server Edition 8.00 Update 5 (Apache httpd, Nginx, IIS; not FreeBSD)
SiteGuard Server Edition 7.00 Update 6 (Apache httpd and Nginx on FreeBSD)
Vendor patch replacing the statistics processing files, for versions that cannot be upgraded
verify: Confirm in the web management screen that the version is 8.00 Update 5 or 7.00 Update 6 or later, or that the vendor patch is applied.
Confirm the diagnostic information captured before patching was kept and reviewed.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve the diagnostic information, logs and a disk image.
Treat the host as fully compromised, since commands ran as root or SYSTEM: rebuild from a known-good image with a fixed version.
Rotate credentials, certificates and keys stored on or used by the server, including website and database secrets.
Report to JPCERT/CC or your national CERT (US federal agencies to CISA), and contact the vendor support desk.

CVE-2026-106931.caveats: The vendor and JPCERT/CC publish few technical details: how attackers reach the statistics feature, who exploited it and what they did next are not public. JVN rates the attack vector as local with low privileges, yet some reports call it critical and remote; CyberView records exposure as local per JVN. No independent technical write-up was found. Disabling statistics was not stated as a workaround in the pages read.

CVE-2026-107154.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported as of 19 Nov 2026: MS-ISAC (10 Nov) says SonicWall reported none; not in CISA KEV; no public exploit code reported. The exploited flaw in the same advisory is the separate SSLVPN SAML bypass CVE-2026-19868.
CVE-2026-107154.how_exploited: A session validation flaw in the SonicOS web management interface; SonicWall's CVE record classes it as reliance on an IP address for authentication (CWE-291). Under specific conditions a remote attacker without credentials may have requests treated as part of a valid session and so carry out unauthorised operations on the firewall. SonicWall has not published the conditions; the CVSS vector says user interaction is needed.
preconditions: SonicOS Gen7 hardware or NSv at 7.3.3-7015 or earlier, or Gen8 hardware or NSv at 8.2.2-8015 or earlier.
The attacker can reach the firewall's management interface over the network; MS-ISAC says internet-exposed management interfaces face higher risk.
No credentials are needed, but the CVSS vector published with the CVE (8.8) requires user interaction, so a person, most likely an administrator, has to take some action.
SonicWall says it works only under specific conditions, which it has not detailed publicly.
attack_path: Initial access: a remote attacker targets the management interface without logging in, relying on weak session validation and on some action by a user.
Impact: unauthorised operations on the firewall with high impact to confidentiality, integrity and availability per the CVSS vector; SonicWall has not said which operations.
No attacker activity after access has been reported, because no exploitation has been seen.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running SonicWall Gen7 or Gen8 firewalls, hardware or NSv virtual, on the affected builds.
Most of all, those whose HTTPS management interface is reachable from the internet or from untrusted networks.
Administrators who manage firewalls from everyday workstations that also browse the web.
detect: Check every firewall's SonicOS build against the affected ranges (7.3.3-7015 or earlier, 8.2.2-8015 or earlier).
Scan from outside your network to confirm whether any management interface answers from the internet.
Review firewall audit logs for configuration changes, new admin accounts or admin sessions that no administrator recognises, and their source addresses.
SonicWall and MS-ISAC have published no indicators or detection rules for this flaw.

steps: Upgrade every affected Gen7 and Gen8 firewall, hardware and NSv, to the fixed SonicOS build named in SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0014, after testing.

Scan from outside your network to confirm whether any management interface answers from the internet.

CVE-2026-107412.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported. Citrix's bulletin CTX697305 (12 Nov 2026) says nothing of exploitation; CERT-EU (12 Nov 2026) says Citrix reports none and no public proof of concept is confirmed. Not in CISA's KEV catalog on file.
CVE-2026-107412.how_exploited: Citrix describes CVE-2026-107412 as several memory overflow flaws (CWE-119) in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. They sit in the code that serves Gateway functions (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) and AAA authentication virtual servers. According to the vendor and CERT-EU, a remote attacker can reach them over the network without logging in by sending crafted traffic to such a virtual server. Citrix states the impact as unpredictable behaviour or denial of service, but its CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5 rates confidentiality, integrity and availability all high, so memory corruption leading to data exposure or code execution cannot be ruled out.
preconditions: The appliance is configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or as an AAA virtual server (Citrix).
Network reach to that virtual server; Gateway and AAA services are normally internet-facing. No authentication or user interaction is needed (CVSS vector PR:N, UI:N).
Citrix's vector marks attack requirements as present (AT:P), meaning some deployment condition beyond reachability applies; the bulletin does not detail it.
Customer-managed NetScaler ADC or Gateway 14.1 before 14.1-73.57, 13.1 before 13.1-64.39, ADC FIPS before 14.1-73.58 FIPS, or FIPS and NDcPP before 13.1-37.293.
attack_path: Initial access: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted traffic to an internet-facing Gateway or AAA virtual server, triggering a memory overflow.
Impact stated by the vendor: unpredictable or erroneous behaviour and denial of service, which takes remote access for users offline.
Possible further impact: the high confidentiality and integrity ratings suggest memory disclosure or code execution on the appliance; no attack of this kind has been reported for this flaw.
No post-exploitation activity has been reported, because no attacks using this flaw are known as of 19 Nov 2026.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running customer-managed NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway 14.1 or 13.1, including FIPS and NDcPP builds, configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server.
Secure Private Access hybrid deployments that use NetScaler instances (Citrix lists them as affected).
Appliances without Gateway or AAA virtual servers are not exposed to this flaw, but CERT-EU notes the companion flaw CVE-2026-120868 affects every deployment, default configuration included.
detect: Version check: compare each appliance's build with the fixed builds; anything older is vulnerable.
Configuration check: review the running configuration for VPN (Gateway) virtual servers and AAA authentication virtual servers, as Citrix advises.
Watch for unexpected restarts, crashes or core dumps of the packet engine and for Gateway or AAA services dropping, which a memory overflow attempt can cause.
Review Gateway and AAA access logs and firewall logs for unusual traffic volumes or malformed requests to authentication endpoints from unfamiliar sources.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules have been published for this flaw by Citrix or CERT-EU.

steps: Inventory all customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances, their builds and whether they host Gateway or AAA virtual servers.
Upgrade internet-facing Gateway and AAA appliances first (CERT-EU), then all remaining appliances, to the fixed builds.
Upgrade the rest of the estate as well, because the same release fixes CVE-2026-120868, which affects default configurations.
Check Secure Private Access hybrid deployments and upgrade the NetScaler instances they use.
If an upgrade must wait, restrict who can reach Gateway and AAA services where the business allows and increase monitoring; Citrix gives no official workaround.
fixed_versions: NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.57 and later releases of 14.1
NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.39 and later releases of 13.1
NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.58 and later releases of 14.1-FIPS
NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.293 and later releases
verify: Confirm each appliance reports a build at or above the fixed build for its line after the upgrade, including every node of HA pairs and clusters.
Confirm Gateway and AAA virtual servers came back up and authenticate users normally after the upgrade.
if_compromised: If crashes, unexplained configuration changes or unknown files suggest compromise, isolate the appliance and preserve its logs, core dumps and configuration before rebuilding.
Rebuild from a clean, fixed image rather than patching a suspect appliance in place.
Terminate active Gateway and AAA sessions and rotate credentials, keys and certificates held on or passing through the appliance.
Hunt from the appliance into the internal network for lateral movement, and report the incident to Citrix and your national CERT.

CVE-2026-107412.caveats: Only the vendor bulletin and CERT-EU's advisory are available; no technical write-up from researchers exists. Citrix describes the impact only as unpredictable behaviour or denial of service while scoring confidentiality and integrity high, so whether code execution is possible is unclear. Citrix does not say what the 'attack requirements present' condition is. Detection advice here is general, not from the vendor.

CVE-2026-107484.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported for this flaw. Rescana (Nov 2026) says Check Point lists it as not exploited and it is not in CISA's KEV catalog. Its companion CVE-2026-123039, fixed in the same update, is exploited (CISA KEV 13 Nov 2026).
CVE-2026-107484.how_exploited: An input validation and authorisation flaw in the backend handlers of the Gaia Portal, the web administration interface of Check Point's Gaia operating system. The Canadian Cyber Centre says it lets an authenticated user escalate privileges; Rescana, citing Check Point's sk1000291, says an authenticated, non-administrative portal user can carry out operations meant only for administrators. An attacker who holds or steals a low-privileged portal account can therefore change the firewall or management server as if they were an administrator.
preconditions: A valid Gaia Portal account; a non-administrative role is enough (Cyber Centre, Rescana).
Network reach to the Gaia Portal web interface of a gateway, management or log server.
An affected Gaia release; Rescana reports sk1000291 lists R82.20 as not affected, with fixes in R82.10, R82 and R81.20 Jumbo takes. Exact ranges are in Check Point's sk1000291.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker logs in to the Gaia Portal with a low-privileged account, obtained legitimately or through stolen or guessed credentials.
Privilege escalation: crafted requests to Gaia Portal backend handlers are accepted without the proper role check, giving administrator-level operations.
Impact: administrator control of the device lets an attacker change policy or configuration, add accounts or weaken protections; no attacks using this flaw have been reported.
Context: in the October and November 2026 campaign Check Point Research describes, attackers entered through the Mobile Access portal and used CVE-2026-123039, not this flaw, to gain root.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Check Point Force firewalls, management and log servers, Multi-Domain Security Management and Log Servers, and Maestro Orchestrator on affected Gaia releases (Cyber Centre).
Deployments where Gaia Portal accounts are shared with non-administrative staff, contractors or monitoring tools.
Devices whose Gaia Portal is reachable from broad internal networks or the internet, which makes stolen low-privileged credentials more useful.
detect: Version check: compare each device's Gaia release and Jumbo Hotfix take with the fixed takes in sk1000291.
Gaia Portal and web server logs: actions by non-administrative accounts that only an administrator should be able to perform.
Audit logs: unexpected new users, role changes, configuration or policy changes made through the Gaia Portal.
Because the same update fixes the exploited CVE-2026-123039, also review the Dynamic CLI log and check the indicators Check Point published in sk1000362.

steps: Install the November 2026 Jumbo Hotfix take for your release, which fixes this flaw and the exploited CVE-2026-123039; follow sk1000291 and sk1000362.
Patch gateways with internet-facing Mobile Access first, then management, log and Multi-Domain servers and Maestro Orchestrator.
Until patched, limit Gaia Portal access to a dedicated management network and review which accounts can log in to it.
Remove unused Gaia Portal accounts and reset passwords of non-administrative accounts that could have been exposed.
Move devices on R81.10 or R81, which no longer receive fixes, to a supported release.
fixed_versions: Fixed in the November 2026 Jumbo Hotfix takes for R82.10, R82 and R81.20 per sk1000291, as reported by Rescana; take numbers to be confirmed in sk1000291
R82.20 listed as not affected by sk1000291, as reported by Rescana
verify: Confirm the installed Jumbo Hotfix take on every gateway and server is at or above the take named in sk1000291.
Test that a non-administrative Gaia Portal account can no longer perform administrator-only operations.
if_compromised: Isolate the device's management interface and preserve Gaia Portal, audit and Dynamic CLI logs before changes.
Revert unauthorised configuration and policy changes and remove unknown accounts.
Rotate all administrator and portal passwords and any keys or certificates stored on the device.
If root-level compromise is suspected, rebuild from a clean image, check the sk1000362 indicators, and report to Check Point and your national CERT.

CVE-2026-107484.caveats: Check Point's own sk1000291 could not be read (the page loads only with scripts), so this relies on the Canadian Cyber Centre and a secondary summary of the SK. Affected and fixed takes are not confirmed from the vendor. Rescana notes Check Point's blog table differs from the SK. The urgency of this item comes mostly from the exploited companion flaw CVE-2026-123039 fixed in the same update.
