CVE-2026-116606.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Barracuda reported exploitation affecting a small number of organizations on 9 November 2026; CISA added it to KEV on 10 November and Singapore's CSA reports public proof-of-concept code. No actor named.
CVE-2026-116606.how_exploited: Authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the Barracuda Email Security Gateway administrative interface. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach that interface invokes a configuration-import function without logging in and restores a crafted backup archive the appliance accepts as compatible, changing the appliance's global configuration. Barracuda and CISA say it can be chained with CVE-2026-111560, a command injection that needs administrative access, to run operating system commands as root.
preconditions: Barracuda ESG without patch BNSF-40425 (9.4.017 and later) or BNSF-40430 (earlier versions); Mandiant lists versions before 9.4.0.030 as affected.
The administrative interface is reachable by the attacker; Barracuda says devices whose admin interface is not exposed to the internet are less at risk.
No credentials or user interaction needed.
Root access additionally uses CVE-2026-111560 on the same unpatched appliance.
attack_path: Initial access: an unauthenticated request to the exposed admin interface reaches the configuration-import function.
Configuration tampering: a crafted backup is restored, changing the appliance's global settings.
Execution: chained with CVE-2026-111560, the attacker runs commands as root on the appliance.
Barracuda has not described what attackers did after access; on an email gateway, mail flow and stored credentials are at risk.
who_is_exposed: Organizations running Barracuda Email Security Gateway appliances (hardware or virtual) whose administrative interface is reachable from the internet.
ESG appliances with automatic patching turned off or firmware several versions behind.
CVE-2026-116606 affects ESG only; the chained command injection also affects Barracuda Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center and Web Security Gateway.
detect: Patch check: confirm in the appliance that BNSF-40425 or BNSF-40430 is applied and the firmware is the latest the device shows.
Exposure check: whether the ESG administrative interface answers from the internet.
Appliance logs: configuration imports or backup restores that no administrator performed, since at least 2 November 2026.
Configuration review: compare the current global configuration, admin accounts, relay and routing settings with a known-good backup.
Barracuda's advisory publishes no indicators of compromise; check the advisory and Barracuda support for later updates.

steps: Apply BNSF-40425 (ESG 9.4.017 and later) or BNSF-40430 (earlier ESG) and upgrade to the latest firmware; appliances several versions behind may need more than one update.
Turn automatic patching back on if it was disabled, and apply patches manually if they did not install automatically.
Restrict the administrative interface to trusted internal networks with network access controls.
Patch CVE-2026-111560 on any other Barracuda ADC, BMA, WAF, WCC or WSG devices.
Check the appliance for signs of compromise (US federal agencies must do forensic triage under BOD 26-04) and contact Barracuda Support if anything is unexplained.
workarounds: Restrict administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and do not expose them to the internet (Barracuda, CSA Singapore); this reduces exposure but is not a fix.
verify: Confirm in the appliance's firmware and patch view that the BNSF patch is applied and no newer firmware is offered.
Confirm from an outside network that the administrative interface does not answer.
if_compromised: Take the appliance out of the mail path and preserve its logs and configuration backups.
Contact Barracuda Support for incident guidance before rebuilding.
Restore a configuration from a backup taken before 2 November 2026 or rebuild it, and rotate admin passwords and any credentials stored on the appliance (directory, relay, LDAP).
Review mail flow and routing for interception, and report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-116606.caveats: Barracuda gives patch identifiers but no version numbers; 9.4.0.030 comes from Mandiant. Mandiant does not report exploitation; Barracuda does but gives no technique, indicators or scale beyond a small number of organizations. CVSS is 9.3 (v4.0) from Barracuda and Mandiant, 9.8 (v3.1) per CSA.

CVE-2026-116779.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: SignalWire's advisory (28 October 2026) says exploitation has been observed, and CISA added it to KEV on 9 November 2026 with forensic triage required. No actor has been named publicly.
CVE-2026-116779.how_exploited: Command injection through an exposed dangerous function (CWE-77, CWE-78, CWE-749). FreeSWITCH's SIP profiles route inbound SIP MESSAGE requests to a chat handler chosen from part of the recipient address, and nothing stopped a sender from selecting the built-in API chat handler, which passes the message text to FreeSWITCH's API command executor. A remote peer whose MESSAGE is accepted can therefore run API commands, including ones that reach the operating system, with the FreeSWITCH process's privileges, read configuration and credentials, and take control of calls. Where mod_lua is loaded, as in the stock configuration, the advisory describes a second route to run Lua code.
preconditions: FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 or earlier.
A SIP profile that accepts inbound MESSAGE requests from the attacker (chat is enabled on profiles by default).
If MESSAGE authentication is enforced, any one registered account on that profile; stock configurations that still hold a default directory user with no password need no authentication at all.
Inbound ACLs do not cover MESSAGE traffic, so an ACL alone does not prevent the attack on a reachable profile.
attack_path: Initial access: a single crafted SIP MESSAGE sent to an exposed FreeSWITCH profile selects the API chat handler.
Execution: FreeSWITCH API commands run with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process, including commands that reach the operating system or, with mod_lua, inline Lua.
Collection: configuration files and credentials (SIP accounts, gateways, trunks) can be read.
Impact: arbitrary call control, which can enable toll fraud or call interception. Public sources do not describe what attackers did after access.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted FreeSWITCH servers, PBXs and VoIP platforms with a SIP profile reachable from the internet or from untrusted SIP peers.
Products and services that embed FreeSWITCH; CISA notes the flaw is in an open-source component other products may use.
Deployments built from the sample or vanilla configuration, which keep a passwordless default directory user or leave chat enabled.
detect: Version check: list every FreeSWITCH instance, including those inside vendor appliances, and compare with 1.11.3.
Configuration review: which SIP profiles have inbound chat enabled, and whether any directory user has no password or hash.

SIP traffic and logs: inbound MESSAGE requests from unexpected sources or addressed to unusual recipient names; after upgrading, 1.11.3 logs rejected API chat attempts with the sender and requested command.
Host telemetry: the FreeSWITCH process starting shells or other programs, and unexpected changes to dialplan or configuration files.
Call records: unexpected outbound calls, transfers or eavesdrop sessions that could indicate call control abuse.

steps: Upgrade every FreeSWITCH instance to 1.11.3 or later and leave the new per-profile API chat setting (enable-chat-api-proto) off, which is its default.
Until upgraded, disable inbound chat on every SIP profile that does not need it; SignalWire says this is the only workaround that fully closes the route.
Keep MESSAGE authentication on and remove directory users that have no password or hash.
Restrict system API commands as an extra layer, knowing SignalWire says this does not close the path.
Check exposed servers for signs of compromise (US federal agencies must do forensic triage under BOD 26-04), then rotate SIP and trunk credentials stored in the configuration.
workarounds: Disable inbound chat on every SIP profile that does not need it (fully closes the route, per SignalWire).
Keep MESSAGE authentication enabled and remove directory users without a password or hash (reduces, does not close, exposure).
Disable system API commands in the switch settings (partial: other API commands remain reachable).
verify: Confirm the running FreeSWITCH version is 1.11.3 or later on every server and embedded product.
Confirm the API chat setting is absent or off on every profile, and that chat is disabled where not needed.
From a test peer, confirm that a MESSAGE selecting the API handler is refused and appears in the log as rejected.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve FreeSWITCH logs, SIP captures, call records and a disk image.
Rotate every credential in the FreeSWITCH configuration: SIP user passwords, gateway and trunk credentials, and database or event socket secrets.
Rebuild the host from a clean image and restore only reviewed configuration.
Ask your carrier to check for fraudulent call traffic, and report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-116779.caveats: Neither SignalWire nor CISA has said who exploited the flaw, at what scale, or what attackers did after access. A researcher write-up (Bitsight) refused automated reading; the technical detail here comes from the vendor advisory, CISA and a secondary briefing that agree.

CVE-2026-116928.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported. Microsoft (10 Nov 2026) marks it not exploited, not publicly disclosed and 'Exploitation Less Likely'; not in CISA's KEV catalog. OPSWAT (12 Nov) and CrowdStrike also report no exploitation.
CVE-2026-116928.how_exploited: An out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component. Microsoft says an unauthenticated attacker can send an email with a specially crafted attachment to an organisation running Exchange Server; Exchange automatically hands the attachment to Windows Search for indexing, so nobody has to open the message or the attachment. The memory corruption during indexing lets the attacker run code with the permissions of the processing service on the mail server. Rapid7 advises assuming SYSTEM-level privileges.
preconditions: The attacker can deliver an email with an attachment to a mailbox on the target Exchange server; no account, credentials or user interaction needed (CVSS AV:N/PR:N/UI:N).
Exchange content indexing processes the attachment through Windows Search, which OPSWAT says is enabled on most Exchange servers.
The Windows host lacks the November 10, 2026 cumulative update; every supported Windows client and server release from Windows 10 1607 and Server 2016 onward is listed.
attack_path: Initial access: a crafted attachment arrives by ordinary email delivery to the Exchange server.

Execution: Exchange queues the attachment for indexing and the Windows Search component parses it; the out-of-bounds write gives code execution in the indexing service, before any user sees the message.
Foothold: the attacker controls a process on the mail server, which holds mailbox data and usually has broad rights in Active Directory.
Follow-on (no attacks seen yet): an attacker would be expected to read mail, steal credentials and move laterally from the Exchange server.
who_is_exposed: On-premises Exchange Server deployments, including Exchange Server Subscription Edition, whose mail flow reaches Windows Search indexing; mail delivery makes them reachable from the internet.
Any Windows client or server release Microsoft lists (Windows 10 1607 to Windows 11 26H2, Server 2016 to 2025) that indexes untrusted files.
File servers with Windows Search enabled on shares that accept uploads, which OPSWAT names as a second exposure path.
detect: Check every Exchange server and DAG member for the November 2026 Windows cumulative update build (see fixed versions); an unpatched node is exposed.
Endpoint telemetry: unexpected child processes started by the Windows Search indexer or by Exchange transport components (OPSWAT).
Windows Application and System event logs: repeated crashes or restarts of the Windows Search service or Exchange search components with no matching change.
Mail gateway logs: unusual attachment types or malformed attachments sent to many mailboxes from external senders.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules have been published for this flaw as of 19 Nov 2026.

steps: Install the November 10, 2026 Windows cumulative update on all Exchange servers first, every DAG member, not just a test node; the fix ships in Windows updates, not in the Exchange security update (IT-Connect).
Also apply the current Exchange Server security update so Exchange flaws patched alongside it, such as CVE-2026-118207, are closed in the same window (OPSWAT).
Then patch file servers that run Windows Search on shares accepting uploads, followed by the rest of the Windows estate.
Keep Exchange on a supported release (Subscription Edition); Rapid7 notes earlier Exchange versions are out of support.
Review the Exchange server's outbound connections and the accounts it can use, to limit what a compromised mail server could reach.
fixed_versions: Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 1809: KB5131085, build 10.0.17763.9487
Windows Server 2016 and Windows 10 1607: KB5131291, build 10.0.14393.9688
verify: Confirm each server's OS build is at or above the fixed build for its release (winver or the update history).
Confirm every Exchange DAG member and every file server running Windows Search reports the November 2026 update installed.
Confirm the Windows Search and Exchange search services restarted cleanly after the update.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected Exchange or file server from the network while keeping it powered on for memory capture.
Preserve event logs, Exchange transport and message tracking logs and the suspicious messages before cleaning.
Reset credentials and secrets the server held or used, including service accounts and any privileged Active Directory accounts.
Rebuild the server from known-good media, patch it, then restore Exchange from a clean configuration.
Hunt for lateral movement from the mail server and report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-116928.caveats: Only Microsoft's short FAQ describes the attack; no researcher write-up exists. Microsoft's record also carries an 'Exchange Server' description, but its affected-product list names only Windows; IT-Connect says the fix is in Windows updates only, while OPSWAT advises patching both. Microsoft lists no workaround. Exact service privileges are not stated by Microsoft.

CVE-2026-118527.exploitation_status: Known exploited: chained since at least 1-3 Oct 2026 by UTA0576 (Volexity; low-confidence criminal motive) for root on patched appliances; CISA added it to KEV on 30 Oct 2026 (due 13 Nov).
CVE-2026-118527.how_exploited: A predictable-identifier flaw (CWE-340) in an upload handler of Ivanti Connect Secure. The handler saves an uploaded file before validating it and names it from the client-supplied filename, so the location is predictable; an attacker can place a file with content of their choosing at a known place on disk and use it before it is deleted (Volexity, CISA). On its own it needs an authenticated session and scores 4.3, but UTA0576 reached it through the authentication bypass CVE-2026-104935 and combined it with the privilege escalation CVE-2026-111357 to run code as root without logging in.
preconditions: The Connect Secure web interface is reachable by the attacker, normally from the internet.
An authenticated session, or the authentication bypass CVE-2026-104935 on appliances not yet updated past it.
Connect Secure 22.8R2 through 22.8R2.5, or 25.1 releases before 25.1.1.3; appliances patched only for CVE-2026-104935 (22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2) remain affected.
attack_path: Initial access: an authentication bypass in a public login handler lets the attacker reach protected internal scripts (CVE-2026-104935).
File placement: the attacker uploads attacker-controlled content to the predictable location created by this flaw and triggers it in the short window before the handler deletes it.
Privilege escalation: a trusted maintenance service is manipulated to run the attacker's code as root, then restored (CVE-2026-111357).

Actions on objective: no web shell or malware; the actor re-exploited for each command and stole appliance and Active Directory credentials, LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, ran Kerberoasting and password spraying, and exfiltrated data.
Defence evasion: the actor edited debug and audit logs, deleted temporary scripts and restored altered memory, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool did not detect it.
who_is_exposed: Every organisation running Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances below 22.8R2.6 or 25.1.1.3, physical or virtual; Shadowserver tracks over 5,000 internet-exposed instances (BleepingComputer).
Organisations whose appliance holds a directory service account, since the actor targeted Active Directory secrets from the appliance.
detect: Version check: confirm each appliance runs 22.8R2.6, 25.1.1.3 or later.
Web and access logs: unusually high volumes of requests to the public login handler and mismatches between the requested path and internal routing, as Volexity describes.
Authentication failures originating from the appliance's internal interface, which Volexity noticed first in its investigation.
Temporary directories on the appliance: leftover scripts or files; treat missing log entries as possible tampering, not as proof of a clean device.
Active Directory: queries from the appliance's service account for LAPS, BitLocker and password attributes, Kerberoasting and password spraying from the VPN's address.
Integrity Checker Tool alone is not enough here (Volexity, CISA); confirmation needs memory and disk acquisition and network forensics. Use Volexity's published indicators by reference.

steps: If compromise is suspected, acquire memory and disk images and network evidence before upgrading.
Upgrade Connect Secure to 22.8R2.6 or 25.1.1.3 or later; the earlier fixes for CVE-2026-104935 do not close this flaw.
Rotate the appliance's directory service account credentials and any secrets stored on the appliance.
Rotate local administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys in Active Directory if the appliance may have been reached, as Volexity advises.
Restrict management interfaces to trusted networks and forward appliance logs off-box so tampering is harder.
verify: Confirm the running Connect Secure version in the admin console after the upgrade.
Confirm no requests matching the reported pattern continue to succeed, and that internal-interface authentication failures stop.
Confirm rotated service account credentials are the only ones in use.
if_compromised: Preserve memory, disk and network evidence; the Integrity Checker Tool cannot be relied on for this activity.
Isolate the appliance, upgrade or rebuild it on a fixed release, and reset all credentials it stored.
Assume Active Directory secrets reachable by the appliance's account are exposed: rotate LAPS passwords, BitLocker keys and Kerberoastable service account passwords.
Hunt for lateral movement originating from the appliance and for password spraying across the domain.
Report to Ivanti support and your national CERT.

CVE-2026-118527.caveats: Ivanti's own advisory page did not load for automated reading (it needs a browser), so versions and status come from CISA's catalog, NVD ranges on file and news reports quoting Ivanti; confidence is capped at medium. Ivanti said no alternative mitigation exists. Motive and attribution rest on Volexity alone, at low confidence. Ivanti says few customers were hit.

CVE-2026-119618.exploitation_status: Reportedly exploited in the wild with public proof-of-concept code, per Singapore's CSA alert AL-2026-164 (17 Nov 2026). Earlier research notes saw no confirmed attacks; no attacker is named.
CVE-2026-119618.how_exploited: A race condition (concurrent use of a shared resource without proper synchronisation) in the header-handling code of mod_http2, the module that serves HTTP/2 in Apache HTTP Server. mod_http2 processes the streams of one connection on several threads, and the bug lets one thread write into memory that belongs to another, corrupting the heap. An unauthenticated remote attacker who opens HTTP/2 connections and sends crafted request streams can turn that corruption into code execution with the privileges of the Apache worker process. Red Hat says public research showed a reliable exploit against a default configuration with mod_http2 enabled.
preconditions: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, or standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.
mod_http2 loaded and HTTP/2 enabled through the Protocols setting, over TLS (h2) or cleartext (h2c), server-wide or on any one virtual host; HTTP/1.1-only servers are not affected.
The attacker can reach the server over the network; no credentials or user interaction are needed.
Red Hat rates RHEL 9 and 10 Important rather than Critical because per-stream memory allocators there make exploitation harder; RHEL 8 and earlier are not affected.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers find web servers that advertise HTTP/2 and run an affected Apache version.
Initial access: crafted concurrent HTTP/2 streams trigger the race and corrupt the worker process heap.
Execution: arbitrary code runs as the Apache worker user; failed attempts usually crash worker processes.
Follow-on: no campaign details are published; researchers expect web shells, credential theft and lateral movement to back-end systems, and Orca notes wormable potential.
who_is_exposed: Internet-facing Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 to 2.4.70 with HTTP/2 enabled, including reverse proxies and load balancers built on Apache.
Distribution packages: RHEL 9 and 10 (fixed), Debian stable releases (fix pending when Orca wrote), Amazon Linux (pending); check your distributor.
Users of the standalone mod_h2 from GitHub, which is archived and has no fixed release.
detect: Version and configuration check: list Apache versions and every server-wide and virtual-host Protocols setting that enables h2 or h2c.
Apache error log: bursts of worker child crashes (segmentation faults) or restarts, which can signal failed exploitation.
Process telemetry: the Apache worker user starting shells or unexpected programs, or new files in web roots.
Network egress logs: unexpected outbound connections from web servers.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules have been published by Apache or CSA.

steps: Find every Apache HTTP Server instance and note its version and whether HTTP/2 is enabled anywhere in its configuration.
Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or your distribution's patched package, internet-facing HTTP/2 servers first.
Replace standalone mod_h2 with the mod_http2 bundled in 2.4.71, since the standalone project has no fix.

If you cannot patch at once, disable HTTP/2 by leaving only HTTP/1.1 in the Protocols setting, server-wide and in every virtual host (Orca Security interim advice; expect some client performance loss).
Restart Apache fully so no old worker processes remain, then check hosts for signs of compromise because exploitation is reported.
fixed_versions: RHEL 9 and 10: Red Hat's fixed httpd packages; other distributions: the distributor's patched package
verify: Confirm the running server reports version 2.4.71 or a distribution build that includes the fix, after a full restart.
If HTTP/2 was disabled instead, confirm from outside that the server no longer negotiates HTTP/2 on any virtual host.
Rerun a vulnerability scan against all public web servers.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve Apache access and error logs, system logs and a disk image.
Rotate TLS private keys, application secrets and credentials readable by the Apache user or stored on the host.
Rebuild from a known-good image with a fixed Apache, and review back-end systems the server could reach.
Report to your national CERT (in Singapore, SingCERT).

CVE-2026-119618.caveats: CSA says exploitation is reported but gives no detail, and earlier research found no confirmed attacks; it was not in CISA's KEV catalog on file. Severity differs: Apache critical, Red Hat 9.8, cve.org and CSA 8.1. Apache gives no workaround; disabling HTTP/2 is Orca's advice. Distribution fix status changes quickly.

CVE-2026-119958.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported. Microsoft (10 Nov 2026) marks it not exploited, not publicly disclosed and 'Exploitation Less Likely'; not in CISA's KEV catalog. CrowdStrike and OPSWAT (12 Nov) report no exploitation.
CVE-2026-119958.how_exploited: An out-of-bounds write in the Windows LDAP service. Microsoft says an unauthenticated attacker who can reach a server's LDAP service can send a specially crafted sequence of LDAP calls that corrupts memory and runs the attacker's code inside the LDAP service. No credentials or user interaction are needed. On a domain controller, where LDAP serves Active Directory, that would put the attacker inside the domain's trust boundary.
preconditions: Network access to the LDAP service of an unpatched Windows server, typically a domain controller on TCP 389 or 636 (CrowdStrike, OPSWAT).
No authentication and no user interaction (CVSS AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N).
Windows without the November 10, 2026 cumulative update; Microsoft lists every supported release from Windows 10 1607 and Server 2016 to Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker, already on a network that can reach a domain controller (any domain-joined host by default), connects to its LDAP service.
Execution: crafted LDAP calls trigger the out-of-bounds write and run code in the LDAP service on the domain controller.
Follow-on (CrowdStrike's assessment, no attacks seen): credential extraction, abuse of directory replication and lateral movement across the domain.
Impact: control of a domain controller amounts to control of the Active Directory domain.
who_is_exposed: Every Active Directory domain controller, because LDAP runs on all of them and cannot be turned off without breaking the domain (CrowdStrike).
Domain controllers reachable from guest, remote-access or OT segments, which OPSWAT warns is common, or worse, from the internet.
Other Windows servers that run an LDAP service, such as Active Directory Lightweight Directory Services, on the listed releases.
detect: Version check: confirm every domain controller runs at least the fixed November 2026 build for its release.
System and Directory Service event logs: LDAP service or LSASS crashes, or unexpected domain controller restarts, with no matching change record (OPSWAT).
Network: map which segments can reach domain controllers on ports 389 and 636, and look for LDAP traffic from hosts that do not normally query the directory.
Post-compromise signs on a domain controller: new privileged accounts or group changes, unexpected replication requests, and new services or scheduled tasks.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules have been published for this flaw as of 19 Nov 2026.

steps: Patch domain controllers first with the November 10, 2026 Windows cumulative update, before the general server estate (OPSWAT, IT-Connect).
Use the same maintenance window for the other unauthenticated flaws on domain controllers patched this month, such as Windows DNS (OPSWAT).
During rollout, restrict which networks can reach domain controllers on LDAP ports; this buys time but does not remove the bug (OPSWAT).
Patch remaining Windows servers that run LDAP services, then all other Windows systems.
Enforce LDAP signing if it is not already enforced, as general hardening (OPSWAT); Microsoft does not list it as a mitigation for this flaw.
fixed_versions: Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 1809: KB5131085, build 10.0.17763.9487
Windows Server 2016 and Windows 10 1607: KB5131291, build 10.0.14393.9688
verify: Confirm every domain controller reports a build at or above the fixed build for its release.
Confirm the update installed on all domain controllers in every domain and forest, including read-only and DR site controllers.
Confirm LDAP and Active Directory replication work normally after the restart.
if_compromised: Treat a compromised domain controller as a compromise of the whole domain; isolate it and engage incident response.
Preserve memory, event logs and directory state from the affected controller before cleaning.
Reset the KRBTGT account twice and reset privileged and service account passwords.
Rebuild affected domain controllers from known-good media and review all privileged group membership and trusts.
Report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-119958.caveats: Only Microsoft's short FAQ describes the attack; no researcher has published a technical write-up. Exposure and follow-on stages are vendors' assessments, not observed attacks. Microsoft lists no workaround. Restricting LDAP reach and LDAP signing are OPSWAT's suggestions; signing is not stated to block this flaw.

CVE-2026-119977.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: CISA added it to KEV on 3 Nov 2026 (due 6 Nov), citing a Canadian Centre for Cyber Security advisory per eSecurity Planet. Wordfence saw attackers repeatedly polling for the window. No attacker named.
CVE-2026-119977.how_exploited: A time-of-check time-of-use race (CWE-367) in WordPress Core's full-package upgrade. While a site upgrades itself, WordPress unpacks the new release into a staging folder under the web root whose name is predictable and which the web server will serve and execute. An unauthenticated attacker who keeps requesting the staged installer files can reach them during the few seconds the upgrade runs and get the server to run code as the web server user. That gives database credentials, the chance to plant a web shell that outlives the upgrade, and a foothold to reach internal services.
preconditions: The site is reachable over the web; no login and no user interaction are needed.
A full-package core upgrade must be in progress, either started by an administrator or run by unattended background auto-updates.
The attacker must win the race: the window lasts seconds, so attackers poll repeatedly (high attack complexity, CVSS 8.1).
An affected WordPress version from 4.7 through 7.1.3 that lacks its branch's backported fix.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers find WordPress sites and repeatedly request the predictable staging location, waiting for an upgrade to start.
Initial access: during the upgrade window, a staged installer file is reached and executed by the server without authentication.
Execution: code runs as the web server user.
Persistence: attackers can drop a web shell elsewhere in the site, or create administrator accounts, so access survives the upgrade.
Follow-on: theft of database credentials and secrets from the site configuration, and outbound connections to reach other services.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted WordPress sites on 4.7 through 7.1.3 without their branch's security release, especially those with automatic background core updates, which upgrade unattended.
Hosting where PHP runs with broad file and database permissions, which raises the impact.
Sites already on 7.1.4 or a backported security release for their branch are not affected.
detect: Version check: confirm each site runs 7.1.4 or its branch's fixed release, and that the last automatic update actually completed.

Web server logs: compare recent core upgrade times with requests to staged installer files in the upgrade folder under the content directory, especially the configuration setup file, and repeated automated requests to that area.
File review: look for unexpected PHP files in the upgrade folder and elsewhere under the content directory after updates.
WordPress users: look for unfamiliar administrator accounts and unauthorised configuration changes.
Network: watch for unusual outbound connections from the web server user. A suspicious request alone does not prove compromise.

steps: Update to WordPress 7.1.4, or the security release for your branch, as soon as possible.
Check that automatic updates finished on every site rather than assuming they did.
Until patched, deny direct web access to the temporary upgrade folder at the web server and avoid running core upgrades on exposed sites without that block.
Run PHP as a least-privilege user and limit file and database permissions to reduce the impact of any compromise.
Review logs around recent upgrade times for signs of exploitation (see detect).
US federal agencies: follow BOD 26-04 and CISA's forensics triage requirements, which the KEV entry marks as required.
fixed_versions: Backported security releases for every branch from 4.7; Wordfence names 7.0.8, 6.9.11, 6.8.12 and 4.7.39 among them
Other branches: NVD's affected ranges (CyberView's KEV copy) end before 6.7.11, 6.5.14, 5.9.20 and similar per-branch releases
verify: Confirm the dashboard or version file reports the fixed release for the branch on every site.
Confirm the staging folder is no longer predictable and is not reachable from the web during the next upgrade.
Run a file integrity check of core files against the official release.
if_compromised: Preserve web server logs, the database and a copy of the site files before removing anything, and involve incident responders.
Take the site offline or into maintenance mode and look for web shells and unknown administrator accounts.
Rotate the database password, authentication keys and salts, administrator passwords and any API keys the site holds.
Rebuild from a clean WordPress release and known-good content, then patch before going back online.
Record the fix and findings, and report to your national CERT (US federal agencies to CISA).

CVE-2026-119977.caveats: The WordPress release note describes the flaw only briefly, and Wordfence's page did not load; the mechanism comes from SAFE Security and eSecurity Planet, which agree. Reported attack volumes vary widely between outlets and were not used. WordPress rated the issue lower than the CVE record's 8.1. Blocking the upgrade folder is advice from researchers and press, not from WordPress itself, so it is listed as a step, not a vendor workaround.

CVE-2026-120017.exploitation_status: No exploitation and no public exploit code reported in the sources read (SAP, RedRays, The Hacker News) as of 19 Nov 2026. Not in CISA's KEV catalog. Fixed on SAP Patch Day, 10 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-120017.how_exploited: Improper verification of a cryptographic signature (CWE-347) in the SAML2 service provider of SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform. Under certain configurations the service provider did not check the identity provider's signature on incoming SAML responses and assertions. An unauthenticated attacker who reaches the service provider's logon endpoint can submit a forged assertion naming any user and be logged on as that user, including privileged accounts. SAP rates the scope as changed: a forged administrator session can reach connected systems through trusted RFC and other integrations.
preconditions: The AS ABAP system uses SAML2 for browser logon on at least one client, for example Fiori Launchpad or Web GUI behind an identity provider.
The SAML2 configuration is one of those in which signatures on responses or assertions were not verified (SAP does not detail which publicly).
Network access to the system's web logon endpoints, often from the internet for Fiori systems.
SAP_BASIS 702, 731, 740, 750 to 758, 816 or 920 to 922 without the correction; no login or user interaction needed.
attack_path: Initial access: a forged SAML assertion is accepted by the service provider, giving a logged-on session as a chosen user.
Privilege: the attacker picks a privileged ABAP user, so no escalation step is needed.
Impact: full access to business data and functions the impersonated user has, with SAP warning of full system compromise.
Lateral movement: trusted RFC connections and integrations from the compromised system to connected components (per SAP's changed-scope rating and RedRays).
who_is_exposed: SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform systems (including S/4HANA) on the affected SAP_BASIS releases that have SAML2 logon enabled on any client.
Internet-facing Fiori Launchpad and Web GUI systems that use an external identity provider are at highest risk (RedRays).
Systems without SAML2 configured are not described as exposed, but SAP's note text is not public, so treat SAML2-enabled clients as in scope until checked.
detect: In transaction SAML2, list every client with SAML2 enabled and every trusted identity provider, and confirm signature checks are required for responses and assertions.
Search the Security Audit Log for SAML2 logons by privileged users, emergency and technical accounts from unexpected sources, times or user agents.
Compare service provider logons with the identity provider's own sign-in logs: a logon on the SAP side with no matching identity provider sign-in is a strong sign of a forged assertion.
Check the SAP_BASIS support package level, or whether the correction instructions of Note 3849308 are implemented (transaction SNOTE). No public indicators or detection rules exist.

steps: Identify every AS ABAP system and client with SAML2 logon enabled, internet-facing Fiori systems first.
Apply SAP Security Note 3849308, by its correction instructions or the support package it lists; read FAQ Note 3849602.
Review each trusted identity provider in transaction SAML2 and remove any that are not needed.
Confirm the service provider requires signed responses and assertions after the fix.
Review recent SAML2 logons of privileged users before and after patching.
fixed_versions: SAP_BASIS 702, 731, 740, 750 to 758, 816 and 920 to 922: apply SAP Note 3849308 correction instructions or the support package it lists
Exact support package levels are in SAP Note 3849308 (needs an SAP for Me login)
workarounds: None: SAP gives no workaround, according to RedRays' reading of the note. Patching is the only fix.
verify: SNOTE shows Note 3849308 fully implemented, or the system is at or above the support package the note lists.
In transaction SAML2, each trusted identity provider is set to require signed responses and assertions.
Normal SAML2 sign-in through the real identity provider still works after the change.
if_compromised: Lock the impersonated accounts, end their sessions and preserve the Security Audit Log, HTTP logs and change documents.
Review changes made by those users: new users, role and authorization changes, transports, RFC destinations and business transactions.
Rotate credentials of technical users and RFC destinations, and check connected systems for activity from the affected system.
Report the incident to your national CERT and data protection authority where personal data was reached.

CVE-2026-120017.caveats: SAP's note is behind a login and no finder write-up is public, so which configurations are affected is unclear. RedRays' release list (adds 804 and 918) differs slightly from SAP's CVE record. Status could change; check KEV.

CVE-2026-120704.exploitation_status: No in-the-wild use of this CVE reported as of 25 Nov 2026. It is the final step of an unauthenticated chain that Eye Security published on 24 Nov; watchTowr reports attacks on the chain's first step, CVE-2026-120705.
CVE-2026-120704.how_exploited: Remote code execution through SQLite JDBC extension loading in GeoServer's JDBC security services (rated High by GeoServer). An administrator can register a JDBC user or role service whose database connection is allowed to load native extensions. Eye Security used an SQLite connection to load a native library the attacker had uploaded, which ran code on the server on both Linux and Windows. Admin rights are needed, but the attacker can get them without a password through CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129245.
preconditions: The attacker has a GeoServer administrator session, through stolen credentials or the forged remember-me session described for CVE-2026-129245.
GeoServer before 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7 with JDBC security services available; Eye Security says the chain works on default configurations and verified it on 3.0.1.
The attacker can place a native library file on the server; Eye Security did this through GeoServer itself.
The admin interface can be reached by the attacker.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker reads credential material through CVE-2026-120705, then forges an administrator session through CVE-2026-129245.
Staging: as administrator, the attacker uploads a native library file to the server.
Execution: the attacker registers a JDBC security service with an SQLite connection that loads the library, which runs code with the rights of the GeoServer process.
Follow-on: not described for this CVE. Code running as the GeoServer service can read data store credentials and spatial data and reach internal networks.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted GeoServer on the 3.0, 2.28 and 2.27 lines before 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7, on Linux and Windows.
Most at risk: servers with the admin interface reachable from the internet and still open to CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129245, which remove the need for a password.
Products that bundle GeoServer until they ship the fixed release.
detect: Check the version on the About GeoServer page (Build Information); anything older than 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7 is exposed.
Review the security configuration in the data directory for new or changed JDBC user or role services, especially ones using SQLite, that your team did not create.
Search the data directory and temporary folders for native library files (.so or .dll) that do not belong to the installation.
Watch endpoint telemetry for the GeoServer Java process starting shells or other programs, or making unexpected outbound connections.
Correlate admin sessions without a normal login with earlier WFS GetFeatureById or stored-query requests from the same source.

steps: Upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7 (tracked as GEOS-12292). The 2.27 line is end-of-life, so plan a move to 2.28 or 3.0.

Apply the same upgrade for the other October 2026 fixes, including CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129245 that make this step reachable without a password, and the related JDBC deserialization flaw CVE-2026-129242.
Limit access to the GeoServer web admin interface to trusted networks and review who holds administrator rights.
Remove JDBC user or role services that are not needed.
verify: Confirm the new version on the About GeoServer page.
Confirm that every configured JDBC user and role service is one your team created and still needs.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and keep logs, the data directory, unknown library files and a disk image for investigation.
Treat the host as fully compromised: rebuild it from a clean image and restore only checked configuration.
Rotate GeoServer admin and user passwords, the remember-me key, and every database or service credential stored in GeoServer.
Check connected databases and internal systems for follow-on access, and report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-120704.caveats: GeoServer's GitHub advisory (GHSA-wc3v-48j7-xf57) returned 403 and was not read; GeoServer's own posts give only the title and fixed releases. The mechanism comes from Eye Security alone. The exact vulnerable version range for this CVE is not stated by GeoServer. GeoServer gives no workaround.

GeoServer 3.0.2 Release
GeoServer 2.28.6 Release
Eye Security: Unauthenticated RCE in GeoServer
The Hacker News: Hackers exploit two GeoServer flaws

CVE-2026-120705.exploitation_status: Exploitation attempts in the wild: The Hacker News (25 Nov 2026) cites watchTowr seeing probes that abuse it with CVE-2026-129243. Researchers have published RCE chain write-ups. Not in CISA KEV as of 25 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-120705.how_exploited: An unauthenticated XML injection in GeoServer's Web Feature Service (WFS) stored query handling. Text in a stored query is parsed again as XML with file inclusion enabled, so an anonymous attacker can make GeoServer read local text files the GeoServer process can access, or fetch attacker-chosen web addresses, and return the contents. Attackers read the security configuration and user database to obtain the administrator password digest and the remember-me signing key, then forge an administrator session (CVE-2026-129245) and use administrator-only JDBC features (CVE-2026-120704 or CVE-2026-129242) to run code as the GeoServer user.
preconditions: Network access to the GeoServer WFS service; no credentials are needed. Researchers say default settings are enough.
GeoServer 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, or 2.27.6 and earlier.
Creating stored queries is normally restricted; anonymous exploitation in the reported chain relies on the service rule bypass CVE-2026-129243, or on WFS write access being open.
For the full chain to code execution: the default admin account in the default user service and an unchanged remember-me configuration.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: scanning for internet-facing GeoServer; watchTowr saw error-based probes that create and invoke stored queries.
Initial access: anonymous WFS requests create a stored query (via the CVE-2026-129243 rule bypass) that pulls local files into the response.

Credential theft: the attacker reads the security configuration and user files, obtaining the admin password digest and the remember-me signing key; the same flaw also allows server-side requests to other hosts.
Privilege escalation: a forged administrator remember-me cookie gives admin access without the password (CVE-2026-129245).

Execution: as admin, the attacker configures a JDBC user service that loads attacker-supplied code or deserialises attacker data, running commands as the GeoServer process (often root in the official container).
Next steps: no post-exploitation activity has been published; expect web shells, data theft from connected spatial databases and use of stored data store credentials.
who_is_exposed: Internet-facing GeoServer instances on affected 3.0.x, 2.28.x and 2.27.x releases, including the official container images.
Products and platforms that bundle GeoServer (the fix is in the gs-wfs-core module and the GeoTools gt-metadata library).
Internal GeoServer instances are exposed to anyone on the network who can reach WFS.
detect: Version check: the About GeoServer page in the web admin shows the build version; anything below 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7 is affected.
Data directory: review the WFS stored query storage for queries nobody on your team created (recommended by the Rapid7 researcher).
Request and access logs: anonymous WFS stored query creation, description or deletion requests, and bursts of stored query errors, which match the probes watchTowr reported.
Security configuration: unexpected changes to user and role services (especially new JDBC services), remember-me settings or administrator accounts.
Host and network: the Java process starting shells, new native library files written to disk, and outbound connections from GeoServer to unknown hosts.
No indicator lists or detection rules were published in the sources read.

steps: Upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2 or 2.28.6, or to 2.27.7 if you must stay on the end-of-life 2.27 line; this also fixes the other chain steps.
If GeoServer is internet-facing and cannot be upgraded at once, restrict access to it (VPN, IP allow lists or a reverse proxy) until it is patched.

After upgrading, change the admin password and any account passwords, because their digests may already have been read; do not rely on changing the remember-me key on an unpatched server, since the flaw can read the new key.
In clusters, set the same remember-me key on every node in the way the fixed release documents, because fixed releases generate a new key at each start.
Review the server for signs of compromise (see detect), especially if it was exposed between October and the upgrade.
verify: The About GeoServer page shows 3.0.2, 2.28.6, 2.27.7 or later.
For embedded copies, confirm the deployed gs-wfs-core and gt-metadata libraries are at the fixed versions.
Confirm that old remember-me cookies no longer work after restart and that only known accounts and stored queries exist.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve the data directory, logs and a disk or container image.
Remove unknown stored queries, JDBC user or role services and accounts, but rebuild from a clean, patched install rather than cleaning in place if code execution is suspected.
Rotate every secret GeoServer held: admin and user passwords, database and data store credentials, cloud keys and anything in readable configuration files.
Check connected databases and file shares for access from the GeoServer host.
Report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-120705.caveats: GeoServer's GitHub advisory could not be read (403); its summary page calls this an XML injection in WFS GetFeatureById, while researchers describe a stored query file read. Exploitation is watchTowr's report relayed by news; the post itself was not read. Release dates differ between sources. Researcher interim measures (proxy filtering, disabling remember-me) are not vendor guidance.

CVE-2026-120868.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported: Citrix reports none and no public proof of concept was confirmed (CERT-EU, 12 Nov 2026). Not in CISA's KEV catalog as of 13 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-120868.how_exploited: A memory overflow (CWE-119) in the core packet processing of NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. An attacker on the network sends specially formed traffic to the appliance; mishandling of it overflows memory and, per Citrix, causes unpredictable or erroneous behaviour or a denial of service. Citrix does not describe code execution, but its CVSS 4.0 vector rates confidentiality, integrity and availability impact high, so a more serious outcome cannot be ruled out. It needs no login and no special feature, so default configurations are affected.
preconditions: Network access to the appliance's traffic-handling interfaces; no authentication and no user interaction (CVSS 4.0 score 9.3).
No feature needs to be enabled: Citrix says all deployments, including the default configuration, are affected.
Customer-managed NetScaler ADC or Gateway 14.1 before 14.1-73.57, 13.1 before 13.1-64.39, 14.1-FIPS before 14.1-73.58 FIPS, or 13.1-FIPS and NDcPP before 13.1-37.293.
attack_path: Reach the appliance: NetScaler appliances usually sit at the network edge, so any internet-facing virtual server is a reachable target.
Trigger: the attacker sends traffic that overflows memory in packet processing.
Impact per Citrix: unpredictable behaviour or denial of service, which can take down the gateway, load balancing or remote access the appliance provides.
who_is_exposed: Every customer-managed NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway on an affected build, physical, virtual or cloud-hosted.
Secure Private Access hybrid deployments that use NetScaler instances (Citrix says these must be upgraded).
Not affected: Citrix-managed cloud services and Citrix-managed Adaptive Authentication, which Citrix patches itself.
detect: Version check: compare each appliance's build with the fixed builds in Citrix bulletin CTX697305.
Appliance health: unexplained crashes, packet engine restarts, core dumps or reboot loops on unpatched builds deserve investigation (Rescana), though they are not proof of attack.
Monitoring: sudden gaps in availability of Gateway, AAA or load-balanced services, and spikes of malformed traffic to virtual server addresses.
Citrix says it is not releasing indicators of compromise for this bulletin.

steps: Upgrade every customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway to a fixed build as soon as possible (Citrix), internet-facing Gateway and AAA appliances first (CERT-EU).
Include FIPS and NDcPP appliances and Secure Private Access hybrid NetScaler instances.
Keep the management addresses (NSIP) off untrusted networks while patching (Rescana guidance, for a separate management-plane flaw in the same bulletin).
Upgrade for the other 27 flaws in the same bulletin at the same time, including CVE-2026-107412 (CVSS 9.5) on Gateway and AAA.
fixed_versions: NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.57 and later releases of 14.1
NetScaler ADC and Gateway 13.1-64.39 and later releases of 13.1
verify: Confirm each appliance, including every node of a high-availability pair or cluster, reports a fixed build after the reboot.
Confirm services on the appliance are healthy and no unexplained crashes recur.
if_compromised: Collect core dumps, crash logs and system logs from the appliance before rebooting or upgrading where possible.
Upgrade to a fixed build and check the configuration for unexpected changes.
If code execution or tampering is suspected, rotate credentials and certificates on the appliance, rebuild it from a clean image and report to Citrix and your national CERT.

CVE-2026-120868.caveats: The 'exploitation or exploit code reported' tag on the assignment is not supported by the sources read: Citrix and CERT-EU report no exploitation and no confirmed proof of concept. Citrix describes only unpredictable behaviour or denial of service; whether code execution is possible is not stated. No researcher write-up was found. Citrix gives no workaround and the bulletin did not address end-of-life builds.

CVE-2026-121653.exploitation_status: Public exploit code reported; no exploitation in the wild reported. NCSC-NL (NCSC-2026-0493, 13 Nov 2026) says a proof of concept is public. Ivanti saw no exploitation (10 Nov); not in CISA KEV on 19 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-121653.how_exploited: An SQL injection flaw in the Core server of Ivanti Endpoint Manager (EPM). An attacker who can reach the Core over the network sends input that the server places into a database query without proper neutralisation, so the attacker's own database instructions run. Ivanti and NCSC-NL state this lets a remote attacker with no account run code on the Core server. Because the Core manages software, scripts and settings for every enrolled endpoint, control of it is a likely route to the wider managed estate.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the EPM Core server over the network; no credentials and no user action are needed (CVSS 3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N, score 9.8).
The Core runs Ivanti Endpoint Manager before 2024 SU8 (2024 SU7 and earlier).
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker finds an EPM Core server reachable from the internet or from a network they already control and sends crafted input to it.
Execution: the injected database instructions are turned into code running on the Core server, per Ivanti's description.

Likely next steps (not yet observed for this flaw): from a compromised management server, attackers can read stored credentials and push software or scripts to managed endpoints, so treat the Core as a path to every device it manages.
No incident responder has yet published an observed attack chain for this CVE.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running an on-premises Ivanti Endpoint Manager Core server on 2024 SU7 or earlier.
Highest risk: Core servers reachable from the internet or from large untrusted internal networks.
Every endpoint managed by an affected Core is indirectly exposed, since the Core distributes software and configuration to them.
The separate EPM Agent flaw fixed in the same release (CVE-2026-18128, cleartext traffic) affects networks where an attacker can sit between agents and the Core.
detect: Version check: confirm the version of every EPM Core server; anything below 2024 SU8 is affected.
Exposure check: find Core servers reachable from the internet with your external attack surface scan or firewall rules.

Database and web logs on the Core: look for database errors, unusual query failures and spikes of malformed requests from unfamiliar addresses, especially since 13 Nov 2026 when exploit code became public.
Process behaviour on the Core: new child processes started by the database service or the EPM web services, unexpected command interpreters, and new files written by those services.
Management activity: unexpected new software distribution tasks, scripts or policies pushed from the Core, and new or changed console administrator accounts.
Ivanti published no indicators of compromise with the advisory; watch Ivanti and NCSC-NL for later detection guidance.

steps: Upgrade every Ivanti Endpoint Manager Core server to 2024 SU8 or later, starting with any Core reachable from the internet.
Until upgraded, remove internet access to the Core and limit network access to it to the hosts and agent networks that need it.
Review each Core for signs of compromise (see detect) before and after upgrading, given that exploit code is public.
Update agents as part of the same release to close CVE-2026-18128, the cleartext agent traffic flaw.
workarounds: Neither Ivanti (as summarised in its CVE record and secondary reports) nor NCSC-NL gives a workaround; upgrading is the only fix. Restricting network access is general hardening, not a vendor workaround.
verify: Confirm each Core server reports 2024 SU8 or later in the EPM console or installed software list.
Confirm from outside your network that the Core is not reachable from the internet.
Re-check logs after the upgrade for continued attempts and confirm no unexpected distribution tasks or administrator accounts remain.
if_compromised: Isolate the Core server from the network and stop distribution tasks, while preserving disk images, database and web server logs for investigation.
Treat every managed endpoint as possibly affected: review recent distribution jobs and scripts the Core pushed and check endpoints for unknown software.
Rotate all credentials the Core stores or uses (service accounts, domain accounts used for deployment, database accounts) and console administrator passwords.
Rebuild the Core from clean media at 2024 SU8 or later rather than cleaning it in place, and restore only reviewed configuration.
Report the incident to your national CERT (NCSC-NL in the Netherlands, CISA in the US) and to Ivanti support.

CVE-2026-121653.caveats: Ivanti advisory page did not render for an automated reader, so vendor facts come from Ivanti CVE record, NCSC-NL and a secondary summary quoting Ivanti. No technical write-up or proof of concept was read, by design, and no attack in the wild is reported, so the attack path beyond code execution on the Core is a general assessment. NCSC-NL says the public code raises the short-term chance of exploitation.

CVE-2026-121810.exploitation_status: No exploitation and no public exploit code reported for this flaw as of 19 Nov 2026; it is not in CISA's KEV catalog. The public proof of concept CERT-FR mentions is for the separate HTTP/2 flaw CVE-2026-123007.
CVE-2026-121810.how_exploited: A use-after-free in NGINX's HTTP/3 module (ngx_http_v3_module), disclosed by F5 on 18 Nov 2026. A remote attacker without credentials sends crafted HTTP/3 traffic that makes an NGINX worker process use memory it has already freed. Usually this crashes and restarts the worker, a denial of service. F5's CVE record says code execution is possible only where ASLR is disabled or the attacker can get around it, and that success also depends on conditions outside the attacker's control. Only the data plane is affected, not the control plane.
preconditions: NGINX Open Source 1.25.0 to 1.30.6 or 1.31.0 to 1.31.8, or NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1, 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1, or R34 to R36.
The configuration serves HTTP/3; F5 says the issue affects only configurations that use HTTP/3.
The attacker can reach the HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP) listener; no login or user interaction is needed.
For code execution rather than a crash, ASLR must be off or bypassable, and timing conditions outside the attacker's control must line up (high attack complexity in the CVSS vector).
attack_path: Initial access: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP/3 traffic to an internet-facing NGINX listener.
Execution: the worker process uses freed memory; most attempts crash the worker, which the master process restarts.
Possible code execution in the worker process where ASLR is absent or defeated, giving the attacker the worker's privileges.
No attacker activity after access has been reported, because no exploitation has been seen.
who_is_exposed: Web servers, reverse proxies, load balancers and API gateways running affected NGINX Open Source or NGINX Plus with HTTP/3 turned on.
NGINX Plus R34 to R36 users, for whom F5's listing names no fixed release in those branches.
Sites that do not enable HTTP/3 are outside the affected configuration according to F5.
detect: Inventory NGINX and NGINX Plus versions and check each configuration for HTTP/3 (QUIC) listeners, including UDP 443 exposed to the internet.
Review the NGINX error log for worker processes exiting on a signal and restarting, especially in bursts tied to HTTP/3 clients.
Watch for core dumps from NGINX workers and for unexpected child processes or outbound connections started by the worker account.
F5, nginx.org and KrCERT/CC publish no indicators or detection rules for this flaw.

steps: Find every NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus instance that serves HTTP/3, starting with internet-facing ones.
Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.31.9 or 1.30.7 and NGINX Plus to 37.3.0.1 or 37.0.8.1, as listed in F5 article K000163927.
Move NGINX Plus R34 to R36 to a fixed 37.x release, since no fix is listed for those branches.
Apply the same update for the HTTP/2 flaws CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 fixed in the same releases, which have a public proof of concept.
Keep ASLR enabled on NGINX hosts; F5 says code execution needs it to be off or bypassed.
fixed_versions: NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fixed version listed
verify: Confirm the version NGINX reports on each host is at or above the fixed release and that the running workers were restarted on the new binary.
Check that container images and packaged distributions bundling NGINX were rebuilt with the fixed version.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve the NGINX error and access logs, core dumps and a disk image before changes.
Look for files, scheduled tasks or processes created by the NGINX worker account and remove them, or rebuild from a known-good image.
Rotate TLS private keys and any upstream credentials or tokens stored in the NGINX configuration.
Report to your national CERT and to F5 support.

CVE-2026-121810.caveats: F5's own article K000163927 could not be loaded (script-only page); this rests on F5's CVE record, nginx.org's advisory list and KrCERT/CC. nginx.org rates it medium while the CVE record gives CVSS 8.1 (v3.1) and 9.2 (v4.0). No vendor or government workaround was found for this HTTP/3 flaw; the HTTP/2 workaround in CERT-FR's alert is for other CVEs. The CyberView event on file is about the HTTP/2 flaws.

CVE-2026-123007.exploitation_status: Public proof of concept: Rapid7 published one at disclosure on 18 Nov 2026 and CERT-FR (CERTFR-2026-ALE-017) knows of it. No exploitation in the wild reported; CISA's CVE record rated exploitation none on 18 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-123007.how_exploited: An integer underflow (CWE-191) leading to an out-of-bounds heap write in the NGINX HTTP/2 module's flow-control accounting. A remote, unauthenticated client manipulates how NGINX tracks how much response data the client allows it to send, by cancelling queued data and adjusting window counters, until a counter wraps past its valid range; a later response copy then uses an invalid length. This corrupts memory in the worker process and usually crashes it, and can lead to code execution as the worker's account where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed (F5).
preconditions: HTTP/2 is enabled for client connections; Rapid7's tested setup used HTTP/2 over TLS.
NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6 or 1.31.0 to 1.31.8, or NGINX Plus 37.0.x before 37.0.8.1, 37.1.x to 37.2.x before 37.3.0.1, or R33 and later Rx releases.
No authentication or user interaction is needed, but the attack is complex: Rapid7 needed roughly 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic over one connection.
Rapid7's code-execution method relied on a specific x86-64 glibc memory-copy routine chosen on CPUs with AVX-512; other methods may exist but none are known.
Under NGINX's default one-hour connection lifetime, Rapid7 estimates links slower than about 300 Mbit/s would time out first; proxied HTTP/2 connections probably do not pass the needed frames intact.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: find internet-facing NGINX servers that negotiate HTTP/2.

Initial access: hold one long HTTP/2 connection and send a very large volume of traffic that drives the flow-control counter out of range (about two and a half minutes on a fast link in Rapid7's test).

Execution: the resulting heap corruption in the worker process is turned into code execution as the NGINX worker account; on systems where this fails the worker crashes and restarts, a denial of service.
Follow-on: Rapid7 and CERT-FR describe no campaigns; a foothold on a reverse proxy would typically expose TLS keys, proxied traffic and backend credentials.
who_is_exposed: Any NGINX Open Source or NGINX Plus server in an affected version that serves HTTP/2 directly to clients, most often public HTTPS web servers, reverse proxies and load balancers.
NGINX Plus R33 to R36: listed as affected with no fix in Rapid7's table; check F5's bulletin K000163926 for current guidance.
Servers behind a proxy that terminates HTTP/2 itself are probably less exposed, per Rapid7.
Products and container images that embed affected NGINX builds; check each vendor's bulletin.
detect: Version check: list every NGINX binary and container image and compare the version against 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 (Open Source) or 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (Plus).
Configuration check: find server blocks with HTTP/2 enabled on their listen lines or through the http2 directive.
NGINX error log and system log: repeated worker processes exiting on a signal (segmentation fault) and being restarted.
Network and flow data: single client HTTP/2 connections lasting a long time and moving tens of gigabytes, far beyond normal use.
Host: the NGINX worker account starting shells or other child processes, or writing files outside its cache and log folders.
Rapid7 and CERT-FR published no indicators of compromise; watch Rapid7's write-up and F5's bulletin for detection content.

steps: Inventory NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus servers and images, starting with internet-facing ones that serve HTTP/2.
Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 or later, and NGINX Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1 or later, as listed in F5 bulletin K000163926; restart so new workers run the fixed binary.
Install the same update (1.30.7 or 1.31.9) to also close CVE-2026-123633 and the other flaws F5 fixed on 18 Nov 2026.
Where you cannot upgrade at once, disable HTTP/2 on exposed servers until patched (CERT-FR).
NGINX Plus R33 to R36: move to a fixed 37.x release; Rapid7 lists no fix for those releases.
Rebuild container images and update third-party appliances that bundle NGINX once their vendors ship fixes.
fixed_versions: NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 (nginx.org advisory, F5 K000163926)
NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (Rapid7 table and CVE record from F5)
workarounds: Disable HTTP/2 until the update is applied (CERT-FR): on 1.25.1 and later remove the http2 option from the listen line, or set the http2 directive off; test the configuration and reload.
verify: Confirm the running binary reports a fixed version, and that the running master and worker processes were restarted after the upgrade.
If you used the workaround, confirm HTTP/2 is no longer offered in TLS negotiation (ALPN) on each listener, as CERT-FR suggests.
Rescan with a vulnerability scanner check for CVE-2026-123007.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve NGINX error and access logs, system logs, a memory image if possible and a disk image.
Look for processes started by the NGINX worker account and for new files or changed configuration.
Replace the TLS private keys and certificates on the server and rotate backend credentials and secrets it held.
Rebuild from a clean image with a fixed NGINX version.
Report to your national CERT (CERT-FR in France, CISA in the US).

CVE-2026-123007.caveats: F5's own bulletin pages did not render for automated reading; F5's text was read through its CVE record and the nginx.org advisory list. NGINX Plus version numbers differ between sources (CERT-FR prints 3.7.x where Rapid7 and F5 give 37.x); check K000163926. Rapid7's attack needed fast links and specific CPUs, but others may find easier methods.

CVE-2026-123039.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per Check Point: chained after PHP2Shell on unpatched gateways from 30 Oct to 4 Nov 2026, about two dozen systems compromised. In CISA KEV since 13 Nov 2026 (federal due date 16 Nov).
CVE-2026-123039.how_exploited: Incorrect permission assignment (local privilege escalation) in the Gaia Dynamic CLI service. The component runs as root and accepts commands over a local control socket that any process on the device can write to, without checking the sender. An attacker who already runs code as a low-privileged account, in the observed attacks the Mobile Access portal's web service account after PHP2Shell exploitation, can have commands executed as root and so take full control of the gateway.
preconditions: The attacker already has code execution as some local account on the appliance; this flaw alone is not a remote entry point.
In the observed attacks, that foothold came from PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) on an internet-facing Mobile Access Portal.
Gaia R82.20, R82.10, R82 or R81.20 below the fixing Jumbo Hotfix take, or end-of-support R81.10 and R81, which get no fix.
The Dynamic CLI service is running (it is by default; stopping it is the vendor's temporary mitigation).
attack_path: Initial access: unauthenticated PHP2Shell exploitation of the Mobile Access Portal gave code execution as the portal's service account (Check Point Research).
Privilege escalation: the attacker used the Dynamic CLI flaw to run commands as root on the gateway.

Persistence: web shells planted among the portal's login page templates, then a backdoor Check Point Research names TSGA that relaunches at boot and injects a proxy component into appliance processes to hide its traffic.
Discovery and lateral movement: an internal network scanner mapped assets, then the attacker reached a VMware ESXi host over SSH with a service account.

Impact: in the first wave against Israeli organisations, a wiper deleted files on ESXi and left a politically themed note with no ransom demand; the second wave from 2 Nov hit several countries without destruction.
who_is_exposed: Check Point Security Gateways, Force firewalls, Management and Log Servers, Multi-Domain servers and Maestro Orchestrator on the affected Gaia releases.
Highest risk: gateways with the Mobile Access Portal reachable from the internet, because PHP2Shell gives the foothold this flaw needs.
Spark firewalls and Smart-1 Cloud are reported as not affected by this flaw.
detect: Review the Dynamic CLI log for unexpected requests, especially ones that create users or download files (reported guidance relaying Check Point).
Look for unexpected files among the Mobile Access portal templates, PHP session files carrying the upload-progress marker Check Point describes, and a spike in web server worker crashes.

Look for a process posing as a Check Point component with a name resembling a configuration daemon, unfamiliar background processes, new boot-time persistence entries, and tools dropped in temporary folders.
Check firewall traffic logs for unexplained gaps, especially after a logging daemon crash, and SSH logins from the gateway to ESXi or other servers.
Match file hashes and the two scanning addresses against the indicator list in the Check Point Research PHP2Shell report; Check Point warns a clean result does not rule out compromise.

steps: Install the November Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator on every Security Gateway and Management Server, starting with gateways whose Mobile Access Portal faces the internet; it also fixes the PHP2Shell flaws used for entry.
If the hotfix cannot be installed at once, use Check Point's temporary mitigation of stopping the Dynamic CLI service and keeping it from restarting (some extra command-line functions stop working).
Plan an upgrade for appliances on end-of-support R81.10 or R81, which receive no fix.
Because patching does not remove backdoors already planted, hunt each exposed gateway for the signs in the detect list before returning it to trust.
US federal agencies: apply BOD 26-04 and CISA's forensics triage requirements for systems patched after exploitation began.
fixed_versions: R82.20 Jumbo Hotfix Take 14 and later
R82.10 Jumbo Hotfix Take 52 and later
R82 Jumbo Hotfix Take 132 and later
R81.20 Jumbo Hotfix Take 174 and later
R81.10 and R81: no fix (end of support)
workarounds: Stop the Dynamic CLI service and prevent it from restarting until the hotfix is installed; some extended command-line functions will not work meanwhile.
verify: Confirm in the Gaia portal or command line that the installed Jumbo Hotfix take is equal to or higher than the fixed take for the release.
Confirm every gateway and management server in the estate was updated, including cluster members and Maestro components.
If the workaround was used, confirm the Dynamic CLI service stays stopped after a reboot.
if_compromised: Contact Check Point Support, which asks affected customers to get help assessing exposure and installing the hotfix.
Isolate the gateway and preserve its logs, the Dynamic CLI log and a disk image before cleaning anything.
Rotate credentials stored on or used by the gateway, including administrator, VPN and service accounts, and accounts used to reach ESXi or other servers.
Check reachable ESXi hosts and internal servers for SSH logins from the gateway and for the scanner and wiper tools Check Point Research names.
Rebuild the appliance from a clean image at a fixed release rather than trusting an in-place cleanup, and report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-123039.caveats: Check Point's knowledge base article sk1000362 did not load, so the fixed takes and the temporary mitigation come from Check Point's blog advisory and press reports relaying sk1000362; confirm them there before patching. Check Point Research links the tools to a family ESET tied to UNC5221 but calls attribution uncertain.
