CVE-2026-123158.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild according to CISA, which added it to KEV on 9 November 2026 with forensic triage required. Disclosed 5 November 2026 by Özgün Kültekin ("SSHole"); public proof-of-concept code is reported. No actor named.
CVE-2026-123158.how_exploited: Unexpected return value (CWE-394) in sshd's password check when built without PAM on musl libc. sshd hashes the offered password and compares it with the stored password field. musl's hashing function signals failure with the same marker that disabled, key-only accounts store as their password field, so an overly long password makes the hash fail and the failure marker matches. A remote attacker can thus log in with a password to an account that should accept no password, reliably and in one connection, and may reach root where root login with a password is allowed or the account can escalate.
preconditions: OpenSSH before 10.6p2 built without PAM (or with UsePAM off) on a musl libc system, such as Alpine Linux, OpenWrt or musl-based Buildroot and Yocto builds.
Password authentication enabled in sshd, which is the default.
An account whose password field is the no-password marker (Alpine base images' root since about 3.16, key-only users, some cloud images' alpine user).
At least one local account with a real SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt password hash on the same machine.
sshd reachable by the attacker; no credentials or user interaction needed.
attack_path: Initial access: a password login to a no-password account over SSH succeeds because of the failed-hash comparison.
Privilege escalation: direct root where root password logins are permitted, or through passwordless doas, which Alpine notes for the alpine user in tiny-cloud images.
Persistence (per Alpine's compromise checks): new local users, added authorized keys and changed files.
Public reporting does not describe specific campaigns after access.
who_is_exposed: Alpine Linux hosts, VMs and containers running openssh-server without PAM and with password logins on.
Alpine tiny-cloud images 3.18.11 to 3.24.3 once any account gains a real password hash (safe on first boot, per Alpine).
Routers, appliances and embedded devices using musl with OpenSSH (OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto).
Container images built or pinned before 5 November 2026, including cached CI layers. glibc-based distributions are not affected.
detect: Authentication logs: successful password logins for accounts that have no password, such as root, alpine or key-only users (Alpine's main indicator).
A successful password login following failed attempts in the same session, as StepSecurity suggests alerting on.
Package check: compare the installed openssh package revision with Alpine's fixed revisions; do not trust the SSH version banner, since backported fixes keep the old version string.
Configuration check: effective sshd settings for password authentication and PAM on every musl host and image.
Host review on exposed machines: doas use, recently created users, recently changed files and authorized keys.

steps: Upgrade OpenSSH to 10.6p2, or to your distribution's fixed package (Alpine lists one per branch).
Restart sshd after the upgrade; Alpine warns that upgrading the package does not restart the running daemon.
Rebuild container images and appliance firmware from current repositories, and remove sshd where it is not needed.
Where keys are in use, turn password authentication off permanently.
Check exposed machines for signs of compromise (US federal agencies must do forensic triage under BOD 26-04).
workarounds: Disable password authentication in the sshd configuration and restart sshd; first confirm key login works and keep a session open (Alpine, NCSC New Zealand).
Disable SSH entirely where it is not needed (NCSC New Zealand).
Use the PAM-enabled sshd package with PAM switched on, which Alpine lists as not affected.
verify: Confirm the installed openssh package revision with the package manager matches or exceeds the fixed revision for your branch.
Confirm sshd was restarted after the upgrade (the running process start time is later than the package install).
If using the workaround, confirm the effective sshd configuration reports password authentication off.
if_compromised: If a login to a no-password account cannot be ruled out, treat the machine as compromised, as Alpine advises.
Isolate it and preserve authentication logs and a disk image.
Remove unknown users and authorized keys, rotate any secrets and keys stored on the host, and rebuild from a patched image.
Report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-123158.caveats: CISA lists it as exploited but gives no details; Alpine's advisory, the OpenSSH notes, NCSC New Zealand and StepSecurity (6 November) do not report exploitation themselves. The OpenSSH release notes do not print the CVE number; CISA's record links it. Fixed revisions for musl distributions other than Alpine were not checked.

CVE-2026-123218.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per CISA, which added it to KEV on 9 Nov 2026 (federal deadline 12 Nov). IBM's bulletin of 7 Nov reports no exploitation. No actor, scale or public exploit code reported.
CVE-2026-123218.how_exploited: Incorrect authorisation (CWE-863) in IBM Aspera Faspex 5, the managed file-transfer server. IBM says a user can send a specially crafted message that bypasses the product's authorisation checks and gives full administrative privileges in Faspex. IBM has not described the message, the affected function or what attackers did with admin access; the stated impact is administrative control of Faspex itself, not code execution on the server.
preconditions: The Faspex 5 web service is reachable by the attacker over the network.

IBM's description says an authenticated user, but its CVSS vector lists no privileges required; treat a login requirement as an unreliable barrier, especially if self-registration or external accounts exist.
Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 without Fix Pack 1 (5.0.19 PL1).
attack_path: Initial access: an attacker with access to the Faspex service (per IBM, an authenticated user) sends a crafted message that the authorisation check fails to stop.
Privilege escalation: the attacker gains full Faspex administrator rights.
Likely next steps are not published; an administrator can typically manage users, packages and settings, so files exchanged through Faspex should be treated as exposed.
Neither IBM nor CISA has published attack timelines, indicators or attribution.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 to 5.0.19 on Linux (containerised deployment), especially instances published to the internet for partners and customers.
Instances with many external or self-registered user accounts, since IBM's description requires only an authorised user.
detect: Check the faspex-core container image on every instance: it must be version 5.0.19, build 1ce4b13, Fix Pack 1; plain 5.0.19 is still vulnerable.
Review Faspex administrator accounts and role changes for users promoted to admin without a change record.
Review Faspex audit and web access logs for unusual account, package or settings changes and for downloads by unexpected users since early November 2026.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules have been published for this flaw.

steps: Upgrade to Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1 (Linux) using IBM's documented procedure for patching container images.
Confirm the running faspex-core image is the fixed build on every instance.
Until patched, limit who can reach the Faspex service and review accounts, removing ones that are not needed (interim exposure reduction, not an IBM workaround).
Because CISA reports exploitation, check each instance for misuse of admin rights before and after patching (CISA BOD 26-04 asks federal agencies for forensic triage).
fixed_versions: IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1 (Fix Pack 1) on Linux: faspex-core image 5.0.19, build 1ce4b13
verify: The faspex-core container image reports version 5.0.19, build 1ce4b13, Fix Pack 1, as IBM's bulletin specifies.
if_compromised: Preserve Faspex logs and container state before changes, then restrict access to the service.
Remove unauthorised administrators and accounts, and reset passwords and API credentials for remaining users.
Identify packages and files that could have been read or changed and notify affected partners where needed.
Report to IBM support and your national CERT; CISA asks federal agencies to report findings under BOD 26-04.

CVE-2026-123218.caveats: IBM's bulletin gives few technical details and lists no workaround; CISA's catalog is the only source for exploitation and gives no detail. IBM's text (authenticated user) and CVSS vector (no privileges) disagree. Attack-path stages after privilege escalation are not published and are described only in general terms. Only Faspex 5.0.0 to 5.0.19 are listed; Faspex 4 is not mentioned.

CVE-2026-123633.exploitation_status: No exploitation or public exploit code reported as of 18 Nov 2026: CERT-FR (CERTFR-2026-ALE-017) names a public proof of concept only for CVE-2026-123007, and CISA's CVE record rated exploitation none.
CVE-2026-123633.how_exploited: A use-after-free (CWE-416) in the NGINX HTTP/2 module. When NGINX accepts HTTP/2 from clients and proxies their requests to a backend, an unauthenticated attacker sends a specially crafted request while the worker process is running low on worker_connections; the worker then uses memory it has already freed. This can crash the worker (denial of service), and F5 says attackers can execute code as the worker's account where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed. F5 states it is a data plane issue with no control plane exposure.
preconditions: HTTP/2 is enabled for client connections and NGINX proxies those requests to a backend server.
The worker process is running low on worker_connections, which an attacker may try to bring about with many connections.
NGINX Open Source 1.19.7 to 1.30.6 or 1.31.0 to 1.31.8, or affected NGINX Plus 37.x and R33 and later Rx releases.
No authentication or user interaction; F5 rates attack complexity high (CVSS 3.1 score 8.1, CVSS 4.0 score 9.2).
Code execution additionally needs ASLR disabled or an ASLR bypass, per F5.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: find NGINX reverse proxies that accept HTTP/2 from clients.
Initial access: push the worker toward its connection limit and send a crafted HTTP/2 request that triggers the use-after-free.
Execution: crash and restart of the worker, or, with ASLR absent or bypassed, code running as the NGINX worker account.
Follow-on: no campaigns described in the sources read; a foothold on a reverse proxy would typically expose TLS keys, proxied traffic and backend credentials.
who_is_exposed: NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus deployments that terminate HTTP/2 from clients and proxy to backends: reverse proxies, API gateways and load balancers, often internet-facing.
Busy servers near their worker_connections limit, and servers where an attacker can exhaust connections.
Systems with ASLR disabled are at higher risk of code execution rather than only crashes.
Products and container images that embed affected NGINX builds; check each vendor's bulletin.
detect: Version check: compare every NGINX binary and image against the fixed Open Source releases 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and the fixed NGINX Plus releases.
Configuration check: list server blocks with HTTP/2 enabled that also proxy to backends.
NGINX error log: warnings that worker_connections are not enough, followed by workers exiting on a signal (segmentation fault).
Network: bursts of many simultaneous HTTP/2 connections from a few sources aimed at reaching the connection limit.
Host: the NGINX worker account starting shells or other child processes, or writing unexpected files.
No indicators of compromise were published by F5 or CERT-FR.

steps: Inventory NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus servers and images, starting with internet-facing reverse proxies that serve HTTP/2.
Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 or later and NGINX Plus to the fixed release in F5 bulletin K000163928; restart so new workers run the fixed binary.
This is the same update that fixes CVE-2026-123007, which has a public proof of concept, so treat the combined update as immediate.
Where you cannot upgrade at once, disable HTTP/2 on exposed servers until patched (CERT-FR).
Keep ASLR enabled on NGINX hosts, which F5 says is needed to block code execution.
Rebuild container images and update appliances that bundle NGINX once their vendors ship fixes.

NGINX Plus: fixed releases listed in F5 K000163928; CERT-FR and Rapid7 give 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 for this update
workarounds: Disable HTTP/2 until the update is applied (CERT-FR): on 1.25.1 and later remove the http2 option from the listen line, or set the http2 directive off; test the configuration and reload.
verify: Confirm the running binary reports a fixed version and that NGINX was restarted after the upgrade.
If you used the workaround, confirm HTTP/2 is no longer offered in TLS negotiation (ALPN) on each listener.
Rescan with a vulnerability scanner check for CVE-2026-123633.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve NGINX logs, system logs and a disk image.
Look for processes started by the NGINX worker account and for new files or changed configuration.
Replace TLS private keys and certificates and rotate backend credentials the proxy held.
Rebuild from a clean image with a fixed NGINX version.
Report to your national CERT (CERT-FR in France, CISA in the US).

CVE-2026-123633.caveats: Only F5's short CVE description is public; no technical write-up was found, and F5's bulletin pages did not render for automated reading. The NGINX Plus ranges in the CVE record (37.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1 as upper bounds) differ from those given for the same update by CERT-FR and Rapid7; confirm the fixed Plus release in K000163928.

CVE-2026-123634.exploitation_status: No exploitation or public exploit code reported as of 18 Nov 2026; CISA's CVE record rated exploitation none, and CERT-FR's alert names a proof of concept only for CVE-2026-123007.
CVE-2026-123634.how_exploited: A use-after-free (CWE-416) in the NGINX resolver, not in HTTP/2. When NGINX proxies to a server name built from variables, so it resolves the name at run time, and a Server Side Includes (SSI) or mirror directive sends a subrequest to a location that resolves the same name, a specially crafted HTTP request can make the worker use freed memory during response processing. This can crash the worker or corrupt its memory, and F5 says code execution is possible where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed.
preconditions: NGINX is configured as a proxy and the proxied server name contains variables, so names are resolved at run time with the resolver.
An SSI or mirror directive sends a subrequest to a location that resolves the same server name.
NGINX Open Source 0.6.18 to 1.30.6 or 1.31.0 to 1.31.8, or NGINX Plus before 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, including R33 and later Rx releases.
No authentication or user interaction; F5 rates attack complexity high (CVSS 3.1 score 8.1).
Code execution additionally needs ASLR disabled or an ASLR bypass, per F5.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: an attacker needs to find a site whose NGINX configuration matches the narrow conditions, which is hard to see from outside.
Initial access: a crafted HTTP request to the affected location triggers the use-after-free during name resolution handling.
Execution: worker crash and restart, or, with ASLR absent or bypassed, code running as the NGINX worker account.
Follow-on: no campaigns described in the sources read.
who_is_exposed: NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus reverse proxies that use variables in proxied server names together with SSI or mirror subrequests to the same name.
Configurations without that combination are not affected by this flaw, according to F5's description.
Products and container images that embed affected NGINX builds; check each vendor's bulletin.
detect: Version check: compare every NGINX binary and image against 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 (Open Source) and the fixed NGINX Plus releases.
Configuration check: search for proxy targets that use variables together with a resolver, and for SSI or mirror directives that reach the same names.
NGINX error log: workers exiting on a signal (segmentation fault), especially around requests to locations using SSI or mirroring.
Host: the NGINX worker account starting shells or other child processes, or writing unexpected files.
No indicators of compromise were published by F5 or CERT-FR.

steps: Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 or later and NGINX Plus to the fixed release in F5 bulletin K000163925; this is the same update that fixes the urgent HTTP/2 flaws CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, so apply it with them.
Before the upgrade, review configurations for the affected combination of variable proxy targets and SSI or mirror subrequests, and patch those servers first.
Keep ASLR enabled on NGINX hosts, which F5 says is needed to block code execution.
Rebuild container images and update appliances that bundle NGINX once their vendors ship fixes.

Rescan with a vulnerability scanner check for CVE-2026-123634.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve NGINX logs, system logs and a disk image.
Look for processes started by the NGINX worker account and for new files or changed configuration.
Replace TLS private keys and rotate backend credentials the proxy held.
Rebuild from a clean image with a fixed NGINX version and report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-123634.caveats: The map's event groups this CVE with the HTTP/2 flaws, but F5 and nginx.org describe it as a resolver use-after-free that needs a specific proxy, SSI or mirror setup; nginx.org rates it medium. F5's bulletin pages did not render for automated reading, so no vendor workaround was seen, and no technical write-up was found.

CVE-2026-123890.exploitation_status: Exploited as a zero-day since early September 2026 by ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor (formerly UNC5221), per Google and Mandiant. Fixed 19 Nov 2026 (VMSA-2026-0009); CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-123890.how_exploited: Authentication bypass (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service that vCenter Server uses for single sign-on, rated 9.8 by Broadcom. Broadcom says an attacker with network access to vCenter can bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access; Google describes a weakness in the directory service's password-based (SRP) login exchange, including predictable session identifiers, that lets an attacker obtain a session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as the vsphere.local administrator, which gives full control of vCenter and, through it, of the ESXi hosts and virtual machines it manages.
preconditions: Network access to the vCenter Server appliance and its directory service; no credentials and no user interaction (Broadcom, CVSS 9.8).
vCenter 7.0, or 8.0 before 8.0 U3m; Cloud Foundation or vSphere Foundation 9.0 before 9.0.2.0200, 9.1 before 9.1.1.0200, 5.x before 5.2.5; affected Telco Cloud releases.
In the campaign Google describes, the attacker was already inside the network after compromising a remote support appliance and an internal Linux appliance.
attack_path: Initial access: ARMORY CASTLE gained a foothold on a remote support appliance and an internal Linux appliance, then reached vCenter over the internal network (Google).
Execution: a custom Go tool Google calls BONESAW abused the directory service flaw to obtain a vsphere.local administrator session.

Identity persistence: new single sign-on administrator and backdoor machine accounts, a copy of the directory database, the stolen token-signing key, and forged administrator SAML assertions (also via a tool called SAWSNAKE).
Appliance access: SSH enabled through the appliance management (VAMI) interface, a local administrator created, the vCenter master key and database credentials extracted, then SSH disabled again.
Lateral movement: the vCenter service account and root SSH on ESXi hosts were used to add SSH keys, enumerate datastores and copy Windows domain secrets from virtual disks.
Long-term access: a systemd service on an internal Linux appliance ran the LAZYBONES backdoor using Slack for command and control; Google also names SLIMSAVAGE, CAGEMATCH and BEARBONES.
who_is_exposed: Every organisation running vCenter Server 7.0 or 8.0 below 8.0 U3m, on-premises or in a self-managed cloud.
VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 5.x, 9.0 and 9.1 deployments below the fixed builds, and Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure customers.

vCenter 7.0 users without an extended support contract: Broadcom publishes no public fix for 7.0 and tells customers with extended support to contact Broadcom Support; Google says the exploitation tool works against 7.x and 8.x appliances.

Any vCenter reachable from the internet or from broad internal networks is at higher risk; internal-only placement reduces but does not remove exposure, since the observed attacker moved in from other compromised appliances.
detect: Check each vCenter build against Broadcom VMSA-2026-0009; Rapid7 said an unauthenticated scanner check was due in its 20 Nov 2026 content release.
Review single sign-on for administrator accounts, machine accounts and identity sources nobody created, and Global Administrator rights on the root folder; look back to September 2026.

Forward appliance logs to remote syslog and look for VAMI API requests that turn SSH on, base64-encoded shell commands, downloads into temporary folders, and temporary copies of the directory database or signing keys (Google).
On ESXi hosts, check root's authorized SSH keys, SSH logins by root or the vCenter service account, and access to virtual disks of domain controllers.
Use the YARA rules (G_Hunting_ names for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, SLIMSAVAGE, CAGEMATCH, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES), Google SecOps rules and network indicators in Google's ARMORY CASTLE report.
On internal Linux appliances, look for unfamiliar systemd services and outbound connections to Slack from servers that should not use it.

steps: Upgrade vCenter to the fixed build for its line (8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200 or 9.1.1.0200; Cloud Foundation 5.2.5; Telco per KB463116). Rapid7 notes Quick Patch cannot apply it and management interfaces pause during the update while workloads keep running.
If a move to VCF 9.1.1 is planned, read Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0009 FAQ first: Rapid7 reports that 8.0 U3m and 9.0.2.0200 block some later upgrade paths.
Systems already fixed for CVE-2026-59309 still need this update; Broadcom says the two flaws are distinct.
For vCenter 7.0, contact Broadcom Support if you hold extended support; otherwise CISA's required action is to stop using the product when mitigations are unavailable, so plan migration.
Until patched, restrict network access to vCenter to dedicated administration networks and hosts.
Federal agencies must complete CISA's forensic triage under BOD 26-04; everyone should hunt for the activity above even after patching, because exploitation began in September.
fixed_versions: vCenter 7.0: contact Broadcom Support (extended support contracts)
Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure: KB463116
workarounds: None: Broadcom's advisory states there is no workaround.
verify: Confirm the vCenter version and build in the vSphere Client or appliance management interface match a fixed build listed in VMSA-2026-0009.
Rerun an authenticated or unauthenticated vulnerability scan for CVE-2026-123890 against every vCenter instance, including lab and disaster-recovery copies.
Confirm SSH on the appliance is disabled unless needed, and that remote syslog forwarding is working.
if_compromised: Isolate the vCenter appliance and affected ESXi hosts from untrusted networks while keeping them running for evidence; take snapshots or forensic copies first.
Preserve appliance logs, the directory database and ESXi logs before rebuilding.

Assume the single sign-on signing key and all vCenter, ESXi and stored service credentials are stolen: rebuild vCenter or replace the STS signing certificate, reset the vsphere.local administrator and all local and service passwords, and remove unknown accounts, machine accounts and SSH keys.
Treat Windows domains whose controllers ran as virtual machines on affected hosts as exposed: reset privileged and krbtgt credentials following Active Directory recovery guidance.
Hunt internal Linux and remote support appliances for the backdoors Google names, and report the incident to CISA or your national CERT.

CVE-2026-123890.caveats: Broadcom's advisory gives no detection or response guidance; the attack details come from Google and Mandiant's report on one actor and may not cover other attackers. Google's dating of exploitation to early September 2026 rests partly on build timestamps, which can be altered. Google names no victims. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix. The CISA catalog entry was read through a partly summarised copy of the page.

CVE-2026-123903.exploitation_status: No in-the-wild exploitation reported as of 25 Nov 2026. Rapid7 says a public proof-of-concept exists and it validated it; SOCRadar had found none. The related vmdir flaw CVE-2026-123890 was exploited as a zero-day.
CVE-2026-123903.how_exploited: An authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service (vmdir), the directory behind vCenter Single Sign-On. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach vCenter over the network sends crafted directory requests (Rapid7 says the flaw is reachable over LDAP) and gets past authentication. That gives unauthorized access to the vCenter identity store. From there an attacker can control vCenter and, through it, every ESX host and virtual machine it manages. Broadcom has not published the root cause.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the vCenter Server's directory service over the network; no credentials or user interaction are needed (CVSS 9.8, AV:N/PR:N/UI:N).
vCenter is on a version older than the fixed builds: 9.1.x before 9.1.2, 9.0.x before 9.0.2.0300, 8.0 before 8.0 U3m, VCF 5.x before 5.2.5, and every 7.0 build.
Applying the earlier emergency fix for CVE-2026-123890 on 9.x (9.1.1.0200 or 9.0.2.0200) does not fix this flaw. On 8.0, U3m fixes both.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers find vCenter servers whose directory service is reachable from their network position, either from the internet or after getting into the internal network.
Initial access: crafted directory requests bypass authentication and give access to the vCenter SSO identity store.

Persistence: not described for this CVE. With the related CVE-2026-123890, Armory Castle created SSO domain accounts, briefly enabled appliance SSH and added root SSH keys on ESX hosts (SOCRadar, ThaiCERT).
Next steps: in that related campaign, the attackers stole data. Control of vCenter can also be used to reach, copy or disrupt every managed host and virtual machine.
who_is_exposed: On-premises vCenter Server 9.1.x, 9.0.x, 8.0 and 7.0, including vCenter in VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x and 9.x and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.x.
vCenter in VMware Telco Cloud Platform 3.0, 4.x and 5.x, and in Telco Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 (see Broadcom KB463501).
vCenter 7.0 customers have no public fix. Only customers with an extended support contract can get one from Broadcom support.
The highest risk is vCenter that can be reached from outside dedicated management networks. ESX hosts are not affected directly but are controlled by an affected vCenter.
detect: Version check: compare each vCenter build with the fixed versions in VMSA-2026-0011. Flag 9.x systems that only got last week's CVE-2026-123890 patch.
Network exposure: find which networks can reach vCenter's directory service ports (LDAP and the vmdir RPC service on TCP 2012). Treat any reach from user, guest or internet networks as exposure.

Identity audit: look in the vsphere.local SSO domain for administrator, solution or machine accounts nobody recognises, unexplained group changes and identity source changes. An authentication bypass may leave no failed logon records.
Appliance logs: in the vCenter appliance management logs, look for SSH being enabled and then disabled outside change windows, as seen with the related CVE-2026-123890 campaign (SOCRadar).
ESX hosts: look for new root SSH authorized keys and for root or vpxuser logins at unusual times or from unusual sources.

Scanning: Rapid7 offers an unauthenticated vulnerability check (content release of 25 Nov 2026). No public indicators of compromise are specific to this CVE. Clean results do not prove a system was not compromised, especially without EDR telemetry.

steps: List every vCenter instance and its build, including vCenters inside VCF, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud stacks.
Update vCenter to the fixed version for its release line now, outside normal patch cycles (Rapid7). Broadcom says these updates are not eligible for Quick Patch, so use the standard update mechanism.
Update 9.x systems that only got the CVE-2026-123890 emergency build again; the earlier build does not fix this flaw.
vCenter 7.0: if you have an extended support contract, ask Broadcom support for a fix. Otherwise, plan an upgrade to a supported release and isolate the system until then.
Until patched, allow access to vCenter management and directory services only from dedicated administrative hosts (ThaiCERT and SOCRadar recommend this; Broadcom lists it as no workaround).
Run the identity and host checks under detect, because exploitation could have happened before the patch.
fixed_versions: VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.1.x.x: 9.1.2
VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.0.x.x: 9.0.2.0300
vCenter 7.0: contact Broadcom Support if you have an extended support contract
Telco Cloud Platform vCenter 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2 and Telco Cloud Infrastructure vCenter 3.0: see KB463501
workarounds: None. Broadcom lists no workaround for this CVE. Restricting network access to the management interfaces reduces exposure but does not fix the flaw.
verify: Check the build number on the vCenter appliance summary or management page and compare it with the fixed version for your release line.
Re-run an authenticated or unauthenticated vulnerability scan and confirm this CVE is no longer reported.
Confirm with a scan from a non-management network that the directory service ports are not reachable.
if_compromised: Isolate the vCenter appliance from untrusted networks, but keep it running long enough to preserve logs and a snapshot for investigation.
Preserve vCenter appliance logs, SSO and directory audit data, and ESX host logs before you make changes.

Remove unknown SSO accounts and ESX SSH keys. Then rotate the vCenter STS signing certificate, the master key and all SSO and administrator credentials, following Broadcom's guidance for your version.
Rotate credentials stored in or used by vCenter, such as service accounts, backup and integration accounts. Review every managed host and virtual machine for changes.
If you cannot be sure the appliance is clean, rebuild it from known-good media at a fixed version. Report the incident to your national CERT, and to Broadcom support if you have a contract.

CVE-2026-123903.caveats: Broadcom has published no root cause. Sources disagree on a public proof-of-concept (Rapid7: exists and validated; SOCRadar: none found). No in-the-wild use is reported, but the related vmdir bypass CVE-2026-123890 was exploited as a zero-day; post-access stages here come from that campaign, not from observed use of this CVE. HKCERT lists the CVE without per-CVE detail.

CVE-2026-123910.exploitation_status: No in-the-wild exploitation or public exploit code reported as of 25 Nov 2026 (Broadcom VMSA-2026-0011; SOCRadar). The advisory's 'exploit code' flag on CyberView refers to the vCenter flaw CVE-2026-123903.
CVE-2026-123910.how_exploited: A heap out-of-bounds write in the ESX I/O filter service, a host service that listens on the management network (TCP 9080, per Broadcom KB463535). An unauthenticated attacker who can reach that service over the network sends crafted traffic that corrupts the service's memory. Broadcom says this may let the attacker run code on the ESX host. Code on the hypervisor host puts every virtual machine on it at risk. Broadcom has not published further technical detail.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the ESX host's I/O filter service over the network. No credentials or user interaction are needed (CVSS 9.8, AV:N/PR:N/UI:N).
ESX is on a version older than the fixed builds: 9.1.x before ESXi-9.1.2.0-25946735, 9.0.x before ESXi-9.0.2.0200-25953133, 8.0 before ESXi80U3m-25926933, VCF 5.x before 5.2.5, and every 7.0 build.
On ESX 8.0, the interim firewall workaround in KB463535 limits who can reach the service. With it in place, the attacker would need to come from an allowed address, normally vCenter.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: an attacker who already has a foothold on a network that can reach ESX management interfaces, or finds ESX exposed more widely, identifies hosts running the I/O filter service.
Initial access and execution: crafted network traffic to the service triggers the memory corruption and runs code on the ESX host. Broadcom gives no detail on the privilege level.

Next steps: no attacks using this flaw are described. Typical hypervisor follow-on is theft of VM disks, SSH-key persistence, or encrypting or powering off VMs; this is general, not observed for this CVE.
who_is_exposed: VMware ESX 9.1.x, 9.0.x, 8.0 and 7.0, including ESX in VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x and 9.x and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.x.
ESX in VMware Telco Cloud Platform 5.0.x and 5.1.x (see Broadcom KB463501).
ESX 7.0 customers have no public fix. Only customers with an extended support contract can get one from Broadcom support.
The risk is highest where ESX management interfaces can be reached from user, server or guest networks, or from the internet, rather than only from a dedicated management network and vCenter.
detect: Version check: compare each host's ESXi image profile and build with the fixed builds in VMSA-2026-0011, for example from vCenter inventory or a vulnerability scanner.
Network exposure: find which networks can reach TCP 9080 on ESX hosts. Anything other than vCenter and the management network is unnecessary exposure (KB463535 limits the service to vCenter).
Firewall and flow logs: look for connections to ESX hosts' I/O filter service from addresses other than vCenter.

Host behaviour: look for crashes or restarts of the I/O filter service in ESX host logs, unexpected new processes or files on the host, new root SSH authorized keys, SSH or ESXi Shell being enabled outside change windows, and unusual root logins.
No public indicators of compromise or detection rules specific to this CVE had been published in the sources read.

steps: List all ESX hosts and their builds, including hosts in VCF, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud stacks.

Update ESX to the fixed build for its release line. Hosts in VCF 5.x go to 5.2.5, and Telco Cloud Platform follows KB463501. Do this together with the vCenter update for CVE-2026-123903 from the same advisory.
If ESX 8.0 cannot be patched right away, apply Broadcom's interim workaround KB463535. It sets the ESXi firewall so that only vCenter can reach the I/O filter service.
ESX 7.0: if you have an extended support contract, ask Broadcom support for a fix. Otherwise, plan an upgrade and limit network access to the hosts' management interfaces until then.
Keep ESX management interfaces on a dedicated management network that can be reached only from vCenter and administrative hosts.
fixed_versions: VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation ESX 9.1.x.x: ESXi-9.1.2.0-25946735
VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation ESX 9.0.x.x: ESXi-9.0.2.0200-25953133
ESX 7.0: contact Broadcom Support if you have an extended support contract
Telco Cloud Platform ESX 5.0.x, 5.1.x: see KB463501
workarounds: ESX 8.0 only: Broadcom KB463535 is a manual, interim workaround. It restricts the ESXi firewall rule set for the I/O filter service so that only the vCenter Server address (or subnet) is allowed. It does not fix the flaw, and Broadcom lists no workaround for 9.1 or 9.0.
verify: Check the build number of each host in vCenter or the host client and confirm it matches or is later than the fixed build.

Where the workaround is used, confirm that the host's allowed-address list for the I/O filter rule set contains only vCenter (the last step in KB463535). Then scan from another network to confirm the port cannot be reached.
Re-run a vulnerability scan and confirm this CVE is no longer reported.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected host on the network. Preserve its logs and a support bundle before you reboot or reimage it, because ESX logs may not survive a reboot.
Rotate the host's root password and remove unknown SSH keys and accounts. Also rotate the vCenter and service credentials the host could reach.
Rebuild the host from known-good media at a fixed build rather than cleaning it in place. Check its virtual machines for tampering before moving them back.
Check the rest of the estate (other hosts and vCenter) for the same signs. Report the incident to your national CERT, and to Broadcom support if you have a contract.

Exposure is marked internal because ESX management services usually sit on management networks; hosts reachable more widely are at higher risk.

CVE-2026-124194.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Microsoft marks it Exploitation Detected (10 Nov 2026), not publicly disclosed. Attackers, targets and scale are not named. In CISA KEV since 10 Nov 2026, federal due date 24 Nov.
CVE-2026-124194.how_exploited: A user-interface flaw (CWE-356, no warning for an unsafe action) in Outlook. An unauthenticated attacker sends a specially crafted message file or Office file; when the victim opens it, Outlook connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning. Windows then sends the user's NTLMv2 authentication data to that server, which the attacker can crack offline or relay to authenticate as the user. It does not give code execution by itself.
preconditions: The victim opens the crafted message or Office file; Microsoft says the Preview Pane is not an attack vector.
The victim's computer can reach the attacker's server over the network (outbound SMB or similar authentication traffic is not blocked).
An unpatched Outlook in Microsoft 365 Apps, Office LTSC 2021 or Office LTSC 2024.
No account or prior access is needed by the attacker.
attack_path: Delivery: a crafted message file or Office file is sent to the target, typically by email.
Trigger: the user opens it and Outlook silently connects to the attacker's server with no external-content prompt.
Credential access: the user's NTLMv2 hash reaches the attacker.
Follow-on: the hash can be cracked offline or relayed to internal services to act as the user; Microsoft has not said whether stolen credentials were used further in the observed attacks.
who_is_exposed: Windows users of Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021 and Office LTSC 2024 (32-bit and 64-bit) below the November 2026 builds.
Organisations that still accept NTLM on internal services and allow outbound SMB to the internet face the most risk from captured hashes.
detect: Outlook initiating SMB (TCP 445) or other authentication connections to external or unfamiliar hosts shortly after a message file is opened (endpoint and firewall logs).
Outgoing NTLM authentication to internet destinations, seen in the Windows NTLM Operational log or with the outgoing NTLM restriction policy set to audit.
Logons to internal services from unusual systems or addresses soon after suspicious Outlook activity, which can indicate relayed or cracked credentials.
Inventory installed Office builds per update channel and compare them with the November 2026 release builds; no indicators of compromise have been published.

steps: Install the November 2026 Office security updates on every device running Outlook, and confirm each Microsoft 365 Apps update channel has received its November build.
Block outbound SMB to the internet at the perimeter and on endpoints where it is not needed.
Audit outgoing NTLM with the Restrict NTLM outgoing traffic policy in audit mode, build an exception list, and move towards denying it and reducing NTLM use.
Warn users not to open unsolicited message files or Office files from unclear senders.
US federal agencies: meet the 24 Nov 2026 KEV deadline and BOD 26-04 forensics triage requirements.

CVE-2026-125343.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported as of 19 Nov 2026: Google's 9 Nov release notes say only CVE-2026-125350 (fixed in the same update) is exploited in the wild; this CVE is not in CISA's KEV catalog and no public exploit code has been reported.
CVE-2026-125343.how_exploited: A heap buffer overflow in Chrome's Compositing component, rated High by Chromium (reported by Google on 15 Sep 2026). Per the NVD description, an attacker who has already compromised the renderer process can use a crafted HTML page to run arbitrary code outside the sandbox. It is therefore a sandbox-escape class bug: on its own it does not give access, but paired with a separate renderer flaw it could let a malicious web page take over the user's session on the device.
preconditions: The victim runs Chrome (or another Chromium-based browser) older than the fixed build.
The victim visits an attacker-controlled or compromised web page.
The attacker must already control the renderer process, which requires a second, separate flaw (such as a renderer code-execution bug); NVD rates attack complexity high for this reason.
attack_path: Delivery: the victim is lured to or redirected through a malicious web page.
Renderer compromise: a separate flaw gives the attacker code execution inside the sandboxed renderer.
Sandbox escape: from the renderer, the attacker triggers the Compositing overflow to run code outside the sandbox with the browser user's rights.
No in-the-wild use and no follow-on activity have been reported for this CVE.
who_is_exposed: Chrome desktop users on Windows and macOS before 157.0.8103.50/.51 and on Linux before 157.0.8103.50.
Users of other Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge until their vendor ships the matching Chromium fix (CSO Online notes Chromium browsers need the fix too).

CVE-2026-125350.how_exploited: A use-after-free memory-safety bug in Chrome's XML handling. Code running in the sandbox normally needs a second, separate flaw to escape to the operating system.
preconditions: The victim runs Chrome (or another Chromium-based browser) older than the fixed build.
The victim opens or is redirected to an attacker-controlled or compromised web page that delivers crafted content; user interaction is limited to visiting the page.

attack_path: Delivery: the victim is lured to, or redirected through, a web page carrying the crafted content (Google has not said how victims were reached).
Execution: the page triggers the use-after-free in XML processing and gains code execution inside the browser's sandboxed renderer process.
Follow-on stages (sandbox escape, malware install, data theft) have not been described by Google or any investigating firm.

CVE-2026-126187.exploitation_status: No exploitation in the wild reported: as of 11 Nov 2026 React, Vercel and CISA reported none and it is not in KEV (Cloudflare). Public proof-of-concept code is claimed (Hash Security lab PoC; ThreatDefence, 8-9 Nov), unverified.
CVE-2026-126187.how_exploited: A framing error in the Flight protocol that React Server Components use to stream data from server to browser and back. When a response carries several typed arrays that share one memory buffer, the writer can announce a chunk it then skips, so the reader falls out of step and treats attacker-influenced bytes as protocol instructions. One such instruction loads and runs a module or Server Action from the application's own bundle with attacker-chosen arguments. An unauthenticated remote attacker can thereby run code on the server, provided the application has the rare data pattern and a Server Action that does something dangerous with its inputs.
preconditions: The application renders React Server Components on a server or edge runtime; client-only apps are not affected (React advisory).
It uses react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-parcel or react-server-dom-turbopack 19.0.0 to 19.0.8, 19.1.0 to 19.1.9, 19.2.0 to 19.2.8 or 19.3.0, directly or through a framework.
A response carries multiple typed-array views over one shared buffer and an attacker can influence bytes in one of them; React calls this extremely rare.
For code execution, a reachable Server Action or module that performs a dangerous operation with the arguments it receives (Cloudflare).
No authentication or user interaction is needed (CVSS 4.0 9.5).
attack_path: Reconnaissance: the attacker identifies an internet-facing application built on a React Server Components framework, such as Next.js App Router.
Initial access: the attacker supplies data that ends up in a typed array of a server response with the shared-buffer pattern, desynchronising the Flight stream.
Execution: the corrupted stream is read as instructions that invoke a Server Action or bundle module with attacker-chosen arguments, running code in the server process.
Follow-on: no in-the-wild attacks are reported; code running in the server process would have the application's secrets, environment variables and network access.
who_is_exposed: Web applications using React Server Components through Next.js, React Router framework mode, Vite RSC plugins or custom bundler setups on affected versions.
Next.js 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 apps using the App Router with Cache Components and cached functions that return several typed arrays (Cloudflare, citing the Next.js advisory).
Next.js 15.5 apps: not listed as affected, but 15.5.28 includes React's transport fix (Cloudflare).
Applications bought from suppliers or hosted by agencies that embed these packages without the owner knowing.
detect: Inventory: search lockfiles, monorepos, container images and deployed artifacts for next and react-server-dom packages and compare resolved versions, not declared ones.
For Next.js 16 apps, note App Router use, whether Cache Components is enabled and whether cached functions return typed arrays (Cloudflare).
Runtime: unexpected child processes, file writes or outbound connections from Node.js server or edge workers.
Responses whose binary-row length declarations exceed the bytes present, and client 'Connection closed' errors on responses with large typed arrays (StepSecurity).
No indicators of compromise or detection signatures have been published by React, Vercel or Cloudflare.

steps: Find every application that uses React Server Components, including those built by suppliers, and list the resolved react-server-dom and next versions.
Update react-server-dom-webpack, -parcel and -turbopack to the fixed release on your 19.x line, or update the framework to a release that includes it.
For Next.js, update 16.x to 16.4.1 or later and 15.5 to 15.5.28 or later; updating React alone does not fix Next.js, which ships its own compiled copy.
Rebuild and redeploy every affected application; a fixed lockfile does not fix code already running.
Block the affected versions in your package registry policy and keep egress controls on server and edge workloads.
fixed_versions: Next.js 16.4.1 and 15.5.28 (per Cloudflare's summary of the Next.js advisory)
verify: Check the package version inside the deployed build artifact or container image, not just the lockfile.
Confirm the running deployment was built after the upgrade, for example by build ID or image digest.
if_compromised: Take the affected deployment out of service or isolate it, and preserve server logs, container images and runtime telemetry.
Rotate every secret the application could read: environment variables, database credentials, API keys and cloud tokens.
Rebuild from clean source with fixed dependencies and redeploy to fresh infrastructure.
Review cloud and database audit logs for use of the application's identities, and report the incident to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-126187.caveats: React's advisory gives little technical detail; the mechanism comes from StepSecurity and Cloudflare, which agree. Public PoC claims are unverified, and React says the triggering condition is extremely rare, so real-world exploitability is uncertain. Vercel says there is no workaround; StepSecurity's stopgap of copying typed arrays before rendering is not vendor guidance. The Cyber Centre's notice names no CVE.

CVE-2026-127063.exploitation_status: Abused in the wild from 11 Nov 2026 per Huntress, which links the SCKit attacks to RMM+ but has not confirmed it as the entry point; ConnectWise said on 11-12 Nov the access vector was unconfirmed. Not in CISA KEV as of 22 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-127063.how_exploited: Use of default credentials (CWE-1392) in RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension by DataComm. The extension lets another tool drive ScreenConnect sessions with a shared API secret instead of ScreenConnect user accounts, roles and MFA. It ships with a static default secret (Huntress: versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank key when none was set). Where the default is kept, a remote attacker can call the extension's API without logging in and send commands to managed agents, which run as SYSTEM on endpoints.
preconditions: The ScreenConnect instance (cloud-hosted or on-premises) has the RMM+ extension installed and enabled; instances without it are not affected (CVE record).
The extension's API secret was never changed from its default (or left blank in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, per Huntress).
The ScreenConnect web server is reachable by the attacker, typically from the internet; no user interaction or account is needed (CVSS 4.0 score 9.3 from ConnectWise).
attack_path: Initial access: commands reach endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances through the extension, with no matching ScreenConnect logins (Huntress).

Execution: the operator uses the Run Command feature to push commands as SYSTEM to groups of endpoints; one panel reached 190 clients, and 288 hosts at 48 organisations were hit within about 90 minutes on 11 Nov.

Persistence: a second, attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client is installed silently, disguised as a Windows update service, backed by a scheduled task, a Run key, Defender exclusions and redirect rules (Huntress).
Tooling: a dropper fetches SCKit, an encrypted 16-file script toolkit keyed to each machine, which stops the real client so the rogue one takes its place.
Spread attempt: SCKit tries to steal a technician's ScreenConnect session cookie and reuse it on the panel to reach more endpoints; Huntress saw no success in any log it recovered.
A second wave on 13 Nov reached 205 hosts at 41 organisations.
who_is_exposed: Managed service providers and IT teams running ScreenConnect with the RMM+ extension (also listed as RMM Plus, Labtech Plus and the Password Link variants), on-premises or cloud-hosted.
Every endpoint managed from an affected ScreenConnect panel, since commands run there as SYSTEM.
Technician workstations that connect to infected endpoints, which SCKit targets for session theft.
detect: List installed ScreenConnect extensions on every instance and check whether RMM+ or its related extensions are present or enabled, and whether its API secret was ever changed.
Review ScreenConnect Run Command and Shared Toolbox history and the audit log for mass commands that no technician started, especially from 11 Nov 2026 on.

On managed endpoints, look for a second ScreenConnect client service, new LocalSystem services named like Windows Update in ProgramData folders, new scheduled tasks and Run keys, Defender exclusions, and a modified hosts file.
Look for the legitimate ScreenConnect service switched to manual start, and for new port-proxy or application control rules that block ScreenConnect's temp folders.
Compare against the indicators in Huntress's SCKit blog (updated for the second wave); Huntress notes file hashes are weak because the scripts are rebuilt per victim.

steps: On-premises: disable the RMM+ extension now, confirm it stays disabled, and do not re-enable or reinstall it until the vendor gives further guidance (ConnectWise, CVE record).
Disable the related third-party extensions ConnectWise named (Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM Plus Password Link, RMM + Password Link) on on-premises servers too.
Cloud-hosted: ConnectWise says it has disabled and removed the extension, so no action is needed for this CVE; still review the instance for signs of the attacks.
Confirm every technician client runs ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later (separate flaw CVE-2026-84869, which ConnectWise urged partners to patch).
Review Run Command, Toolbox and audit history, and check endpoints for a second ScreenConnect client.
From a trusted device, revoke active ScreenConnect sessions, rotate ScreenConnect passwords and enforce MFA (ConnectWise via Cybersecurity Dive).
workarounds: ConnectWise: disable the RMM+ extension; no fixed extension version is published. Where an extension of this kind must stay, Rapid7 and the CVE record note the default secret can be changed, but the vendor advises disabling it.
verify: Check the ScreenConnect extension list on each on-premises server shows RMM+ and related extensions disabled, and recheck after restarts and upgrades.
Confirm the technician client version shown in ScreenConnect is 26.6.5 or later.
After cleanup, confirm each endpoint runs only the legitimate ScreenConnect client and that no rogue service or scheduled task returns.
if_compromised: Do not connect to suspect hosts through ScreenConnect; use WinRM or another out-of-band tool, and investigate technician workstations from a clean device (Huntress, ConnectWise).
Isolate affected endpoints; Huntress saw hosts reinfected once isolation was lifted, so remove persistence before reconnecting.
Preserve authentication, extension installation, Run Command and Toolbox records before cleanup (ConnectWise).
Remove the rogue client service, scheduled task, Run key, toolkit folder, Defender exclusions and added application control rules, after verifying which client is legitimate.
End all ScreenConnect web sessions, rotate ScreenConnect and identity provider credentials, and revoke browser and identity sessions.
Report the incident to affected customers and your national CERT (in the US, CISA).

CVE-2026-127063.caveats: ConnectWise's advisory pages and its GitHub disclosure refused automated reading (403); the vendor's text here comes from its CVE record as CNA. Whether this flaw was the entry point for SCKit is not confirmed by ConnectWise or Huntress, and CVE-2026-84869 has also been linked by others. No fixed RMM+ version is stated. Huntress's note on current ScreenConnect builds being affected is ambiguous.

CVE-2026-129243.exploitation_status: Exploitation attempts in the wild: The Hacker News (25 Nov 2026) cites watchTowr seeing probes that abuse it with CVE-2026-120705. A researcher has published an RCE chain write-up using it. Not in CISA KEV as of 25 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-129243.how_exploited: An incorrect authorization flaw in GeoServer's OGC web service (OWS) security. The request dispatcher strips a prefix from the requested service name before routing it to the real service, but the security check compares its rules against the unstripped name, so service security rules do not match. An unauthenticated attacker who adds a prefix to the service name can call operations the administrator restricted, such as creating and deleting WFS stored queries. Attackers combine this with the stored query file read (CVE-2026-120705) to steal credentials and keys and reach code execution.
preconditions: Network access to GeoServer's OWS endpoints; no credentials are needed.
GeoServer 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, or 2.27.6 and earlier.
Impact depends on which operations the administrator protected with service security rules; in the reported chain it opens stored query management to anonymous users on a default install.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: scanning for internet-facing GeoServer; watchTowr saw probes that create and invoke stored queries.
Access control bypass: requests using a prefixed service name skip the service rules and reach protected operations anonymously.
Chained file read: the attacker stores a query that abuses CVE-2026-120705 to read the security configuration and user files, obtaining the admin password digest and remember-me key.
Privilege escalation and execution: a forged admin session (CVE-2026-129245) and admin-only JDBC features (CVE-2026-129242 or CVE-2026-120704) give code execution as the GeoServer process.
Next steps: no post-exploitation activity has been published.
who_is_exposed: Internet-facing GeoServer instances on affected 3.0.x, 2.28.x and 2.27.x releases, including the official container images.
Deployments that rely on service security rules to block anonymous write or management operations.
Products that bundle GeoServer's gs-ows module.
detect: Version check: the About GeoServer page shows the build version; anything below 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7 is affected.
Access logs: OWS requests whose service name carries an unexpected prefix rather than a plain service name, from anonymous clients.
Data directory: WFS stored queries nobody on your team created, and stored query errors in the GeoServer log.
Security configuration: unexpected user or role services, remember-me changes or new administrator accounts.
No indicator lists or detection rules were published in the sources read.

steps: Upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2 or 2.28.6, or to 2.27.7 if you must stay on the end-of-life 2.27 line; this fixes the whole reported chain.
If GeoServer is internet-facing and cannot be upgraded at once, restrict who can reach it (VPN, IP allow lists or a reverse proxy) until it is patched.
After upgrading, change administrator and user passwords, because the chained file read may already have exposed their digests.
Review stored queries, security services and accounts for changes (see detect).
verify: The About GeoServer page shows 3.0.2, 2.28.6, 2.27.7 or later.
For embedded copies, confirm the deployed gs-ows library is at a fixed version.
Confirm with an authorised test account that operations protected by service rules are refused to anonymous users.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve the data directory, logs and a disk or container image.
Rebuild from a clean, patched install if unknown stored queries, accounts or JDBC services are found.
Rotate every secret GeoServer held: admin and user passwords, database and data store credentials, and cloud keys.
Check connected databases and file shares for access from the GeoServer host.
Report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-129243.caveats: GeoServer's GitHub advisory could not be read (403); its summary page only titles this a service rule bypass via a prefixed service name, and the mechanism comes from a Rapid7 researcher's write-up. Exploitation is watchTowr's report relayed by news; the post itself was not read. A researcher's proxy filtering suggestion is not vendor guidance.

CVE-2026-129245.exploitation_status: No in-the-wild use of this CVE reported as of 25 Nov 2026. watchTowr reports attacks on CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, which are earlier links in the same published chain (The Hacker News, Rapid7 researcher).
CVE-2026-129245.how_exploited: A predictable signing key in GeoServer's remember-me login feature (rated Critical by GeoServer). Remember-me cookies are signed with a key that is normally left at a fixed default and stored in the data directory, plus the user's password digest. An attacker who has read the administrator's password digest, for example through the unauthenticated file-read flaw CVE-2026-120705, can forge a valid remember-me cookie. GeoServer then treats them as the administrator without the password being known or cracked.
preconditions: GeoServer 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, or 2.27.6 and earlier (researcher write-ups); default configuration, per Eye Security.
The attacker needs the administrator's password digest and the signing key. Both can be read through a separate file-disclosure flaw such as CVE-2026-120705; no login is needed for that step.
The GeoServer web interface or services can be reached by the attacker, often from the internet.
attack_path: Reconnaissance and file read: the attacker uses an unauthenticated file-disclosure flaw (CVE-2026-120705, reported exploited by watchTowr) to read user and security configuration files.
Privilege gain: with the password digest and the default key, the attacker forges a remember-me cookie and receives an administrator session.
Execution: as administrator, researchers registered a JDBC security service to run code on the server (CVE-2026-120704 or CVE-2026-129242).
Follow-on: no attacks using this step are described; an admin session also exposes data store credentials and lets the attacker change layers and security rules.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted GeoServer on the 3.0, 2.28 and 2.27 lines before 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7, including ones on default settings.
Most at risk: instances whose web interface is reachable from the internet and that are also open to the file-read flaw CVE-2026-120705.
Products that bundle GeoServer, such as GeoServer Cloud, until they ship the fixed release.
detect: Check the version on the About GeoServer page (Build Information) or in the deployed files; anything older than 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7 is exposed.
Review web and GeoServer access logs for administrator sessions that start from a remember-me cookie without a preceding login, or admin activity from unfamiliar addresses.
Look for unusual WFS GetFeatureById or stored-query requests from the same source shortly before the admin activity; this is the file-read step.
Check the stored-query directories in the data directory for queries nobody created (Rapid7 researcher write-up).
Audit the admin change history and configuration files for new users, new JDBC user or role services, changed security rules or unknown files.

steps: Upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7, the versions GeoServer names in its November 2026 security update. The 2.27 line is end-of-life, so plan a move to 2.28 or 3.0.
Upgrade at the same time for the other October 2026 fixes, especially CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, which watchTowr reports are being exploited.
On clusters, give every node the same remember-me key as the researcher notes describe. Existing remember-me cookies stop working after the upgrade.
Change the administrator password after upgrading, so a digest read earlier cannot be reused.
Limit access to the GeoServer web admin interface to trusted networks.
verify: Confirm the new version on the About GeoServer page.
Confirm that remember-me cookies issued before the upgrade no longer give a session.
On clusters, confirm users stay signed in across nodes, which shows the key is set the same on every node.
if_compromised: Take the server off the network or block outside access, and keep logs, the data directory and a disk image for investigation.
Rotate all GeoServer user passwords and every credential stored in data stores, as these can be read by an admin.
Look for code execution through JDBC security services and for new native library files; if found, rebuild the server from a clean image.
Report the incident to your national CERT and notify data owners as required.

CVE-2026-129245.caveats: GeoServer's GitHub advisory (GHSA-hgm3-wq4h-8vvq) returned 403 and was not read; GeoServer's own posts give only the title. The mechanism comes from Eye Security and a Rapid7 researcher. GeoServer's 2.28.6 and 2.27.7 release notes do not list this CVE, though its November update and researchers say all three releases fix it. Dates for 2.28.6 differ between sources. GeoServer offers no workaround.

CVE-2026-129271.exploitation_status: No exploitation of this flaw reported as of 19 Nov 2026. N-able says the N-central flaws fixed in HF3 were published as zero-days without coordinated disclosure; exploitation reported so far concerns other N-central flaws.
CVE-2026-129271.how_exploited: Local privilege escalation in the Patch Management Engine component of N-central, which runs on managed devices. According to the CVE record written by N-able, the engine trusts metadata that a local attacker can control, so a user with a low-privileged foothold on a managed device can get the component to act on that metadata with its own higher privileges and gain full control of that device. N-able has published no further technical detail.
preconditions: N-central Patch Management Component (Patch Management Engine) older than 2.14.4.5829 on the managed device.
The attacker already runs code or has a low-privileged account on that device (local access, per the CVSS vector); no user interaction is needed.
attack_path: Initial access: obtained separately, for example phishing or another flaw, giving a low-privileged foothold on a managed endpoint.
Privilege escalation: the attacker plants or changes metadata the Patch Management Engine reads, and the engine's privileged process acts on it.
Follow-on: with full control of the endpoint the attacker can disable defences, steal credentials or move to other systems; no in-the-wild use has been described.
who_is_exposed: Every Windows device managed by N-central with the Patch Management Engine below 2.14.4.5829, whether the server is hosted or on-premises.
Managed service providers and their customers, since one MSP's N-central can cover many organisations' devices.
detect: Inventory the Patch Management Engine version on every managed device in N-central and list those below 2.14.4.5829.

In endpoint detection data, look for processes started by the patch management service that are not normal patch installers, and for privilege changes or new local administrators on devices running it.
Watch for files in the Patch Management Engine's working folders being changed by non-administrative users.

steps: On-premises: upgrade the N-central server to 2026.4 HF3 (build 2026.4.1.39) as an emergency change; supported direct upgrade paths start at 2025.4. Hosted (NCOD) servers are upgraded by N-able.

Upgrade all Agents and Probes to 2026.4.1 HF3, including those already on HF2, following the Agent and Probe compatibility rules in the HF2 release notes; N-able warns that unupgraded ones are open to impersonation.
Make sure the Patch Management Engine on every managed device reaches 2.14.4.5829 or later (N-able's PME 2.14.4 release).
Treat low-privileged footholds on managed endpoints as serious until patching is complete.
verify: Check in N-central that every device reports Patch Management Engine 2.14.4.5829 or later.
Confirm the server reports build 2026.4.1.39 and that Agents and Probes report 2026.4.1 HF3.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected endpoint, preserve its logs and memory where possible, and rebuild it if an attacker gained administrative control.
Rotate credentials used or cached on the endpoint and look for the same activity on other managed devices.
Report to N-able support and your national CERT (in Canada, the Cyber Centre).

CVE-2026-129271.caveats: N-able's per-CVE advisory page did not load for automated reading, so details come from the CVE record N-able wrote, its HF3 release notes and the Cyber Centre advisory. The CVE record labels the weakness as missing authentication (CWE-306) while describing a local privilege escalation; the exact mechanism is not public. No source links this flaw to the crypto-mining attacks.

CVE-2026-129272.exploitation_status: No exploitation of this specific flaw reported as of 19 Nov 2026. Public exploit chains for agent impersonation against N-central were released from 12 Nov, and N-able says other N-central flaws were exploited from 13 Nov.
CVE-2026-129272.how_exploited: Improper authentication (CWE-287): N-central before 2026.4.1 HF3 authenticates appliances (Agents and Probes) to an agent-facing interface with a predictable credential. According to N-able's CVE record, a remote, unauthenticated attacker who knows or guesses an appliance identifier can obtain a valid appliance token and session and impersonate that appliance. N-able says impersonation lets an attacker receive the agent's task and script information and set the agent's status and metrics in N-central.
preconditions: N-central server older than 2026.4.1 HF3, or Agents and Probes not yet upgraded to HF3.
The attacker can reach the server's agent-facing interface, which is normally internet-facing so remote devices can check in.
The attacker knows or can guess a target appliance identifier; no login or user interaction is needed.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: the attacker learns or guesses an appliance identifier for a managed device.
Impersonation: using the predictable credential, the attacker gets a valid appliance token and session and connects as that Agent or Probe.
Collection and tampering: the attacker receives task and script details meant for the device, which can reveal configuration and secrets, and can report false status and metrics.
Researchers chained agent impersonation with other flaws to run commands as SYSTEM on managed Windows devices (Agent2Shell, per The Hacker News); which CVEs that chain uses is not stated.
who_is_exposed: On-premises N-central servers below 2026.4.1 HF3 whose agent interface is reachable from the internet.
Hosted (NCOD) customers whose Agents and Probes are not yet on HF3; N-able says unupgraded ones remain open to impersonation.
Devices and customers managed by the server, whose tasks and scripts an impersonator can receive.
detect: After upgrading, open Configuration, Asset Discovery, Discovered Assets, Inactive Assets and investigate inactive or duplicate Agents for the same device that you cannot explain.
Look for the same appliance checking in from unexpected source addresses or from two places at once in server and proxy logs.
Compare device status and metrics in N-central with what the device itself shows; false healthy reports can hide tampering.
Check the indicators N-able published in its 13 Nov update (addresses and URLs) as listed in its remediation update and Rapid7's post; their absence does not prove you were not affected.

steps: On-premises: upgrade the N-central server to 2026.4 HF3 (build 2026.4.1.39) as an emergency change; supported direct upgrade paths start at 2025.4. Hosted (NCOD) servers are upgraded by N-able.

Upgrade all Agents and Probes to 2026.4.1 HF3, including those already on HF2, following the Agent and Probe compatibility rules in the HF2 release notes; N-able warns that unupgraded ones are open to impersonation.
In Administration, Mail and Network Settings, Network Setup, review the Appliance token behaviour setting so inactive or unverified Agents are rejected or made to upgrade.
Review scripts and tasks sent to devices for embedded credentials and rotate any that could have been read.
fixed_versions: N-central 2026.4.1 HF3 (build 2026.4.1.39), with Agents and Probes upgraded to 2026.4.1 HF3
verify: Confirm the server reports build 2026.4.1.39 and every Agent and Probe reports 2026.4.1 HF3.
After Agents reconnect, check the Inactive Assets tab and Set Active only Agents you recognise.
if_compromised: Isolate the N-central server from the internet while you investigate; it can push scripts and software to every managed device.
Preserve server logs, the audit log and a disk image before rebuilding, so the timeline can be established.
Rotate N-central administrator, service and integration credentials and any credentials stored in or pushed by N-central.
Review managed devices for scheduled tasks, scripts or software deployed by N-central that nobody approved, and rebuild the server from a clean, patched install if tampering is confirmed.
Tell customers whose devices the server manages, contact N-able support, and report to your national CERT (in Canada, the Cyber Centre).

CVE-2026-129272.caveats: N-able's per-CVE advisory page did not load for automated reading; details come from N-able's CVE record, its remediation update and HF3 release notes, and the Cyber Centre advisory. N-able's update says agent impersonation needs a foothold on an endpoint, while the CVE record says a remote attacker who knows or guesses an identifier is enough; how hard identifiers are to obtain is not stated.

CVE-2026-129273.exploitation_status: No exploitation of this flaw reported as of 19 Nov 2026. N-able published it among 17 HF3 fixes; reported exploitation concerns other N-central flaws reached through the Legacy API.
CVE-2026-129273.how_exploited: Injection (CWE-74) in the Audit Export feature of the N-central server. According to N-able's CVE record, a setting for exporting the audit log to syslog is written into the server's system logging configuration without removing control characters, so an attacker with product administrator rights can add their own configuration and have the server run commands as root. This turns an administrator account, legitimate or stolen, into full control of the server's operating system.
preconditions: On-premises N-central server older than 2026.4.1 HF3.
The attacker holds an N-central product administrator account, for example through stolen credentials or another flaw that grants admin access.
The web interface is reachable by the attacker; no user interaction is needed.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker logs in as an N-central administrator, possibly after chaining another N-central flaw or credential theft.
Execution: the attacker saves a crafted Audit Export setting that changes the server's syslog configuration, leading to commands running as root.
Impact: root control of the server, which can push scripts and software to every managed device, and can tamper with logs.
Attackers exploiting other N-central flaws installed crypto miners on servers (The Hacker News); no source ties this CVE to that activity.
who_is_exposed: On-premises N-central servers below 2026.4.1 HF3, especially those with the web interface exposed to the internet.
Organisations and MSP customers managed by those servers, since root on the server reaches every managed device.
detect: Review the N-central audit log for changes to Audit Export or syslog settings, and confirm who made them and when.
Inspect the server's system logging configuration for entries you did not create.
Look for unexpected processes running as root, outbound connections from the server and sustained high processor use, which can indicate a crypto miner.
Review administrator account creation, sign-ins from unusual addresses and recent password resets in N-central.

steps: On-premises: upgrade the N-central server to 2026.4 HF3 (build 2026.4.1.39) as an emergency change; supported direct upgrade paths start at 2025.4. Hosted (NCOD) servers are upgraded by N-able.
Limit who holds product administrator rights, require multi-factor authentication for them, and restrict the web interface to trusted networks where possible.

Upgrade all Agents and Probes to 2026.4.1 HF3, including those already on HF2, following the Agent and Probe compatibility rules in the HF2 release notes; N-able warns that unupgraded ones are open to impersonation.
Review Audit Export and syslog settings after upgrading and remove anything unexpected.
verify: Confirm the server reports build 2026.4.1.39.
Confirm the Audit Export settings and system logging configuration contain only entries you configured.
if_compromised: Isolate the N-central server from the internet while you investigate; it can push scripts and software to every managed device.
Preserve server logs, the audit log and a disk image before rebuilding, so the timeline can be established.
Rotate N-central administrator, service and integration credentials and any credentials stored in or pushed by N-central.
Review managed devices for scheduled tasks, scripts or software deployed by N-central that nobody approved, and rebuild the server from a clean, patched install if tampering is confirmed.
Tell customers whose devices the server manages, contact N-able support, and report to your national CERT (in Canada, the Cyber Centre).

CVE-2026-129273.caveats: N-able has not published a detailed advisory page for this CVE that could be read; details come from its CVE record and HF3 release notes. The Cyber Centre advisory AV26-1165 does not list it. Hosted (NCOD) exposure is not stated; N-able upgrades hosted servers itself.
