CVE-2026-129448.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Apache said on 17 Nov 2026 the issue is being actively exploited; CISA added it to KEV on 20 Nov 2026. Attackers, start date and victim count not disclosed; no public exploit code reported.
CVE-2026-129448.how_exploited: Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) in Apache Roller's XML-RPC blogging interface, rated 9.8. The endpoint accepts vendor extension data types and deserializes them while parsing a request, before it checks who is sending it. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the Roller web application sends a crafted XML-RPC request whose embedded object is rebuilt on the server, which Apache says can lead to remote code execution with the rights of the Java application server running Roller. It is the same bug as CVE-2026-82384, which had listed only version 6.1.5.
preconditions: Apache Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.5 (CVE-2026-129448 covers 4.0.0 through 6.1.4; CVE-2026-82384 covers 6.1.5).
Network access to the Roller web application; no account and no user interaction are needed.
No special configuration: the XML-RPC servlet is mapped by default and parses requests even when XML-RPC is switched off in the administration interface.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker sends a request to the XML-RPC interface of an internet-facing Roller blog.
Execution: the server deserializes the attacker's object before authentication and runs code as the account of the Java servlet container hosting Roller.

Follow-on activity: Apache and the news reports read do not describe what attackers did after access; typical next steps for this flaw class are web shells, credential theft from configuration files and database connections, and movement to other hosts, so hunt for them.
who_is_exposed: Any self-hosted Apache Roller blog server on 4.0.0 through 6.1.5, especially those reachable from the internet.
Installations where administrators disabled XML-RPC only in the Roller administration interface, which does not stop the vulnerable parsing on older versions.
Other applications and data on the same servlet container or host, and the blog's database, since code runs as the application server account.
detect: Check the Roller version on every instance; anything from 4.0.0 to 6.1.5 is vulnerable.
Review web server and servlet container access logs for requests to Roller's XML-RPC service, especially from unknown addresses or on sites where no blogging client uses it.
Watch the Java application server process for unexpected child processes such as shells or download tools, and for new files written in the web application folders.
Check servlet container logs for deserialization or class-loading errors around the time of XML-RPC requests.
Watch for outbound connections from the blog server to unfamiliar hosts.
Apache has not published indicators or detection rules for this flaw.

steps: Upgrade Apache Roller to 6.1.6 or later.

If you cannot upgrade at once, apply Apache's workaround in the web application's deployment descriptor (turn off the extensions setting for the XML-RPC servlet, or remove the XML-RPC servlet mapping), then restart Roller; turning XML-RPC off in the administration interface is not enough.
Block or restrict access to the XML-RPC interface at a reverse proxy or firewall if no blogging client needs it.
Hunt for signs of compromise on every instance that ran a vulnerable version while exposed, since exploitation is confirmed.
workarounds: Set the enabledForExtensions parameter of the XML-RPC servlet to false in WEB-INF/web.xml and restart Roller (Apache).
Or remove the XML-RPC servlet mapping from WEB-INF/web.xml and restart Roller (Apache).
verify: Confirm the running Roller version is 6.1.6 or later on every instance, including staging copies.
If using the workaround, confirm the deployment descriptor change survived redeployment and that the XML-RPC service no longer answers.
Rescan with a vulnerability scanner that checks CVE-2026-129448 and CVE-2026-82384.
if_compromised: Take the server offline or isolate it, and preserve web, servlet container and system logs plus a disk image.
Rebuild the server from a known-good image with Roller 6.1.6 or later rather than cleaning it in place.
Rotate the database credentials and any other secrets in Roller's configuration, and reset blog user passwords.
Check the database and published content for tampering, and check other hosts reachable from the server for further intrusion.
Report the incident to your national CERT (CISA in the United States).

CVE-2026-129448.caveats: Apache's advisory is clear on the flaw, versions and workaround, but no technical write-up from the finder or from incident responders was available, and neither Apache nor the news reports say who is exploiting it or what attackers did after access; the attack path beyond initial execution is general for this flaw class, not observed. The CVE.org and NVD web pages did not render; the CVE record was read through the CVE API.

CVE-2026-131914.exploitation_status: Known exploited: Mandiant reported active exploitation (CVE record, 19 Nov 2026); CISA added it to KEV on 24 Nov (due 27 Nov). watchTowr reported honeypot probes, per The Hacker News. No attacker named.
CVE-2026-131914.how_exploited: Insecure deserialisation (CWE-502) in the AntiCsrfModule of Idunno.AntiCsrf, a legacy anti-CSRF module for ASP.NET WebForms. The module deserialises CSRF token data taken from the form field of incoming POST requests using an unkeyed serialisation formatter, with no MAC or signature check. An unauthenticated attacker sends a single crafted POST to any WebForms page protected by the module, with any non-empty value in the CSRF cookie, and the injected object runs code inside the IIS worker process, giving control of the web application and its secrets.
preconditions: An ASP.NET WebForms application has Idunno.AntiCsrf 0.9.1.0 or 0.9.1 Beta (or earlier) registered as an HTTP module.
The attacker can send HTTP POST requests to a page the module handles; no login, valid CSRF token or user interaction is needed.
No official fix exists: the project has been defunct since 2008, so every deployment that still loads the module is exposed.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers probe WebForms pages for the module; watchTowr reported probes that try to make the server redirect to a unique address to confirm code execution.
Initial access and execution: one crafted POST is deserialised by the module and runs code as the IIS application pool identity.

Likely next steps (not described for this campaign): reading secrets such as machine keys and database credentials, and planting files in the web root, which is why Mandiant stresses rotating secrets and checking web roots.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running older ASP.NET WebForms applications on IIS, custom or commercial, that bundle the Idunno.AntiCsrf library; CISA notes it may be embedded in other products.
Internet-facing sites are at greatest risk, but internal applications that load the module are equally vulnerable to anyone who can reach them.
Long-unmaintained legacy applications are the most likely to still carry this 2008-era library.
detect: Inventory: search Web.config files for references to the Idunno AntiCsrf module and the application bin directories for the Idunno.AntiCsrf assembly (Mandiant guidance as reported by The Hacker News).
IIS logs: look for unusual POST requests to .aspx pages that return 302 or 500, especially with large request sizes where bytes received are logged.
Process behaviour: alert on the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) starting command interpreters or other unexpected child processes, or making unexpected outbound connections.
File integrity: look for new or changed files in web roots and application folders since mid-November 2026.
Indicators and detection guidance are in Mandiant advisory MNDT-2026-0048; check your WAF or EDR vendor for published signatures.

steps: Find every application that loads Idunno.AntiCsrf (configuration and bin folder search) and take internet-facing ones offline or restrict access if they cannot be changed today.

Remove the library and replace it with a supported anti-CSRF control, as Mandiant recommends: System.Web.Helpers AntiForgery, ViewState protection tied to a per-user key with MAC-verified or encrypted ViewState, or ASP.NET Core antiforgery.
Redeploy the application and confirm it works without the module.
Follow CISA's required action: apply mitigations and BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements, or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.
fixed_versions: None: no patched release exists; the project is abandoned and the library must be removed and replaced.
workarounds: CISA: discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.
As a stopgap only, watchTowr suggests web application firewall rules to block exploitation attempts (reported by The Hacker News); this is a research suggestion, not vendor guidance.
verify: Rerun the search of Web.config files and bin folders on every server and confirm no reference to the module or assembly remains.
Confirm the application still rejects cross-site requests through its replacement anti-CSRF control.
if_compromised: Isolate the server and preserve IIS logs, memory and disk images before cleaning.
Rotate every secret held in Web.config and applicationHost.config, including machine keys, encryption keys and database credentials (Mandiant guidance).
Inspect web roots for unauthorised files, remove them, and preferably rebuild the server from a known-good image.
Review accounts and connections the application pool identity could reach for lateral movement.
Report the incident; US federal agencies must follow CISA's forensic triage requirements.

CVE-2026-131914.caveats: Mandiant's own advisory (MNDT-2026-0048) refused automated access during this run, so details of the mechanism, detection and replacement guidance come from the CVE record, CISA's catalog and The Hacker News' account of the advisory. There is no software vendor; Mandiant is the disclosing party. Neither Mandiant nor CISA has said who is exploiting it or what attackers did after access. Some aggregators wrongly list 0.9.1.0 as a patched version; it is the last, vulnerable release.

CVE-2026-132165.exploitation_status: Known exploited: Drupal says it was exploited on live sites from 19 Nov 2026 19:00 UTC, a day after the fix; CISA added it to KEV on 24 Nov (due 27 Nov). A proof of concept exists per The Hacker News.
CVE-2026-132165.how_exploited: A fail-open flaw in the installer script that ships with Drupal core and stays on the site after installation. Under specific conditions, an unauthenticated attacker can reach the installer on an already-installed site and drive it to reinstall Drupal, which lets them take over the site or run arbitrary code on the web server. Drupal rates it highly critical; some attack paths are blocked when the web server cannot write to or change permissions on the settings file, but not all.
preconditions: Drupal core below 10.6.22, 11.0.0 up to 11.3.22, or 11.4.0 up to 11.4.13; end-of-life branches (11.2 and earlier, 10.5 and earlier, 8 and 9) get no fix.
The core installer is reachable from the network; Drupal core's default web server rules do not block it.
No authentication or user interaction is needed. Drupal calls the vulnerable configurations uncommon and exploitation complex; a writable settings file widens the attack paths.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers look for Drupal sites whose installer still answers requests.
Initial access: the attacker uses the installer to start a reinstall of the existing site under specific conditions.
Execution and takeover: a successful reinstall gives the attacker administrative control of the site or code execution as the web server user.
Next steps are not described in the sources; typical follow-on for Drupal takeovers is web shells, new admin accounts and theft of database contents.
who_is_exposed: Any self-hosted Drupal 10 or 11 site on an affected version where the installer has not been blocked or removed.
Sites on end-of-life Drupal branches, about 29 percent of reporting sites in early November according to The Hacker News, which cannot get a patch.
Sites using the Drupal Steward service are protected against known attack vectors, per Drupal.
detect: Version check: confirm Drupal core version in the status report or composer lock file against the fixed releases.
Web server logs: look for requests to the core installer script on an installed site, especially from 18 Nov 2026 onward.
Integrity: check the settings file for unexpected changes, new database connection details or changed permissions, and compare core files against a clean release.
Site state: watch for an unexpected reinstall, new administrator accounts, changed site configuration, or new PHP files in public file directories.
Drupal publishes no indicators; it directs sites that suspect compromise to the Drupal Security Team.

steps: Upgrade Drupal core to 11.4.13, 11.3.22 or 10.6.22 for your branch; sites on end-of-life branches must move to a supported branch.

Block or remove the core installer after updating, as Drupal recommends, using its installer-hardening guidance (web server deny rule, access rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed in the build).
Make the settings file and its directory non-writable by the web server.
Check for signs of compromise from 18 Nov 2026 onward before declaring the site clean.
workarounds: If you cannot upgrade immediately, follow Drupal's documentation on securing the installer so it cannot be reached (Drupal SA-CORE-2026-017).
Drupal Steward subscribers are protected from known attack vectors but should still upgrade.
verify: Confirm the status report shows the fixed core version.
Confirm from outside the network that the installer no longer responds (blocked or not found).
Confirm the settings file is read-only for the web server user.
if_compromised: Take the site offline or put it in maintenance mode and preserve web server logs, database and file system copies.
Rebuild from a known-good codebase and a database backup taken before 18 Nov 2026 where possible.
Rotate database credentials, the site hash salt, API keys and all administrator passwords; remove unknown accounts.
Contact the Drupal Security Team and report the incident as required; US federal agencies must follow CISA's forensic triage requirements.

CVE-2026-132165.caveats: Drupal's advisory gives few technical details, and no incident-response write-up of the attacks was found; the exact conditions that make a site exploitable are not public. Some early coverage says the flaw was not exploited; that predates Drupal's update reporting exploitation from 19 Nov. Drupal's advisory page shows the highly critical rating (20 of 25) while The Hacker News reported 18 of 25, likely an earlier score.

CVE-2026-132166.exploitation_status: Not directly exploitable and no exploitation reported as of 19 Nov 2026. Drupal (SA-CORE-2026-018, 18 Nov 2026) rates it moderately critical with exploit maturity theoretical: no public exploit code.
CVE-2026-132166.how_exploited: A gadget chain in Drupal core: a set of existing classes and methods that, when an application deserialises attacker-controlled data, can be chained to run code. On its own it is not a threat; it becomes one only if a separate flaw in core, a contributed module or custom code passes untrusted input to PHP deserialisation. In that case the chain can turn the other flaw into remote code execution with full read and write access to site data.
preconditions: Drupal core before 10.6.22, 11.0.0 to before 11.3.22, or 11.4.0 to before 11.4.13.
A separate insecure deserialisation flaw exists on the site (in core, a contributed module or custom code).
Drupal rates access complexity complex, authentication administrator-level and target distribution uncommon.
attack_path: Prerequisite: the attacker finds a separate flaw that deserialises data they control.
Execution: the attacker supplies data that uses the core gadget chain, turning the deserialisation flaw into code execution on the web server.
Impact: Drupal rates confidentiality and integrity impact as all non-public data readable and all data modifiable.
who_is_exposed: Drupal 10 and 11 sites on unpatched core that also run code which deserialises untrusted input.
Sites on end-of-life branches, which receive no fix.
detect: Version check: confirm Drupal core version on the status report page.
Code review: search custom and contributed modules for deserialisation of data that users or external systems can influence, and follow Drupal advisories for those modules.
Watch web server and PHP logs for errors around deserialisation and for new PHP files or unexpected processes started by the web server account.

steps: Update Drupal core to 11.4.13, 11.3.22 or 10.6.22 (or later); this is the same release that fixes the critical CVE-2026-132165, so in practice apply it urgently.
Move sites on end-of-life branches to a supported branch.
Keep contributed modules updated and remove custom code that deserialises untrusted data.
fixed_versions: Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, 8 and 9: end of life, no fix; move to a supported branch
verify: The status report shows a fixed core version.
if_compromised: If code execution through a deserialisation flaw is suspected, take the site offline, preserve logs and files, and find the separate flaw that was used.
Rebuild from a known good backup, rotate credentials and secrets stored on the site, and report the incident.

CVE-2026-132166.caveats: Drupal gives only a short description; which classes form the chain is not published. Risk depends entirely on whether a separate deserialisation flaw exists on the site.

CVE-2026-132224.exploitation_status: Known exploited: Optimizely says it was exploited on 16 Nov 2026 from 07:51 UTC and fixed at 16:10 UTC; CISA added it to KEV on 24 Nov (due 27 Nov). Unit 42 calls the campaign OPTIMJACK; no actor attributed.
CVE-2026-132224.how_exploited: A flaw in the Optimizely Web Experimentation account signup flow (external control of critical state data) let an attacker act as existing administrator users of customer accounts without their credentials. The attacker used this to write malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript of some customer projects. Optimizely's CDN then served that code, as trusted vendor script, to every visitor of affected customer pages, where it stole payment card data and swapped cryptocurrency addresses.
preconditions: The flaw was in Optimizely's hosted service; the attacker needed only access to the public signup flow.
A customer was affected if one of its Web Experimentation projects was targeted and its pages loaded the Web Experimentation snippet during the exposure window.
Visitors were harmed only if they loaded an affected page; a strong Content Security Policy blocked the script, and cards entered in hosted payment iframes were not reachable.
attack_path: Initial access: abuse of the signup flow to impersonate administrator users on targeted customer accounts (Optimizely).
Tampering: malicious JavaScript written into Project JavaScript fields, served from Optimizely's CDN to visitors.

Execution in visitors' browsers: a loader fetched a second-stage script that swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skimmed card data from forms on the host page, and sent screenshots, readable cookies and page data to the attacker (Zscaler, Unit 42).
Further targeting: iPhone and iPad visitors were served iOS exploit kits (Unit 42 names Coruna and DarkSword).
Scale: at least 178 organisations per Unit 42; Zscaler counted more than 450 domains serving the script.
who_is_exposed: Optimizely Web Experimentation customers; Optimizely says fewer than 5 percent were affected and it has told each customer directly whether it was.
Visitors to affected websites between 07:51 and 22:24 UTC on 16 Nov 2026, especially those who entered card details on the site's own forms, made crypto transfers, or used iOS devices.
Not affected: Feature Experimentation, the SDKs and legacy Full Stack, per Optimizely.
detect: Confirm with Optimizely (customer success manager or support) whether your account was affected.
List pages that loaded the Web Experimentation snippet during 07:51 to 22:24 UTC on 16 Nov 2026 and flag any with card entry or crypto transfers as high risk.

Review CSP violation reports and outbound browser requests to unfamiliar domains in that window; Optimizely lists indicators in section 10 of its incident report and Zscaler publishes indicators in its blog.
Audit Project JavaScript fields and project change history for unexpected code, and review account activity for unknown users or sessions.
Review card and cryptocurrency transactions taken on your site in the window for fraud signals.

steps: No customer patch is needed: Optimizely fixed the flaw in its service on 16 Nov and removed the injected code.
Treat the event as a security incident and investigate impact on your site, as Optimizely advises.
Retain web server, CDN, WAF, CSP report, payment and fraud logs covering at least 16 Nov 2026.
Reset Optimizely administrator credentials, rotate API and session tokens and enforce multi-factor authentication (Zscaler).
Assess with legal advisers any notification duties to customers, card brands or regulators.
Enforce a strong Content Security Policy on pages that load the snippet, and remove the snippet from payment and crypto pages where no experiments run.
fixed_versions: Fixed in the Optimizely-hosted service on 16 Nov 2026; no customer-installed version applies.
workarounds: Optimizely: on sites without CSP protection you may keep the Web Experimentation snippet removed from templates or tag manager while you finish your review; it says re-enabling is now safe.
Optimizely: remove the snippet from pages handling payment or crypto transfers that do not run experiments.
verify: Check that every Project JavaScript field contains only code your team approved.
Confirm production pages load only approved snippet versions and that CSP is enforced and reporting.
Confirm Optimizely has stated in writing whether your account was affected.
if_compromised: Preserve logs and project change history before making changes.
Treat card data entered on affected pages during the window as compromised and inform your payment processor.
Rotate Optimizely credentials and tokens and review all account users.
Notify affected customers and regulators as legally required; advise them to watch statements and crypto transactions and to update iOS devices.
US federal agencies must follow CISA's forensic triage requirements.

CVE-2026-132224.caveats: Optimizely has not published the root cause in detail; its full report is in the customer portal and its forensic investigation was still open on 20 Nov. Victim counts differ between researchers (178 organisations per Unit 42, more than 450 domains per Zscaler). Whether iOS exploit kits succeeded on any visitor device is not established in the sources read.

CVE-2026-133275.exploitation_status: Known exploited: CISA added it to KEV on 25 Nov 2026 (deadline 28 Nov, forensic triage required). No attacker named. Mitel's advisory reports no exploitation. No public exploit code found as of 26 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-133275.how_exploited: An arbitrary file upload flaw in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab. The component does not properly check the type of file it accepts, so an unauthenticated attacker who can reach AWV over the network can place files of their choosing on the server. Mitel rates the upload alone as a low integrity impact. It also warns that exploiting the five AWV flaws together can significantly amplify their impact, and two of the others (an XML injection that runs commands and an information leak) depend on content the attacker has staged beforehand.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the MiCollab AWV web component over the network. AWV is the conferencing part of MiCollab and is often published so outside participants can join.
MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier without the KB000129195 patch.
No authentication and no user interaction are needed, and Mitel rates attack complexity low.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: the attacker finds MiCollab servers whose AWV conferencing component can be reached, usually from the internet.
Initial access: without logging in, the attacker uploads files of their choosing through AWV, because the component does not enforce allowed file types.

Staging and chaining: Mitel warns the five AWV flaws amplify each other. Its XML injection flaw (CVE-2026-133303) runs commands using pre-staged content, which an upload could supply. That link is an inference, not a reported finding.
Follow-on: the sources read do not describe what attackers did after access. Treat a compromised MiCollab server as a foothold in the voice and collaboration network.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier that use the AWV conferencing component.
Highest risk: deployments where AWV can be reached from the internet, for example for external meeting participants.
On-premises and hosted MiCollab installations alike, if the AWV component is reachable and unpatched.
detect: Version check: confirm the MiCollab release and whether the KB000129195 patch is installed. 10.3.0.18 or earlier without the patch is vulnerable.
Exposure check: test from outside your network whether the AWV component answers from the internet.
Web server logs for AWV: look for file uploads from addresses that have no authenticated session, especially from unfamiliar internet addresses.

File system: look for new or recently modified files in AWV content and upload locations that no user or administrator meant to create, especially scripts or files that do not match normal conference content.

Process and network behaviour: look for unexpected child processes of the web or conferencing service and for new outbound connections from the MiCollab server, which could mean the upload was chained with a command execution flaw.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules were published in the sources read.

steps: Inventory every MiCollab server, record its release and patch level, and note whether AWV is reachable from the internet.
Before patching an exposed server, preserve evidence as CISA's forensic triage requirements under BOD 26-04 describe: keep web and system logs and take a snapshot or image where possible.
Apply the Mitel patch for 10.3 (10.3.0.18) described in KB000129195, or upgrade to a later MiCollab release. Patch all five AWV flaws in MISA-2026-0012 together.
If you cannot patch at once, restrict external access to the AWV component as Mitel advises until the patch is installed.
Review the server for signs of compromise (see detect) before returning it to normal exposure.
fixed_versions: MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) with the patch described in Mitel KB000129195
Later MiCollab releases (Mitel states the fix will be included in later releases)
workarounds: Restrict external access to the AWV component until the patch is applied (Mitel MISA-2026-0012, with details in the knowledge base article).
verify: Confirm in MiCollab administration that the KB000129195 patch is installed, or that the server runs a release later than 10.3.0.18.
From an external network, confirm that AWV can be reached only as intended, or not at all if you restricted it.
Rescan with your vulnerability scanner and confirm that the MISA-2026-0012 findings are gone.
if_compromised: Isolate the MiCollab server from the internet and from internal networks while keeping evidence: keep logs, the uploaded files and a disk image.

Look for command execution and persistence, such as new accounts, scheduled tasks, unknown services and outbound connections, because the upload may have been chained with the AWV command injection flaws.
Rebuild from known-good media or a clean backup taken before the compromise, then apply the Mitel patch before reconnecting.
Rotate credentials stored on or used by the server: administrator accounts, directory service bind accounts, integration secrets and certificates.
Report to Mitel and your national CERT. US federal agencies must report to CISA under BOD 26-04.

CVE-2026-133275.caveats: Mitel's advisory is the only detailed technical source, and it gives no mechanism beyond insufficient file type checking. No researcher or responder write-up was found. CISA lists the flaw as exploited but names no attacker, timeline or attack chain, and the role of this upload flaw in attacks is not described. Revision 2.0 of Mitel's advisory changed the CVE numbers, so check the identifiers against the CVE record. The 5.3 score understates the risk when chained.

CVE-2026-133303.exploitation_status: Known exploited per CISA KEV (added 25 Nov 2026, due 28 Nov). Mitel MISA-2026-0012 does not state exploitation; Italy CSIRT saw none as of 20 Nov. Attacker not named; no public exploit code reported.
CVE-2026-133303.how_exploited: An XML injection (CWE-91) in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab, caused by insufficient parameter validation. An unauthenticated attacker uses malicious content they have staged on the system beforehand to inject XML, which Mitel says can lead to running arbitrary commands with system-level rights. Mitel says chaining the five AWV flaws in the same advisory greatly increases the impact; the medium-rated unauthenticated file upload flaw (CVE-2026-133275) is one plausible way to stage the content, but Mitel has not confirmed how the flaws are chained.
preconditions: Network access to the MiCollab AWV conferencing component; no authentication or user interaction.
Malicious content already staged on the system (high attack complexity in the CVSS score).
MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier without Mitel's patch; releases past end of support were not assessed by Mitel.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: finding MiCollab servers whose AWV web conferencing portal is reachable, usually from the internet.
Staging: placing attacker content on the server, possibly through another AWV flaw in the same advisory such as the unauthenticated file upload.
Execution: a request that triggers the XML injection makes the server act on the staged content and run commands with system-level rights.
Next steps: no post-exploitation activity has been published; command execution with system rights would allow persistence, credential theft and movement into the voice and internal network.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier with the AWV component enabled.
Highest risk: MiCollab servers whose AWV conferencing portal is published to the internet, which is common for external conferencing.
End-of-support MiCollab releases, which Mitel did not assess and which should be treated as exposed.
detect: Version check: confirm the MiCollab release and whether the patch from Mitel KB000129195 is installed; 10.3.0.18 without the patch is affected.
Web server logs for the AWV component: unauthenticated requests from unknown addresses, especially file uploads followed by unusual conferencing requests.
File system: new or changed files in AWV web and upload directories that nobody on your team placed there.
Process and network behaviour: the web or conferencing service starting shells or other programs, and outbound connections from the MiCollab server to unknown hosts.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules were published in the sources read.

steps: Apply Mitel's patch for MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) as described in KB000129195, or upgrade to a later release that includes the fix; this also fixes the other four AWV flaws.
Until patched, restrict external access to the AWV component, prioritising servers whose conferencing portal is internet-facing.
Check the server for signs of compromise (see detect); US federal agencies must follow CISA's forensic triage requirements under BOD 26-04.
Replace or isolate MiCollab releases that are past end of support.
fixed_versions: Later MiCollab releases, which Mitel says will include the fix
workarounds: Restrict external access to the AWV component if the fix cannot be applied promptly (Mitel MISA-2026-0012).
verify: The patch from KB000129195 shows as installed on MiCollab 10.3.0.18, or the server runs a later release.
From outside your network, the AWV portal is unreachable while a workaround is in place.
if_compromised: Isolate the MiCollab server and preserve its logs and a disk image.
Rebuild from a clean, patched install rather than cleaning in place.
Rotate credentials stored on or used by MiCollab, including directory service accounts and integrations with MiVoice systems.
Look for movement from the MiCollab server into the voice and internal network.
Report to your national CERT; US federal agencies report to CISA.

CVE-2026-133303.caveats: Mitel's advisory is brief and does not say how the flaw is exploited or that it is exploited; the exploitation claim rests on CISA's catalog. No researcher or incident responder write-up was found. 'Pre-staged malicious content' is not explained, and the link to the file upload flaw is an inference. The CVE record also cites an Accenture page on MiCollab exploitation, which could not be found or read. CVE numbers were added to the advisory only in revision 2.0 on 24 Nov 2026.

CVE-2026-133311.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per CISA, which added it to KEV on 25 Nov 2026 (deadline 9 Dec 2026). No attacker or details named; Mitel's advisory (24 Nov) does not mention exploitation. No public exploit code found as of 26 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-133311.how_exploited: Weak or improper authentication (CWE-1390) in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab. An unauthenticated attacker who reaches the AWV service and knows a specific system-generated random identifier, or has pre-staged content on the system, can get past the authentication check for the affected function. The result is read access to sensitive information handled by that function; Mitel says the flaw does not give access to arbitrary files elsewhere on the system and does not affect integrity or availability (CVSS 5.9). Mitel warns that chaining the five AWV flaws in the same advisory, which include a CVSS 10.0 command injection, can greatly amplify the impact.
preconditions: MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) without the patch from Mitel knowledge base article KB000129195, or any earlier release.
The AWV (conferencing) component is reachable by the attacker over the network; Mitel's interim mitigation of restricting external access implies internet-facing AWV portals are the main exposure.
No login and no user action are needed, but the attacker must know a specific system-generated random identifier or rely on pre-staged content, which is why Mitel rates attack complexity as high.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: finding MiCollab servers whose AWV conferencing portal is reachable, typically from the internet.

Prerequisite: obtaining the system-generated identifier or getting content staged on the server; Mitel does not say how attackers do this, and the same advisory lists an unauthenticated file upload flaw (CVE-2026-133275), but Mitel does not confirm that the two are used together.
Initial access: unauthenticated access to the affected AWV function, bypassing its weak authentication check.
Collection: reading the sensitive information exposed by that function, such as conferencing data; the exact data is not described by Mitel.

Follow-on activity: not described by CISA or Mitel. Because the advisory warns the AWV flaws amplify each other, treat any sign of this flaw as a possible step toward the critical command injection flaws in the same component.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier without the KB000129195 patch, on premises or in a hosted deployment.
Most at risk: deployments that publish the AWV audio, web and video conferencing portal to the internet for external participants.
MiCollab releases past end of support were not assessed by Mitel and should be assumed affected until upgraded.
detect: Check the MiCollab release on every server against 10.3.0.18 and confirm the KB000129195 patch is installed; anything older or unpatched is vulnerable.
Inventory which MiCollab servers expose the AWV component to the internet, from the firewall or reverse proxy configuration and an external scan of your own address ranges.

Review web and reverse proxy logs for the AWV portal for unauthenticated requests from unfamiliar addresses that return data, especially repeated or scripted access to conference resources outside meeting times.

Because the advisory says the AWV flaws can be chained, also look for unexpected files written to the server, unexpected processes or outbound connections started by the MiCollab web services, and new accounts or configuration changes.
Mitel, CISA and Italy's CSIRT have published no indicators of compromise or detection rules for this flaw as of 26 Nov 2026; watch Mitel's advisory and KB000129195 for updates.

steps: Identify every MiCollab server and record its release and whether the AWV component is reachable from the internet.
If the patch cannot be applied right away, restrict external access to the AWV component (Mitel's interim mitigation), for example by allowing only trusted networks at the firewall or reverse proxy.
Upgrade to MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and apply the patch in KB000129195, or upgrade to a later release; this fixes all five AWV flaws in MISA-2026-0012 together.
Patch internet-facing servers first, within CISA's federal deadline of 9 Dec 2026.
After patching, review AWV and system logs from before the patch for signs of misuse of this flaw or the related AWV flaws.
fixed_versions: MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) with the patch from KB000129195
workarounds: Restrict external access to the AWV component, according to Mitel; this reduces risk but is not a fix.
verify: Confirm in the MiCollab administration interface that the server runs 10.3.0.18 with the KB000129195 patch applied, or a later release.
Confirm from outside your network that the AWV portal is either patched or no longer reachable from untrusted networks.
Re-run your vulnerability scanner and confirm it no longer flags CVE-2026-133311 or the other MISA-2026-0012 flaws.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected MiCollab server from the internet while keeping it running long enough to preserve evidence.
Preserve web, reverse proxy and system logs and take a disk image or snapshot before making changes.
Assume conferencing data and any credentials or secrets handled by the server were exposed: rotate service passwords, certificates and integration credentials, and reset affected user credentials.
Check for signs of the related AWV flaws (unexpected files, processes or accounts); if any are found, rebuild the server from a trusted image at a fixed release rather than cleaning it.
Report the incident to Mitel Product Support or the Mitel PSIRT and, for US federal agencies and critical infrastructure, to CISA.

CVE-2026-133311.caveats: No researcher or responder write-up found, so the affected function, the identifier and how attackers obtain it are unknown. CISA lists it as exploited without details; Mitel and Italy's CSIRT (20 Nov) reported no exploitation. Earlier coverage uses the internal ID MTLVULN-1863 (CVEs added 24 Nov). CISA does not require BOD 26-04 forensic triage for this CVE.

CVE-2026-133323.exploitation_status: Known exploited: CISA added it to KEV on 25 Nov 2026 (due 28 Nov, forensic triage required). No attacker named. Mitel's advisory is silent on exploitation, and CSIRT Italy reported none as of 20 Nov.
CVE-2026-133323.how_exploited: A blind OS command injection in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab, caused by insufficient sanitisation of request parameters (Mitel MTLVULN-1864, CVSS 10.0). An unauthenticated remote attacker sends specially crafted requests to the AWV web service, and the parameters are passed into an operating system command. This lets the attacker run arbitrary commands in the system context of the MiCollab server, without seeing command output directly (hence blind). Mitel warns that chaining it with the other four AWV flaws in the same advisory, including an XML injection and an unauthenticated file upload, can significantly amplify the impact.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the MiCollab AWV web component over the network. It is often published to the internet so that external participants can join conferences.
No authentication and no user interaction are needed (CVSS PR:N, UI:N).
MiCollab release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier without the patch from Mitel knowledge base article KB000129195.
Products past End of Support are excluded from Mitel's analysis, but they are not stated to be safe.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers find internet-facing MiCollab servers by their AWV conferencing web pages.
Initial access and execution: an unauthenticated crafted request to the AWV component injects operating system commands, which run with system-level privileges on the MiCollab server.

Possible chaining: Mitel says combining this flaw with the related AWV flaws (unauthenticated file upload, XML injection, authentication bypass) can amplify the impact, for example by staging content on the server first.

Follow-on: with command execution on the server, an attacker can plant web shells or other persistence, read configuration and credentials, and move into the internal network. The sources read describe no specific campaign.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier with the AWV conferencing component, whether installed on-premises or as a virtual appliance.
Highest risk: deployments where AWV is reachable from the internet, typically through a MiCollab edge or teleworker gateway, so that external conference participants can join.
Deployments still on older, end-of-support MiCollab releases, which Mitel did not assess and which will not get this patch.
detect: Version check: confirm the MiCollab release and whether the patch from KB000129195 is installed. Treat any 10.3.0.18 or earlier system without it as vulnerable.

Web logs on the MiCollab server and any reverse proxy in front of it: look for unusual or malformed requests to AWV conferencing pages from unknown addresses, especially from 16 Nov 2026 onward, and for bursts of repeated requests.
Process behaviour: child processes started by the AWV or web server service that are shells, downloaders or scripting interpreters, and unexpected outbound connections from the MiCollab server.
File integrity: new or changed files in AWV and web folders, unexpected scheduled tasks or startup entries, and new local accounts.
Network: outbound connections from the MiCollab host to unfamiliar internet addresses, and connections from it to internal systems it normally does not talk to.
Neither Mitel nor CISA had published indicators or detection rules in the sources read.

steps: Find every MiCollab system and check whether its AWV component can be reached from the internet. Exposed systems come first.

Federal agencies, and anyone who wants to follow CISA's model, should do forensic triage before patching an exposed system: collect volatile data and logs first so the patch does not destroy evidence.
Upgrade to MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) if on an earlier release, then apply the patch from Mitel KB000129195. Alternatively, move to a later MiCollab release that includes the fix.
If the patch cannot be applied at once, restrict external access to the AWV component as Mitel advises, for example by allowing only trusted addresses at the firewall or edge gateway.
Apply the fixes for the four other AWV flaws in MISA-2026-0012 at the same time. The same patch covers them.
fixed_versions: MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) with the patch from Mitel KB000129195
Later MiCollab releases, which Mitel says will include the update
workarounds: Restrict external access to the MiCollab AWV component until the patch is applied, as Mitel advises (details in KB000129195).
verify: Confirm in the MiCollab administration interface or the patch records that the KB000129195 patch is installed on every MiCollab server, including standby and lab systems.
From an external network, confirm that AWV is either patched or no longer reachable from untrusted addresses.
Rerun your vulnerability scanner once its vendor has published a check for this CVE.
if_compromised: Isolate the MiCollab server from the network while keeping it powered on, and capture memory, disk images and web and system logs before making changes.
Look for web shells, unknown processes, new accounts, scheduled tasks, and outbound connections. Check connected systems for lateral movement.
Rotate every credential stored on or used by the MiCollab server, including administrator, integration and directory (LDAP or Active Directory) service accounts and certificates.
Rebuild from known-good installation media at the patched release rather than cleaning the system in place, then restore configuration only after checking it.
Report the incident to your national CERT. US federal agencies must report to CISA under BOD 26-04.

CVE-2026-133323.caveats: No technical write-up by researchers or responders was found, so the detail comes from Mitel's brief advisory, CISA and CSIRT Italy, which agree. Mitel's description of this flaw is garbled. CVSS is 10.0 per Mitel and 9.8 per CISA. It is unknown when exploitation began or who is behind it. Older reports cite only MTLVULN-1864, because the CVE numbers were set on 24 Nov. Patch article KB000129195 needs a login and was not read.

CVE-2026-133324.exploitation_status: Known exploited: CISA added it to KEV on 25 Nov 2026 (deadline 28 Nov, forensic triage required). No attacker named. Mitel's advisory reports no exploitation. No public exploit code found as of 26 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-133324.how_exploited: An authentication bypass in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab. CISA's catalog classes it as 'not failing securely', meaning the component lets a request through when an authentication check does not complete as it should. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach AWV can get past its authentication controls and perform actions in the application's context. Mitel rates the direct impact as low integrity, but warns that chaining the five AWV flaws together can significantly amplify their impact.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the MiCollab AWV web component over the network. AWV is often published to the internet for outside meeting participants.
MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier without the KB000129195 patch.
No authentication and no user interaction are needed, and Mitel rates attack complexity low.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: the attacker finds MiCollab servers whose AWV component can be reached.
Initial access: the attacker gets past AWV authentication without valid credentials and gets access to functions meant for authenticated users.

Chaining: with authentication out of the way, the attacker can combine this with the other AWV flaws in MISA-2026-0012 (file upload, XML injection, data leak, blind command injection), which Mitel says greatly amplifies impact.

Follow-on: the sources read do not describe what attackers did after access. A compromised MiCollab server is a foothold in the unified communications environment and may hold directory and integration credentials.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) or earlier that use the AWV conferencing component.
Highest risk: deployments where AWV can be reached from the internet.
On-premises and hosted MiCollab installations alike, if AWV is reachable and unpatched.
detect: Version check: confirm the MiCollab release and whether the KB000129195 patch is installed. 10.3.0.18 or earlier without the patch is vulnerable.

AWV and web server logs: look for requests that reach functions normally needing a login but have no matching successful login, and for administrative or conference changes made from unfamiliar internet addresses.
Application audit: review AWV conferences, users and settings for entries or changes that no administrator made.

Server behaviour: look for new files in AWV locations, unexpected child processes of the web or conferencing service and new outbound connections. These would suggest the bypass was chained with the upload or command injection flaws.
No indicators of compromise or detection rules were published in the sources read.

steps: Inventory every MiCollab server, record its release and patch level, and note whether AWV is reachable from the internet.

Before patching an exposed server, preserve evidence as CISA's forensic triage requirements under BOD 26-04 describe: keep web, application and system logs and take a snapshot or image where possible.
Apply the Mitel patch for 10.3 (10.3.0.18) described in KB000129195, or upgrade to a later MiCollab release. Patch all five AWV flaws in MISA-2026-0012 together.
If you cannot patch at once, restrict external access to the AWV component as Mitel advises until the patch is installed.
Review the server for signs of compromise (see detect) before returning it to normal exposure.
fixed_versions: MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) with the patch described in Mitel KB000129195
Later MiCollab releases (Mitel states the fix will be included in later releases)
workarounds: Restrict external access to the AWV component until the patch is applied (Mitel MISA-2026-0012, with details in the knowledge base article).
verify: Confirm in MiCollab administration that the KB000129195 patch is installed, or that the server runs a release later than 10.3.0.18.
From an external network, confirm that AWV can be reached only as intended, or not at all if you restricted it.
Rescan with your vulnerability scanner and confirm that the MISA-2026-0012 findings are gone.
if_compromised: Isolate the MiCollab server while keeping evidence: keep logs and a disk image.
Look for command execution and persistence, such as new accounts, unknown files, scheduled tasks, services and outbound connections, because the bypass may have been chained with the other AWV flaws.
Rebuild from known-good media or a clean backup taken before the compromise, then apply the Mitel patch before reconnecting.
Rotate credentials stored on or used by the server: administrator accounts, directory service bind accounts, integration secrets and certificates.
Report to Mitel and your national CERT. US federal agencies must report to CISA under BOD 26-04.

CVE-2026-133324.caveats: Mitel's advisory is the only detailed technical source, and it does not explain how the bypass works or which actions it unlocks. No researcher or responder write-up was found. CISA lists the flaw as exploited but names no attacker, timeline or chain. Revision 2.0 of Mitel's advisory changed the CVE numbers, so check the identifiers against the CVE record. The CVSS score (5.3) understates the risk when the flaw is chained with the critical AWV flaws.

CVE-2026-133335.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per the CVE record (Joomla CNA, 25 Nov 2026), with no date, scale or attacker given. The vendor does not mention exploitation; not in CISA KEV as of 25 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-133335.how_exploited: An unauthenticated local file inclusion in the main controller of the VirtueMart shop extension for Joomla. When the requested controller was not found, the component fell back to loading a controller file whose name came from the request without filtering, so a visitor with no account could use path traversal to make the site load arbitrary PHP files already on the server. Whether this becomes remote code execution depends on what is installed on the host: the CVE record notes that a standard PHP helper script, if present, can be abused to run code, which gives the attacker code execution as the web server user and control of the shop.
preconditions: The Joomla site is reachable by the attacker (normally the public shop); no login or user interaction is needed.
VirtueMart 4.0.0 to 4.8.7 is installed and enabled.

For code execution rather than file loading only, the server must hold a suitable PHP file the attacker can reach through the inclusion; the vendor says it can be misused if the server has the right programs installed.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers identify Joomla sites running VirtueMart, which exposes its component on public shop pages.
Initial access: an anonymous request makes the controller fallback load a local PHP file chosen by the attacker.
Execution: on servers with a suitable helper script present, the inclusion is turned into running attacker code as the web server account.

Persistence and follow-on: the sources read give no campaign details; typical outcomes for this class are planted PHP files (web shells), new administrator accounts, and theft of customer, order and database credential data from the Joomla configuration.
who_is_exposed: Joomla web shops running VirtueMart 4.0.0 through 4.8.7, typically self-hosted or on shared hosting.
Hosts with PHP extras such as the PEAR package tooling installed are at higher risk of code execution.
VirtueMart 3 sites are not covered by the CVE record; the vendor offers only a partial hotfix for older versions, so treat them as at risk.
detect: Version check: in the Joomla administrator, confirm the installed VirtueMart version is 4.8.8 or later; a site fixed by hotfix keeps its old version number, so also check for the vendor's patcher component in the extension list.
Web server access logs: anonymous requests to the VirtueMart component whose controller parameter contains directory traversal sequences or names of files outside the component.
File system: PHP files you do not recognise in the web root, temporary, cache, media and image folders, especially files created since early November 2026.
Joomla users: administrator or super user accounts your team did not create, and unexpected changes to extensions or templates.
Host: the PHP or web server process starting shells or making outbound connections to unfamiliar hosts.
No indicators of compromise have been published by the CVE record or the vendor.

steps: Take a full backup of the site files and database before changing anything.
Update VirtueMart to 4.8.10, the current release, which contains the 4.8.8 fix for this flaw and a later fix for a fake paid order flaw; 4.8.8 is the minimum fixed version.
If a full update is not possible at once, install the vendor's hotfix for your version line (separate hotfixes exist for 4.6 and later and for older versions).
Check the site for signs of compromise (see detect) even after updating, because the update does not remove anything already planted.
Remove unneeded PHP tooling from production web hosts to reduce the chance that file inclusion flaws lead to code execution.
Plan to move VirtueMart 3 sites to a supported VirtueMart 4 or 5 release, as the CVE does not cover them.
fixed_versions: VirtueMart 4.8.10 recommended by the vendor as the current security release
workarounds: Vendor hotfix packages for VirtueMart 4.6 and later and for versions older than 4.6, offered on the vendor's 4.8.10 security announcement, if a full update cannot be made immediately.
verify: Joomla extension manager shows VirtueMart 4.8.8 or later (4.8.10 recommended).
If the hotfix was used, confirm the vendor patcher component is installed and enabled, since the version number does not change.
Clear any full-page cache and confirm the shop still works, including payment plugins.
if_compromised: Put the shop into maintenance mode or take it offline, and preserve web server logs, the site files and a database dump for investigation.
Remove unknown PHP files and unknown administrator accounts, or better, restore from a backup taken before the compromise and then update.
Rotate the database password, Joomla administrator passwords, hosting and FTP or SSH credentials, and payment provider API keys stored in the site.
Check orders and customer data for theft or tampering, and follow your payment card and data protection breach obligations.
Report the incident to your hosting provider and national CERT.

CVE-2026-133335.caveats: Exploitation rests only on the CVE record; the vendor, CISA and others give no confirmation or indicators. The vendor's 4.8.8 note lists only minor fixes; the RCE fix is confirmed in its 4.8.10 post and the CVE record. Code execution depends on which PHP files the server holds. The record's CISA ADP entry says no exploitation, contradicting its own text.

CVE-2026-133469.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Vates VSA-2026-062 (10 Nov 2026) says a threat actor, unnamed, is actively exploiting it. In CISA KEV since 25 Nov 2026 (due 28 Nov). No public exploit code reported.
CVE-2026-133469.how_exploited: An authentication bypass caused by missing type checks in the Xen Orchestra REST API. An unauthenticated attacker sends a login cookie crafted so that it is parsed as an empty object instead of a text token; the token lookup then treats it as a query with no filter and returns the first stored token, so the attacker is logged in as that token's owner, often an administrator. The attacker then reads reusable login tokens from an authenticated route and, with admin rights in Xen Orchestra, can run code on managed pools and take over XCP-ng hosts as root.
preconditions: Network access to the Xen Orchestra web or REST interface; no credentials or user interaction are needed.
At least one unexpired login token stored in Xen Orchestra (normal for an instance in use).
Xen Orchestra before 6.9.2, or 6.10.0 before 6.10.1, including the Xen Orchestra Appliance; xo-server before 5.211.2, or 5.213.0 before 5.213.1.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker reaches an exposed Xen Orchestra instance and authenticates with a crafted empty-object cookie, inheriting another user's session.
Credential access: the attacker lists reusable login tokens through the REST API, which keeps access working after the bug is fixed unless tokens are revoked.
Execution and lateral movement: with admin rights the attacker controls managed pools; Vates lists a VM named pivot2 and VMs whose serial console is redirected to a file as indicators.
Persistence on hosts: Vates lists a dynamic linker preload library, hidden files in the root user's home and cron jobs with a specific naming pattern on XCP-ng hosts.
Impact: full takeover of XCP-ng hosts as root; Vates says theft of credentials and configuration (pool secrets, backup remote credentials) cannot be ruled out.
who_is_exposed: Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance on releases before 6.9.2 (stable channel) and 6.10.1 (latest channel), and source installs not updated to the latest master branch.
Instances reachable from the internet are at highest risk; instances on shared internal networks are reachable by anyone on those networks.
The XCP-ng and XenServer pools, hosts, VMs and backup targets managed by an affected Xen Orchestra.
detect: Version check: compare the Xen Orchestra and xo-server versions against 6.9.2 / 5.211.2 (stable) and 6.10.1 / 5.213.1 (latest).
Xen Orchestra writes no authentication log entry for this bypass, so look in reverse proxy, WAF or web access logs for login cookies carrying an empty JSON object (Vates describes the pattern).

On XCP-ng hosts, use the checks in the Vates advisory: VMs with file-based serial output, XenServer log entries for the pivot VM, unexpected preload library files, hidden files in the root home directory and unfamiliar cron files.
Review Xen Orchestra for VMs, users, tokens or pool changes nobody on your team made, and for connections from Tor or the attacker addresses listed in the advisory.
Vates notes that finding none of these indicators does not prove the system is clean.

steps: Update Xen Orchestra to 6.9.2 or later (stable) or 6.10.1 or later (latest); source installs should update to the latest master branch.
Take Xen Orchestra off the internet and place it on a dedicated management network.
Block the attacker IP address and onion service listed in the Vates advisory, and Tor traffic, at the network edge.
Revoke existing login tokens so that tokens stolen before the update stop working.
Check Xen Orchestra and every managed XCP-ng host for the indicators in the advisory; federal agencies must also follow CISA's forensic triage requirements under BOD 26-04.
workarounds: Keep Xen Orchestra off the internet on a dedicated management network (Vates).
Block the listed attacker infrastructure, including Tor (Vates).
A WAF or reverse proxy rule blocking the empty-object cookie pattern; Vates warns simple pattern rules can be bypassed, so this is not a substitute for updating.
verify: The Xen Orchestra about page or package version shows 6.9.2, 6.10.1 or later and xo-server 5.211.2, 5.213.1 or later.
Old login tokens no longer authenticate after revocation.
Host checks from the Vates advisory come back clean on every managed XCP-ng host.
if_compromised: Isolate Xen Orchestra and the affected hosts from untrusted networks and preserve logs, proxy logs and disk images before cleaning.
Rotate every password and secret the platform used: Xen Orchestra accounts and tokens, pool credentials, backup remote credentials and any stored keys.
Vates recommends a full reinstallation of affected systems, because cleanup alone may not remove backdoors.
Check guest VMs and backup targets reachable from the compromised hosts for follow-on access.
Report to your national CERT; US federal agencies report to CISA.

CVE-2026-133469.caveats: The vendor advisory does not name the threat actor or give a timeline of attacks. BleepingComputer lists fixed releases as 6.9.1 and 6.10.0, but the Vates advisory and the CVE record say 6.9.2 and 6.10.1; this analysis follows the vendor. The advisory was published before the CVE was assigned and does not list the CVE number; the CVE record and CISA's entry link the CVE to VSA-2026-062. A news report mentions a separate advisory, VSA-2026-063, about VM import abuse, which was not read.

CVE-2026-133968.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild as a zero-day (CISA KEV, added 23 Nov 2026). Amazon: a Chinese-nexus actor (moderate confidence) used Cairn AI agents on 8 to 10 Sep 2026 to gain root on servers at two East Asian universities.
CVE-2026-133968.how_exploited: A path traversal flaw (CWE-24) in the MONAI Label server's datastore API. CISA says an unauthenticated remote attacker can write files outside the intended datastore folder. Amazon, as reported by BleepingComputer, says the attackers used this to plant a file that the Python runtime loads automatically at start-up, then called another part of the API so that the file ran, giving them code execution as root on the server.
preconditions: The MONAI Label server API is reachable by the attacker over the network (CVSS AV:N); in the observed attacks the servers were reachable from the internet.
No authentication and no user interaction are needed (CISA: unauthenticated remote attacker; CVSS PR:N/UI:N).
MONAI Label (the monailabel Python package) older than 0.8.6.
Impact is highest where the server process runs with administrative (root) rights, as in the reported compromise.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: AI agents scanned target address ranges given by the operator and mapped the MONAI Label server's API; Amazon says it took 11 minutes from mapping the API to exploitation.
Initial access: the attacker abused the path traversal in the datastore API to write a file outside the datastore folder.
Execution: the planted file was one the Python runtime runs automatically; the attacker then triggered an API function that started Python, gaining a root shell.
Lateral movement: the operator gave the agents a network proxy into a second university running the same software, reused the flaw there, and directed the agents at other machines on that network.
Other attempts in the same campaign (a Log4Shell attempt against a Redis server and over 30,000 password guesses against a GPU server) failed, per Amazon.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running MONAI Label servers older than 0.8.6, typically hospitals, research groups and universities doing medical image annotation and AI model training.
Servers whose MONAI Label API is reachable from the internet or from untrusted networks are at greatest risk; the reported victims were universities.
Self-hosted deployments on workstations, GPU servers and cloud virtual machines alike; the flaw is in the software, not a hosted service.
detect: Version check: list installed Python packages on every server and workstation running MONAI Label and flag monailabel versions below 0.8.6.

File integrity: look for unexpected files recently created or changed in the Python installation and site-packages folders used by MONAI Label, and anywhere outside the configured datastore folder written by the MONAI Label process.
Web and application logs: review MONAI Label server logs for datastore upload requests from unfamiliar addresses, especially from 8 Sep 2026 onwards, and for bursts of API enumeration.
Process behaviour: shells or network tools started as children of the MONAI Label or Python service process, or new outbound connections from the server.
Network: compare traffic logs against the campaign addresses published by Amazon Threat Intelligence in its Cairn report (do not rely on them alone; the actor can change infrastructure).
Use CISA's BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements, which CISA lists as mandatory for this KEV entry, to structure the review.

steps: Find every MONAI Label installation, including researcher workstations and GPU servers outside central IT.
Remove internet exposure of the MONAI Label API at once: place it behind a VPN or firewall rule that allows only known users until patched.
Upgrade the monailabel package to version 0.8.6 or later and restart the server.
Run the MONAI Label service as an unprivileged user rather than root to limit the damage of any future flaw.

Check each server that was reachable before patching for signs of compromise (see detect) and perform CISA's BOD 26-04 forensic triage; if MONAI Label cannot be patched or isolated, CISA says to discontinue use.
fixed_versions: monailabel 0.8.6 (NVD: versions before 0.8.6 are affected; maintainers released the security update on 18 Nov 2026 per BleepingComputer)
workarounds: CISA: apply vendor mitigations; if none are available, discontinue use of the product. Assess each asset's internet exposure.
No vendor workaround could be read for this analysis; restricting network access to the API is a general precaution, not a vendor-stated fix.
verify: Confirm the installed monailabel package version is 0.8.6 or later in every Python environment used to run the server, not just the system default.
Confirm the MONAI Label API is no longer reachable from the internet with an external port check against your own address ranges.
Confirm the service restarted after the upgrade and runs under a non-root account.
if_compromised: Disconnect the server from the network while keeping it powered on, and preserve memory, disk images and MONAI Label and system logs.
Treat the host as fully compromised at root level: rebuild it from a clean image rather than cleaning it.
Rotate every credential, key and token stored on or used from the server, including cloud keys, storage credentials and SSH keys.
Check other machines reachable from the server for lateral movement, as the actor moved into further hosts.
Review whether patient or research imaging data on the server was accessed and follow data-protection notification duties.
Report the incident to your national CERT (in the US, CISA); federal agencies must follow BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements.

CVE-2026-133968.caveats: The maintainers' GitHub advisory and fix pull request could not be read (HTTP 403) and Amazon's blog did not load, so this relies on CISA, NVD and news reports of Amazon's research. Fixed version 0.8.6 is from NVD. Attribution is moderate confidence; victims and full post-exploitation activity are undisclosed.

CVE-2026-134624.exploitation_status: CISA KEV lists it as exploited (added 23 Nov 2026). N-able found it investigating a breach of one hosted Mail Assure server from about 16 Nov 2026 but has not said it was the way in. Attackers are unnamed.
CVE-2026-134624.how_exploited: A server-side request forgery flaw (CWE-918) in the connection check Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronisation when a relay is configured. The check did not restrict where it connected, so an authenticated API user with high privileges could make the email-filtering server connect to internal hosts and ports of their choice, learn which were reachable, and send crafted data to internal services. This gives an attacker a way to probe and attack systems inside the provider's network that are not exposed to the internet.
preconditions: An authenticated account with high-level API access to Mail Assure or SpamExperts (CVSS 4.0 PR:H); a stolen partner or admin API credential would meet this.
Network access to the Mail Assure/SpamExperts API (CVSS AV:N).
A Mail Assure/SpamExperts build earlier than 20261121.1943.
attack_path: Initial access: the attacker obtains or uses a privileged API account on the Mail Assure/SpamExperts platform (how they got access in the real incident has not been disclosed).
Discovery: the attacker uses the LDAP synchronisation connection check to make the server connect to internal addresses and ports and map what responds.
Exploitation of internal services: the attacker sends crafted data through the same check to internal services not reachable from outside.
Observed incident: N-able says an unauthorised party accessed one hosted web server, likely reached some credentials stored there, and N-able took it offline; root cause analysis is pending.
who_is_exposed: N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud: N-able has already patched the hosted platform; partners were affected by the outage and credential revocation.
SpamExperts Local Cloud operators running the software on their own hardware, who must confirm they run build 20261121.1943 or later.
Managed service providers and their customers whose integrations and scripts used Mail Assure API or OAuth tokens, which N-able revoked.
detect: Version check (Local Cloud): confirm the installed build is 20261121.1943 or later.
Mail Assure/SpamExperts audit logs: review changes to relay and LDAP synchronisation settings and repeated LDAP connection checks, especially ones pointing at internal or unusual hosts and ports.
API logs: look for use of privileged API accounts from unfamiliar addresses or at unusual times around and before 16 Nov 2026.
Network (Local Cloud): outbound connections from the filtering servers to internal addresses or ports they normally never contact.
N-able has published no indicators of compromise or detection rules as of 24 Nov 2026; watch for its root cause analysis, promised within about two weeks of 22 Nov 2026.

steps: Hosted Cloud partners: no install is needed; N-able patched the platform. Follow the environment-specific guidance N-able emailed you, and contact N-able support if you did not receive it.
Re-issue credentials for scripts and integrations that used the revoked API or OAuth tokens, and reset local user passwords that N-able reset.
Local Cloud operators: upgrade to build 20261121.1943 or later.
Review which accounts hold high-level API access and remove any that are not needed; require strong, unique credentials for the rest.
Federal agencies: perform CISA's BOD 26-04 forensic triage, which CISA lists as required for this entry, and follow its cloud-service guidance.
fixed_versions: Mail Assure / SpamExperts build 20261121.1943 (versions before 20261121.1943 are affected)
workarounds: CISA: apply vendor mitigations; for cloud services follow BOD 26-04 cloud guidance, or discontinue use if mitigations are unavailable. Assess each asset's internet exposure.
No vendor workaround was found in the pages read.
verify: Local Cloud: confirm the running build number reported by the product is 20261121.1943 or later on every node.
Hosted Cloud: confirm the dashboard and API work with newly issued tokens and that old tokens are rejected.
Confirm all integrations were moved to new credentials and no old API keys remain in scripts or password vaults.
if_compromised: Isolate affected Local Cloud servers from the internal network and preserve their logs and disk images.
Rotate every credential the filtering platform stores or uses, including LDAP bind accounts, relay credentials, API keys and OAuth tokens.
Check internal systems reachable from the filtering servers for unexpected access, since the flaw lets attackers reach internal services.
Rebuild compromised servers from known-good images and reapply the fixed build.
Report to N-able support and to your national CERT (in the US, CISA); notify customers if their data or credentials may be affected.

CVE-2026-134624.caveats: N-able's security advisory page could not be read (it loads only with a script-driven portal), so technical details come from N-able's incident update blog, CISA's KEV entry, the NVD record and SecurityWeek and The Hacker News reports of the advisory. N-able has not said whether this SSRF was the entry point for the breach, how attackers got the privileged access it needs, or which internal services were reached. The root cause analysis is pending.
