CVE-2026-136716.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per Drupal SA-CORE-2026-019 (25 Nov 2026), which also reports exploit code; confirmed by Canadian Cyber Centre AV26-1209 and HKCERT (26 Nov). No attacker named.
CVE-2026-136716.how_exploited: This is an access-control flaw in the Drupal core installer, the script used only once to set up a new site. The fix for the earlier installer flaw CVE-2026-132165 (SA-CORE-2026-017, 18 Nov 2026) left some sites exposed, namely those in an unusual or incomplete installation state, including some production sites. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the installer can use it to get past the site's normal access controls and take over the site. Drupal rates the result as full loss of confidentiality and integrity of site data. In practice the attacker gains control of the site, including the main administrator account (user 1).
preconditions: The site runs a vulnerable Drupal core release: 10.x before 10.6.23, 11.0.0 to 11.3.22, or 11.4.0 to 11.4.13. End-of-life branches have no fix.
The core installer can be reached over the network. Drupal says sites that have secured the installer are not vulnerable.
The site is in an unusual or incomplete installation state. Drupal says this state is not visible in the admin interface and that only uncommon configurations are exploitable.
No authentication or user interaction is needed. Drupal rates the attack complexity as basic.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: the attacker looks for internet-facing Drupal sites where the installer still responds.
Initial access: the attacker sends unauthenticated requests to the installer on a site in the vulnerable state, bypassing access checks.

Takeover: the attacker gains administrative control of the site. Drupal points defenders to unexpected changes to or by user 1, such as a changed email address or password, which would let the attacker keep control.

Follow-on: with administrator rights the attacker can read or change all site data. The sources read do not describe specific post-compromise activity or campaigns. Drupal warns that a compromised site may no longer look vulnerable.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted and hosted Drupal 10 and 11 sites below the fixed releases where the installer is reachable from the internet, in production or staging.
Sites that patched for SA-CORE-2026-017 but left the installer reachable. Drupal says these may already be compromised.
Sites left half-installed or in an incomplete install state, which Drupal says should never be reachable from the internet.
Sites on end-of-life branches (Drupal 11.2.x and older, 10.5.x and older, Drupal 8 and 9), which get no fix and must move to a supported branch.
Sites protected by Drupal Steward's recommended mitigations are, per Drupal, protected from known attack vectors but should still upgrade.
detect: Version check: record the Drupal core version of every site and compare it with 10.6.23, 11.3.23 and 11.4.14.

Installer exposure: from outside your network, confirm that a request to the installer gets a forbidden or not-found response, as described in Drupal's guide to securing the installer. A normal success response means the installer is reachable.
Web server access logs: look for requests to the installer from external addresses since 18 Nov 2026, and keep those logs before routine rotation deletes them (Brandefense).
Drupal watchdog and audit logs: look for unauthorized logins and for changes to or by user 1, especially changes to its email address, password or roles.
Account review: confirm that the user 1 email address is one your organisation controls, and look for new administrator accounts or role changes you cannot explain.
Do not rely on the admin interface alone. Drupal says the vulnerable state is not shown there, so review log and account history as well as versions.

steps: Inventory every Drupal site (production, staging and development) with its core version and whether the installer is reachable, and keep the web and Drupal logs.
Block remote access to the installer at the web server level, following Drupal's guide to securing the installer. Make sure the database update script stays reachable for administrators.
Update Drupal core to the fixed release for your branch: 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23. Sites on end-of-life branches should move to a supported branch.

Run the database updates (through the update script or Drush) on every site. Drupal says an update hook must run to fix production sites already in the vulnerable state, so deploying the new code alone is not enough.
Check that the user 1 email address belongs to you and consider resetting the user 1 password.
Review logs for unauthorized access and changes to user 1 since 18 Nov 2026, and treat any findings as a compromise.
fixed_versions: No fix for end-of-life Drupal 11.2.x and below, 10.5.x and below, Drupal 9 or Drupal 8
workarounds: Secure the installer so it cannot be reached remotely, following Drupal's guide. Drupal says sites that have done this are not vulnerable. The guide recommends a web server rule, combined if possible with removing the installer file after each deployment.
Drupal Steward's recommended mitigations protect against known attack vectors, but Drupal still advises upgrading.
verify: Confirm the reported Drupal core version is 10.6.23, 11.3.23, 11.4.14 or later on each site.
Confirm the database updates ran: the status report shows no pending updates, and your deployment logs show the run completed.
From outside your network, confirm that the installer returns forbidden or not found, including through the alternative addresses the guide lists, and that the site and the update script still work.
Recheck the user 1 email address and the list of administrator accounts after patching.
if_compromised: Take the site offline or restrict it to administrators. Keep web server logs, Drupal logs, the database and the site files as evidence.
Follow Drupal's guide 'Your Drupal site got hacked. Now what?'
Restore from a backup made before the compromise, or rebuild onto a patched release, and check site code and files for anything planted.
Reset all administrator passwords and take back control of user 1. Rotate the database credentials, the site hash salt, API keys and any other secrets in the site configuration.
Report the incident to your national CERT and notify affected users if personal data may have been exposed.

CVE-2026-136716.caveats: Drupal gives few technical details: which install states are exploitable and what attackers did after takeover are not public, and no researcher or responder write-up was found. Brandefense is a playbook drawn from the advisory. Cybersixt returned 403 and was not read. No CISA KEV entry on file.

CVE-2026-18128.exploitation_status: No exploitation and no public exploit code reported for this flaw as of 13 Nov 2026 (NCSC-NL, Ivanti via Rescana). The public proof of concept NCSC-NL reports is for the companion flaw CVE-2026-121653.
CVE-2026-18128.how_exploited: A clear-text transmission flaw (CWE-319) in the Ivanti Endpoint Manager Agent. The agent sends sensitive information over unencrypted HTTP, so an attacker who can sit between an agent and its server (a man-in-the-middle position) can read that traffic and change it in transit. This affects the confidentiality and integrity of agent communication; no authentication is needed beyond that network position.
preconditions: The attacker can intercept traffic between a managed device's agent and the Endpoint Manager server, for example on a shared, wireless or compromised network segment.
Agents from Ivanti Endpoint Manager 2024 SU7 or earlier (all versions before 2024 SU8).
No credentials or user interaction needed once the network position is held (CVSS 6.8).
attack_path: Positioning: the attacker gains a network position on the path between agents and the Endpoint Manager server.
Collection: the attacker reads sensitive information the agent sends in clear text.
Tampering: the attacker alters agent traffic in transit, which NCSC-NL says affects integrity; the practical effect depends on what the altered messages control.
who_is_exposed: Organisations with Ivanti Endpoint Manager agents older than 2024 SU8.
Laptops and devices that talk to the Endpoint Manager server across untrusted networks (home, hotel or public Wi-Fi) or through internet-facing gateways carry the most risk.
detect: Version check: confirm agents and the Core server are on 2024 SU8 or later.
Network monitoring: unencrypted HTTP traffic between agents and the Endpoint Manager server, and ARP or DNS spoofing alerts on segments where agents run.
Endpoint Manager records: unexpected changes in agent inventory or results that do not match the device's real state.
No indicators of compromise have been published by Ivanti or NCSC-NL.

steps: Update Ivanti Endpoint Manager to 2024 SU8 or later and roll the updated agent out to all managed devices; the same release fixes the critical CVE-2026-121653, so in practice do this now.
Until agents are updated, keep agent-to-server traffic on trusted networks or inside an encrypted tunnel such as the corporate VPN (general hardening, not a vendor workaround).
fixed_versions: Ivanti Endpoint Manager 2024 SU8 (2024 SU7 and earlier affected)
verify: Confirm the Core server and agent versions in the Endpoint Manager console report 2024 SU8 or later across the fleet.
Spot-check network captures to confirm agent traffic to the server is no longer sent in clear text.
if_compromised: Identify the network segment where interception happened and remove the attacker's foothold there.
Rotate any credentials or secrets that agents sent in clear text.
Check affected devices for changes that tampered agent traffic could have caused, and report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-18128.caveats: Ivanti's advisory page did not render for an automated reader; this rests on NCSC-NL advisory NCSC-2026-0493 and summaries quoting Ivanti. Which sensitive information the agent sends in clear text, and what an attacker could change by altering it, is not described publicly. No vendor workaround was seen.

CVE-2026-19703.exploitation_status: No exploitation reported as of 19 Nov 2026: MS-ISAC (10 Nov) says SonicWall has not reported exploitation; not in CISA's KEV catalog and no public exploit code reported.
CVE-2026-19703.how_exploited: Weak password hashing on SonicOS virtual appliances (NSv); SonicWall's CVE record files it under hard-coded credentials (CWE-798). An attacker who already has local access with high privileges could recover a platform credential, which gives access to a limited subset of platform settings. It is not a remote entry point; Malwarebytes' Sav Wheeler (via CSO) calls it most useful to an attacker who already has a foothold.
preconditions: SonicOS virtual appliance (NSv) on Gen7 7.3.3-7015 or earlier or Gen8 8.2.2-8015 or earlier.
The attacker already has local access to the appliance with high privileges (CVSS 5.1, local vector).
No user interaction needed.
attack_path: Prior compromise or insider access gives the attacker local access to the virtual appliance.
Credential access: the attacker recovers a platform credential protected only by weak hashing.
Impact: access to a limited subset of platform settings; high confidentiality, low integrity impact per CVSS.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running SonicWall NSv virtual firewalls on affected builds; hardware firewalls are not named for this flaw.
Hypervisor or cloud administrators and anyone else who can reach the appliance locally.
detect: Check each NSv appliance's SonicOS build against the affected ranges.
Review access to the hypervisor or cloud console hosting the NSv and to the appliance's local consoles.
Review appliance audit logs for setting changes no administrator made.
No indicators or detection rules have been published.

steps: Upgrade NSv virtual appliances to the fixed SonicOS build named in SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0014, in the same update as the higher-risk flaws in that advisory.
Restrict who can reach the appliance locally, including hypervisor and cloud console access.
Rotate administrative and local passwords on the appliance after upgrading.
fixed_versions: SonicOS Gen7 NSv: 7.3.4-7013 or later (as reported by ITPro; confirm in SNWLID-2026-0014)
SonicOS Gen8 NSv: 8.2.3-8015 or later (as reported by ITPro; confirm in SNWLID-2026-0014)
verify: Confirm on each NSv that the SonicOS build is at or above the fixed version.
Confirm hypervisor and console access is limited to named administrators.
if_compromised: Treat the appliance and its hosting platform as compromised: preserve logs and a snapshot, then investigate how local access was gained.
Rebuild or restore the NSv from a known-good configuration on a fixed build and rotate all credentials it holds.
Report to SonicWall support and your national CERT.

CVE-2026-19703.caveats: SonicWall's PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 is a script-only page that could not be read automatically; this rests on MS-ISAC, SonicWall's own CVE record text and news reports. Fixed versions come from ITPro only; the Canadian Cyber Centre gives a different Gen8 boundary for a sibling flaw. SonicWall has not named the credential or the settings it reaches. News reports give CVSS 5.2; the CNA vector on NVD scores 5.1.

CVE-2026-19868.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild per CISA (KEV, 6 Nov 2026); SonicWall says it investigated a report of potential exploitation. No attacker, attack details or indicators have been published.
CVE-2026-19868.how_exploited: An authentication enforcement flaw (CWE-308, single-factor authentication) in the SonicOS SSLVPN service. When SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins, a user who holds valid credentials for an alternate authentication method can log in without going through SAML, and so may skip MFA that the identity provider enforces. The attacker gains a VPN session into the internal network with only a stolen or guessed password.
preconditions: SAML authentication is enabled for SSLVPN logins on the firewall.
The attacker has valid credentials for an alternate authentication method accepted by the firewall; it is not an unauthenticated flaw.
The SSLVPN service is reachable, normally from the internet.
Gen7 (7.3.3-7015 and older) or Gen8 (8.2.2-8015 and older) hardware or NSv firewalls.
attack_path: Credential access: obtain a user's password for a non-SAML login method, for example by phishing, reuse or earlier breaches.
Initial access: log in to the SSLVPN with that password, bypassing SAML and any MFA enforced through the identity provider.
Next steps are not published; earlier SonicWall SSLVPN MFA bypasses were followed by ransomware intrusions (Help Net Security cites Akira activity in 2025).
who_is_exposed: SonicWall Gen7 and Gen8 firewalls, physical and NSv, that use SAML for SSLVPN logins and run affected firmware.
Organisations relying on their identity provider's MFA as the main protection for VPN access.
Gen6 firewalls are not listed as affected but are end of support; SonicWall advises moving to Gen8.
detect: Compare successful SSLVPN logins on the firewall with identity-provider sign-in logs; a VPN session for a SAML user with no matching IdP sign-in and MFA check is suspect (Help Net Security).
Firewall logs: SSLVPN logins using a non-SAML authentication method for accounts that should only use SAML.
VPN sessions from unusual countries, hosting providers or at unusual times, and internal scanning from VPN address pools.
Firmware check: confirm each firewall's SonicOS version against the fixed builds; no vendor indicators or detection rules exist yet.

steps: Upgrade SonicOS on every affected Gen7 and Gen8 firewall to the fixed build; CISA's federal deadline is 20 Nov 2026.
Review SSLVPN authentication settings so accounts meant for SAML cannot also log in by another method.
Hunt for VPN logins without a matching identity-provider sign-in since before the patch, and reset credentials for those accounts.
Plan replacement of end-of-support Gen6 devices, as SonicWall advises.
fixed_versions: SonicOS Gen7 7.3.4-7013 and higher (as reported from SonicWall's advisory)
SonicOS Gen8 8.2.3-8015 and higher (as reported from SonicWall's advisory)
verify: Confirm each firewall shows a fixed SonicOS build after reboot.
Test that a SAML-only account cannot complete an SSLVPN login without the identity provider and MFA.
if_compromised: End active VPN sessions for affected accounts, reset their passwords and re-enrol MFA.
Preserve firewall and VPN logs, then review what the sessions reached on the internal network.
Look for follow-on activity such as new accounts, remote access tools or data staging, and report the incident.

CVE-2026-19868.caveats: SonicWall's own advisory page did not load for an automated reader; facts come from the CVE record SonicWall published, MS-ISAC and CISA, and fixed builds from Help Net Security's reading of the advisory. NVD data lists 7.3.4-7015 as the Gen7 bound, which differs. SonicWall scores it 7.1, CISA 7.5. Attack details are unknown.

CVE-2026-20320.exploitation_status: In CISA KEV since 10 Nov 2026 (deadline 24 Nov). Malbear Labs (8 Nov) reports a Chinese-speaking operator used it against a European telecom; CISA has not confirmed that. Cisco says it has no direct evidence of exploitation.
CVE-2026-20320.how_exploited: An out-of-band blind XML external entity (XXE) flaw in the Open Client Interface XML parser of Cisco BroadWorks, which resolves external entities by default. An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted XML message to the OCI-Provisioning (OCI-P) service; the parser follows the external references and the attacker can read files from the server with the privileges of the BroadWorks user, including configuration. In the case Malbear Labs describes, this exposed the platform's system identity private key, SSL credentials and other private keys, which let the attacker impersonate the server to other platform components.
preconditions: The OCI-P provisioning service of a BroadWorks server is reachable by the attacker (Malbear Labs reports TCP port 2208); no authentication or user interaction is needed.
The server runs a BroadWorks release earlier than RI.2026.07; Cisco says configuration does not matter.
Affected products: Application Delivery Platform, Application Server, Profile Server and Xtended Services Platform.
attack_path: Initial access: crafted XML to the OCI-P service on an internet-reachable Xtended Services Platform; files including private keys and keystore credentials were read (Malbear Labs).
Credential access: keystore passwords were reused against other administration interfaces, such as a Cisco Expressway-C admin page.
Lateral movement: further old flaws (JBoss AS 6, Liferay) and a BladeLogic agent gave SYSTEM-level access on Windows hosts; a domain controller credential database was dumped and passwords cracked.
Persistence and control: webshells, tunnels and a Sliver command-and-control beacon; PowerShell scripts, WMI subscriptions and scheduled tasks on Windows.
Impact: the operator mapped and reached 13 organisations hosted by the telecom, including a healthcare database protected only by default credentials.
who_is_exposed: Service providers running Cisco BroadWorks Application Delivery Platform, Application Server, Profile Server or Xtended Services Platform below RI.2026.07.
Deployments where the OCI-P provisioning interface is reachable from the internet or from untrusted networks.
Customers and tenants hosted on a compromised provider's infrastructure, whose credentials or data may be reachable from it.
detect: Compare each BroadWorks server's release with Cisco's Fixed Releases table; Cisco gives no command for this, so use your release records.
Review OCI-P service logs and packet captures for inbound XML that declares external entities or a document type, and for messages from unexpected sources.
Look for outbound connections from BroadWorks hosts to unfamiliar internet addresses, which blind XXE uses to pull data out.

Hunt for the follow-on activity Malbear Labs describes: clusters of PowerShell scripts in Windows temp folders with a watchdog process, JSP webshells, and internal HTTP connections carrying raw TCP tunnels.
Check the four infrastructure indicators (Sliver C2 domain, SSH endpoint, staging server, operator machine) listed in the Malbear Labs Operation Snowball report.

steps: Upgrade every affected BroadWorks component to RI.2026.07; Cisco says there is no workaround.
Until upgraded, restrict the OCI-P provisioning interface to trusted management networks only.
Because private keys and keystore passwords may have been read, rotate the system identity key, SSL certificates and keystore passwords on any server that was reachable before the fix.
Restrict BladeLogic RSCD agents to their application servers and retire or isolate end-of-life JBoss AS 6, as Malbear Labs advises.
Federal civilian agencies: remediate by 24 Nov 2026 under the KEV listing and BOD 26-04.
fixed_versions: Application Delivery Platform: RI.2026.07 (Cisco's table also prints RI.2026.071 as the first-affected boundary; confirm with Cisco)
verify: Confirm every BroadWorks node reports release RI.2026.07 or later in your release records or platform administration tools.
Confirm the OCI-P interface is not reachable from the internet with an external port check from outside your network.
if_compromised: Isolate affected BroadWorks hosts and preserve OCI-P logs, network captures and file access records.
Treat all private keys, certificates and passwords stored on the server as stolen: revoke and reissue them, and change any reused passwords on other systems.
Hunt across Windows hosts and tenants reachable from the platform for webshells, tunnels, scheduled tasks and WMI persistence, and reset domain credentials if a domain controller was touched.
Notify hosted customers whose systems may have been reached and report to your national CERT or CISA.

CVE-2026-20320.caveats: Cisco's advisory briefly said exploitation was known (v1.1, 12 Nov) then withdrew it (v1.2, 13 Nov: no direct evidence). The attack chain comes only from Malbear Labs, based on the attacker's exposed working files; the telecom is unnamed and has not confirmed it, and the Chinese-speaking attribution is the firm's assessment. CISA has not said who exploits it.

CVE-2026-21589.exploitation_status: Exploited: Previdian saw attempts on honeypots from 6 Oct 2026, hours after watchTowr's write-up and checker (Help Net Security, 7 Oct). Atlassian saw none on 5 Oct. CISA added it to KEV on 15 Oct 2026.
CVE-2026-21589.how_exploited: An unauthenticated file read in a web resource library shared by Atlassian's self-managed Data Center products. According to watchTowr, a quirk in the routing code turns certain characters into path separators, which slips past the checks meant to stop directory traversal, so a crafted web request to a plugin resource route returns files from the application's web root. The attacker must know the exact file name and path; directories cannot be listed. watchTowr showed it could read protected configuration files, and that Crowd stores the application's credentials in plain text in one such file; with them an attacker can query Crowd, create users and add them to administrator groups, gaining admin rights in connected Jira, Confluence or Bitbucket.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the web interface of a self-managed Data Center or Server instance; no account and no user interaction are needed.
The instance runs a version before the fixed releases Atlassian lists (Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, Fisheye).
The attacker knows the exact name and path of a file worth reading; the flaw cannot list directories.
The severe escalation watchTowr described needs a readable file holding secrets, such as Crowd's application credentials in a Crowd-integrated setup.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attackers scan for internet-facing Atlassian Data Center login pages; Previdian logged attempts from many addresses in several countries within hours of the technical write-up.
Initial access: an unauthenticated web request to a plugin resource route uses the path-separator quirk to read a known configuration file from the web application folder.
Credential theft: configuration files can expose secrets; in Crowd deployments the application credentials are stored in plain text (watchTowr).

Privilege escalation: with Crowd application credentials the attacker lists users, creates an account and adds it to an administrator group, gaining admin access to connected Jira, Confluence or Bitbucket.
Follow-on: with admin access an attacker can read or change project data and repositories; specific post-exploitation activity has not been published in the sources read.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running self-managed Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo or Crowd Data Center, or Crucible and Fisheye, below the fixed releases.
Internet-facing instances first, and above all Crowd deployments or products connected to Crowd for single sign-on.
Atlassian Cloud customers are not affected: Atlassian patched Cloud and says no action is needed.
detect: Version check: compare each instance's version with Atlassian's fixed-version table in the advisory.

Web access logs: Atlassian's advisory gives patterns to search for; URL-decode request lines (up to two passes) and look for traversal-style requests to plugin resource routes, especially ones that returned success.

Crowd audit logs and the user directory: look for unexpected new users, group membership changes (such as additions to jira-administrators or other admin groups) and Crowd application API use from unfamiliar addresses.
Atlassian product audit logs: new administrators, changed authentication settings or unusual admin sessions after early October 2026.

Network: requests from scanning addresses to Atlassian web interfaces; watchTowr published a checker that defenders can use to test their own instances (link via its GitHub page, named in Help Net Security).

steps: Inventory every self-managed Atlassian instance (Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira, Jira Service Management, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, Fisheye) and its version.
Upgrade each to the fixed release for its line; Atlassian no longer ships binary patches, fixes are in maintenance releases.
Until upgraded, remove the instance from the internet or restrict external access, as Atlassian advises.
If an upgrade must wait, apply one of Atlassian's temporary filtering rules from the advisory and test it after a backup.
Review access logs for the patterns Atlassian lists; if any match, treat secrets in readable configuration files as exposed and rotate them, starting with Crowd application credentials.
US federal agencies: follow CISA's BOD 26-04 guidance and forensics triage requirements named in the KEV entry.
workarounds: Take the instance off the internet, or restrict external access, until it is patched (Atlassian).
A web application firewall or reverse proxy rule using the filtering Atlassian publishes in the advisory (all affected products).
A Tomcat rewrite rule for Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo and Crowd, or a URL rewrite rule for Bitbucket, as described in the advisory; back up first and test afterwards.
verify: Confirm each instance reports a version at or above the fixed release for its line.
Run your scanner or watchTowr's published checker against your own instance from outside to confirm it no longer returns files.
If a temporary rule is in place, confirm with Atlassian's test steps that it blocks the traversal patterns and that the product still works.
if_compromised: Restrict access to the instance and preserve web access logs, Crowd and product audit logs before changing anything.
Rotate every secret held in readable configuration files: Crowd application passwords, database credentials and integration tokens.
Remove accounts and group memberships the attacker added, and review all administrator accounts in Crowd and connected products.
Review repositories, pages and build plans for unauthorised changes; rebuild from a known-good state if admin access was used.
Engage your security team and Atlassian support, and report to your national CERT (US federal agencies to CISA).

CVE-2026-21589.caveats: watchTowr's own write-up and CISA's catalog page were not read: the technical detail comes from Help Net Security's summary of watchTowr, and the KEV listing from CyberView's copy of the catalog feed. Atlassian's advisory said it had no evidence of exploitation at publication; exploitation reports are honeypot attempts, not confirmed intrusions. BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek blocked automated reading.

CVE-2026-40217.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Zenity Labs honeypots logged attempts from 15 Apr to 24 May 2026, starting the day the fix shipped. X41 D-Sec built a proof of concept (Feb 2026). In CISA KEV since 18 Nov 2026.
CVE-2026-40217.how_exploited: Sandbox escape (CISA lists it as an unprotected alternate channel; the vendor as CWE-913) in the LiteLLM proxy's custom-code guardrail test endpoint, which runs administrator-supplied Python inside a home-made sandbox. That sandbox relied on keyword filtering of the source text, which an attacker defeats by rebuilding blocked names at run time or rewriting bytecode. An attacker holding the proxy master key or an admin credential submits guardrail code to the test endpoint and gets arbitrary code execution in the proxy process, which runs as root in the default Docker image.
preconditions: The LiteLLM proxy's management API, including the guardrail test endpoint, is reachable by the attacker.
The attacker holds the master key or a proxy-admin credential; Zenity saw attackers guess default and documented example master keys left unchanged.
Affected release: the vendor lists 1.81.8 up to but not including 1.83.10; X41 tested the main-latest Docker image of early 2026.
Obsidian Security showed that in older releases a low-privilege internal user could first reach admin through CVE-2026-47101 and CVE-2026-47102.
attack_path: Initial access: requests to the guardrail test endpoint cycling through default-style master keys (Zenity counted about 47 distinct values), plus requests with empty authorization.
Capability check: a harmless guardrail that only returns a marker, to learn whether the key works and the endpoint runs code (about 520 such probes on the first day).
Execution: hand-written guardrail code that escapes the keyword filter, reaches Python's import machinery and the operating system, with background processes to outlast the endpoint's short timeout.
Credential theft: reading the proxy's environment to collect LLM provider API keys, the master key, cloud credentials and database connection strings.
Follow-on risk (Obsidian): with admin rights an attacker can also register malicious guardrails, callbacks or MCP servers that persist and run on every request.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted LiteLLM proxy (AI gateway) deployments on releases before the fix, especially with the admin API on the internet.
Deployments still using a default or example master key, or sharing the master key widely.
Containers built from the default Docker image, which runs the proxy as root.
Python environments with the litellm package used as a proxy server; Red Hat ships errata for affected products.
detect: Proxy or reverse-proxy access logs: any POST to the custom-code guardrail test endpoint from outside the admin network; Zenity says it should never face the internet.
Authentication logs: bursts of failed requests rotating through default-looking master keys, or requests with empty authorization headers.

Request bodies (if logged): guardrail code that only returns a marker value, builds names from string pieces, touches generator or coroutine internals, dumps the environment or starts shell subprocesses.
Process telemetry: the LiteLLM Python process spawning shells or long-lived child processes, and outbound connections from the proxy to unknown hosts.
Configuration review: guardrails, callbacks, MCP server entries or admin accounts you did not create; compare against Zenity's published source addresses (do not treat no match as clean).

steps: Upgrade LiteLLM: the vendor advisory names 1.83.10 as first fixed and 1.83.11 as the sandbox replacement; Obsidian advises 1.83.14-stable or later, which also fixes the linked privilege flaws.
Rotate the master key to a long, unique value and limit who holds it and the proxy-admin role.
Move the management API and admin interface off the internet behind a firewall, VPN or private network.
Run the proxy container as an unprivileged user instead of root.
Review all registered custom-code guardrails, callbacks and MCP servers and remove any you did not create.
fixed_versions: litellm 1.83.10 per the advisory's patched field (advisory text says the fix landed in 1.83.11)
litellm 1.83.14-stable or later for the full fix set including CVE-2026-47101 and CVE-2026-47102 (Obsidian Security)
workarounds: Block the custom-code guardrail test endpoint at the reverse proxy or API gateway (vendor advisory and X41).
Restrict the management interface to trusted networks and the master key to the fewest people (X41).
verify: Confirm the running proxy reports version 1.83.11 or later (1.83.14-stable or later preferred) in every container and replica.
From an outside network, confirm the guardrail test endpoint and admin API are not reachable.
Confirm the default or example master key is rejected and the container user is not root.
if_compromised: Isolate the proxy and preserve container images, logs and the database before rebuilding.
Rotate every secret the proxy could read: LLM provider API keys, master and virtual keys, cloud credentials, database passwords and MCP tokens.
Rebuild the container from a clean, fixed image and compare configuration, callbacks and guardrails against a known-good copy.
Review provider billing and usage for abuse of stolen keys, and report the incident as your obligations require.

CVE-2026-40217.caveats: The vendor advisory rates this Moderate (CVSS 4 score 5.9) while the CVE record and Red Hat give 8.8; it is inconsistent on 1.83.10 versus 1.83.11 as the first fix. Zenity's observations come from honeypots; how many real deployments were breached is not known. CISA has not published attack details.

CVE-2026-41709.exploitation_status: Known exploited: CrowdStrike says China-nexus Warp Panda used it as a zero-day against US organisations incl. law firms, as late as early 2026; CISA added it to KEV on 28 Oct 2026 (due 11 Nov).
CVE-2026-41709.how_exploited: An insufficient logging flaw (CWE-778) in VMware ESX. Someone who already has administrator access to an ESX host can carry out certain operations without them being recorded in the host's logs (Broadcom, CISA). It gives no access by itself; its value to an attacker is hiding what they do on a hypervisor they have already taken over. Warp Panda used it to greatly reduce the audit trail of its activity on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has not said which operations go unlogged.
preconditions: The attacker already holds administrator access to the ESX host, for example through stolen credentials or a separate vulnerability.
ESX 8.0 before 8.0 U3j (build ESXi80U3j-25429389), 9.0 before 9.0.2.0100, or other builds listed in VMSA-2026-0006 as unfixed.
No workaround exists, so any unpatched host on an affected release is exposed once an administrator account is compromised.
attack_path: Initial access (Warp Panda): exploitation of internet-facing edge devices such as Ivanti and F5 BIG-IP appliances (CrowdStrike via CSA).
Lateral movement: pivot to vCenter with valid credentials or known vCenter flaws, then to ESXi hosts as administrator.
Defence evasion: this flaw is used so selected administrative operations on ESXi leave no log record; the group also cleared logs and changed file timestamps.
Persistence: BRICKSTORM backdoor and Go implants, one on ESXi posing as a legitimate service and one inside guest VMs talking to the host over VSOCK.
Actions on objective: hidden, unregistered VMs, cloned domain controllers and data taken from guest snapshots.
who_is_exposed: Organisations running VMware ESX 8.0 or 9.0 hosts not updated to the VMSA-2026-0006 builds, including VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud Platform deployments.
ESX 7.0 hosts: do not assume a fix exists for this CVE; plan an upgrade path and compensating monitoring (CSA).
Sectors Warp Panda targets, notably US legal-sector and other organisations with valuable virtualised infrastructure.
detect: Version check: compare every ESX host's build with the fixed builds in VMSA-2026-0006.
Forward ESXi and vCenter logs off-host in real time to a store hypervisor administrators cannot change; keep at least 13 months.
Because host logs can be incomplete, correlate them with network flows to ESXi management interfaces, vCenter task and event history and guest-side EDR.
Reconcile registered VMs against what exists on hosts and datastores to find hidden or unregistered VMs and unexplained snapshots or clones.
Look for listeners on unusual ports on ESXi hosts and unexpected VSOCK traffic; alert on SSH logins by root and vpxuser.
Use the YARA and Sigma content for BRICKSTORM in the joint CISA, NSA and CCCS report AR25-338A by reference.

steps: Apply the ESX builds from Broadcom VMSA-2026-0006 (check the current revision of the advisory); there is no workaround.
Patch the critical vCenter flaws in the same advisory (CVE-2026-59309, CVE-2026-59310), which attackers also exploit to reach hypervisors.
Forward ESXi and vCenter logs to an off-host store administrators cannot alter.
Harden hosts: disable SSH where feasible, restrict vpxuser shell access on ESX 8.0 and later, enforce execInstalledOnly, and require MFA for vCenter.
Segment management networks, limit outbound traffic from ESXi and vCenter, and reduce the number of privileged accounts.
fixed_versions: Telco Cloud Platform 5.0.x and 5.1.x: see Broadcom KB449886
verify: Confirm each host's build number in vCenter or the host client matches or exceeds the fixed build.
Confirm ESXi logs arrive at the off-host collector and test that administrative actions appear there.
if_compromised: Do not treat clean ESXi logs as proof of a clean host; reopen investigations closed on that basis and test against evidence the flaw could not suppress.
Preserve host, vCenter, datastore and network evidence before rebuilding.
Rebuild compromised ESXi hosts from trusted media on fixed builds and check vCenter for implants.
Rotate vCenter, ESXi root and service account credentials, and treat cloned domain controllers as a full Active Directory compromise.
Report to your national CERT; US agencies follow CISA's BOD 26-04 requirements.

CVE-2026-41709.caveats: Broadcom and CrowdStrike have not published which operations escape logging, and when exploitation began is not public. Attribution to Warp Panda rests on CrowdStrike; CISA confirms only that exploitation occurred. CrowdStrike's own report was not read; its findings come via SecurityWeek and the Cloud Security Alliance note. The low CVSS score understates the risk.

sources.name: Broadcom VMSA-2026-0006 (notification 38017)
CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (JSON feed)
SecurityWeek: Chinese hackers used low-severity ESXi logging flaw as zero-day
Cloud Security Alliance research note: Warp Panda ESX logging zero-day

CVE-2026-46300.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: CISA added it to KEV on 28 Oct 2026 on evidence of active exploitation and says it is chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to run commands as root. Public exploit code since May 2026. No actor named.
CVE-2026-46300.how_exploited: Missing initialization (a lost shared-fragment marker) in the Linux kernel's XFRM ESP-in-TCP code, nicknamed Fragnesia and a variant of Dirty Frag. When socket buffers are merged, the marker telling IPsec ESP not to decrypt in place can be dropped, so decryption writes over page-cache-backed file data. A local unprivileged user can thereby change bytes in the cached copy of read-only files, such as a privileged program, without touching the disk, and gain root. Researchers say the technique is deterministic, with no race to win.
preconditions: Local code execution as any unprivileged user, for example a shell, a container workload, a CI job or a web shell planted through another flaw.
A kernel without the fix (kernels released before the 13 May 2026 patch); see fixed versions.
The ESP (esp4, esp6) modules can be loaded; the public technique also creates unprivileged user and network namespaces to get network admin rights inside them (Qualys).
Distributions that restrict unprivileged user namespaces partly block the public exploit, but should still patch.
attack_path: Initial access: attackers first get code running as a normal user; in the case CISA flagged, through the PHP2Shell flaws in PHP, which plant a PHP web shell.
Privilege escalation: the attacker uses this flaw to alter the cached copy of a privileged program and runs it to become root.

Execution as root: Dream Security reported a campaign that gained root on 25 servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, then focused on three servers in a US government-affiliated environment (BleepingComputer).
Follow-on: the same report found target lists, exploitation logs and about 40 custom post-exploitation scripts.
Container risk: Ubuntu says the flaw may allow container escape, since containers share the host's page cache.
who_is_exposed: Shared Linux hosts, container clusters, CI runners and build farms, and multi-tenant services that run other people's code are most at risk (Help Net Security).
Internet-facing web servers whose application flaws give attackers a low-privileged foothold, such as PHP servers open to PHP2Shell.
Red Hat Enterprise Linux, OpenShift, Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE, AlmaLinux, CloudLinux, Amazon Linux and other distributions until their kernel update is installed.
Single-user workstations and single-tenant servers are less exposed but still affected.
detect: Check the running kernel version against your distribution's advisory; a kernel package installed but not booted does not protect you.
Look for unexpected loading of the esp4, esp6 or rxrpc modules on hosts that do not use IPsec.
Watch for unprivileged processes creating user and network namespaces, and for root shells or root processes whose parent is a web server or other service account.
On web servers, hunt for PHP web shells and web server processes spawning shells, the entry seen with PHP2Shell.
The file change lives only in the page cache and the on-disk file is untouched, so disk-based integrity checks will not show it; rely on process, log and module evidence instead.
Qualys customers can find vulnerable hosts with the detection Qualys names for this CVE.

steps: Install your distribution's fixed kernel and reboot into it.
On internet-facing PHP servers, also patch the PHP2Shell flaws, which CISA says are chained with this one.

Until a host can be patched, unload and block the esp4, esp6 and rxrpc modules where IPsec is not used, then drop the page cache so files reload from disk (vendor guidance cited by Qualys and Help Net Security).
Where possible, restrict unprivileged user namespaces, which partly blocks the public exploit.
Prioritise shared, multi-tenant and container hosts and CI runners.
fixed_versions: Upstream stable kernels 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33 and 7.0.10 or later (per NVD ranges on file)
Red Hat: see bulletin RHSB-2026-003 and the errata for your release
workarounds: Unload and block the esp4, esp6 and rxrpc kernel modules, then clear the page cache (Qualys, Help Net Security citing CloudLinux); this breaks IPsec ESP and AFS-related networking that depends on them.
Red Hat publishes a mitigation procedure in security bulletin RHSB-2026-003.
verify: The running kernel version, not just the installed package, matches or exceeds the fixed version from your distribution.
If you used the workaround, the esp4, esp6 and rxrpc modules are not loaded and cannot be loaded.
if_compromised: Treat a host where root was gained as fully compromised: isolate it and preserve memory and logs before rebooting, since the page-cache change disappears on reboot.
Rebuild from known-good media rather than trusting a reboot; anything done as root, such as new accounts, keys or services, persists.
Rotate credentials, SSH keys and secrets stored on or reachable from the host, and check other hosts in the same cluster.
On web servers, remove web shells, patch the entry flaw and review web logs for the initial access.
Federal agencies: follow CISA's BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements and report the incident.

CVE-2026-46300.caveats: The kernel commits on file could not be read (git.kernel.org refused the reader), so the flaw mechanism comes from Ubuntu's and Red Hat's pages and research reports. CISA did not publish details of the attacks; the campaign details come from Dream Security as reported by BleepingComputer. Sources credit the finder, William Bowling, to Zellic or V12. Fixed upstream versions are from the NVD ranges on file.

CVE-2026-48356.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Sansec (which named it PolyShell) saw probing from 16 Mar 2026 and mass scanning from about 19 Mar. CISA added it to KEV on 27 Oct 2026. Adobe's July bulletin said it knew of no exploits. No actor named.
CVE-2026-48356.how_exploited: Unrestricted upload of a dangerous file type (CWE-434) in the Magento REST API. Cart item custom-option handling does not check that a submitted option exists or is a file option, and does not block dangerous extensions; the only check is an image header test. An unauthenticated attacker uploads a file that is both a valid image and a script, and where the web server runs scripts in that upload folder, it becomes a web shell giving code execution on the store.
preconditions: Adobe Commerce, Commerce B2B or Magento Open Source on an affected release (for example 2.4.8-p5 and earlier, or 2.4.9 without the July 2026 fix).
The store's REST API is reachable from the internet; no account is needed (the GraphQL path is not affected, per Sansec).
Code execution needs the web server to hand script files in the upload folder to the PHP handler (some stock nginx setups and older Apache setups do); otherwise the file still lands on disk.
attack_path: Initial access: an anonymous REST API cart request carries a disguised script as a custom-option file upload.
Execution: the attacker calls the uploaded file, a PHP web shell with cookie-based authentication, to run code and commands (Sansec).
Persistence: a secondary backdoor is copied across many directories so that copies survive cleanup; one report describes admin accounts and a GSocket backdoor added.
Impact: obfuscated JavaScript card skimmers are injected into CMS pages and blocks and cached in shoppers' browser storage.
who_is_exposed: Self-hosted and agency-hosted Magento Open Source and Adobe Commerce stores on affected versions with the REST API exposed.
Magento Open Source 2.4.5 and earlier: out of support and no patch, so these must upgrade.
Stores whose web server executes scripts in the media upload folder are at risk of code execution; others still hold the dropped file.
detect: Check the custom-options upload folder under the media directory for any script-type files, and search the whole document root for the secondary backdoor Sansec describes.
Search CMS pages and static blocks for injected or obfuscated script and for the malicious domains Sansec lists.
Compare against Sansec's published indicators (IP addresses, domains, hashes) in its PolyShell research; link, do not copy, them.
Review web server logs for anonymous REST cart requests with file uploads, followed by requests to files in the upload folder.
Check the admin user list for accounts nobody created, and scan the store with a Magento malware scanner.

steps: Apply Adobe's APSB26-73 fix: move to the July 2026 build of your release line, or 2.4.9 with the fix, per the bulletin.
Upgrade unsupported Magento Open Source 2.4.5 and earlier to a supported, fixed release.
Configure the web server to refuse script execution and direct access in the media upload folders before any PHP handler runs.
Put a web application firewall rule in front of the REST API that blocks file uploads in cart custom options until patched (Sansec).
Hunt for web shells, backdoors and skimmers even after patching, since patching does not remove them.
fixed_versions: Adobe Commerce: July 2026 builds per APSB26-73, e.g. 2.4.9-2026-jul
Adobe Commerce B2B: July 2026 builds, e.g. 1.5.3-2026-jul
Magento Open Source 2.4.6 to 2.4.9: July 2026 builds per APSB26-73
workarounds: Sansec: block the vulnerable REST API calls with a web application firewall and make sure the web server denies access and script execution in the upload directory; blocking web access alone does not stop uploads.
verify: Confirm the installed version or patch level matches a fixed build in APSB26-73.
Confirm that requests for script files in the media upload folder are refused by the web server.
Rescan the store and confirm no scripts remain in upload folders and no injected script in CMS content.
if_compromised: Take a full copy of files, database and logs before cleaning.
Remove web shells, all copies of the backdoor and injected CMS scripts, and check cron jobs and admin accounts for persistence.
Rotate admin passwords, API integration keys, payment and database credentials and the store's encryption key settings as appropriate.
If skimming is found, notify your payment provider and follow card-data breach rules; report to your national CERT.

CVE-2026-48356.caveats: Adobe's bulletin said no exploits were known at release; exploitation evidence comes from Sansec and CISA. The share of stores attacked is Sansec's own measurement. Adobe gives no workaround or detection guidance; those come from Sansec. CVSS is 9.6 in Adobe's bulletin and 9.3 at NVD.

sources.name: Adobe security bulletin APSB26-73
CISA: two known exploited vulnerabilities added (27 Oct 2026)
Sansec: Magento PolyShell research

CVE-2026-76418.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026 (advisory 28 Oct 2026); CISA added it to KEV on 29 Oct 2026, due 1 Nov. No actor has been named and no public exploit code is reported.
CVE-2026-76418.how_exploited: A denial-of-service flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco ASA and FTD software. Cisco attributes it to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group; CISA describes it as an unchecked return value leading to a NULL pointer dereference. An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted request to the VPN login service, before any successful login, and the device reloads unexpectedly. Repeating the attack can keep the firewall and its VPN down; Cisco describes availability impact only, not code execution or data access.
preconditions: The device runs an affected ASA or FTD release and the SSL VPN (WebVPN) login service is enabled on at least one interface, usually the internet-facing one.
Secondary authentication (a secondary authentication server group) is configured on at least one tunnel group, including the built-in DefaultWEBVPNGroup.
Hiding the tunnel group list from the login page does not remove the exposure, because the default group still reaches the affected code.
No credentials or user interaction are needed; a successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path.
attack_path: Reconnaissance: attacker finds internet-reachable ASA or FTD SSL VPN login portals.
Exploitation: one or more crafted requests to the VPN login service trigger the fault before authentication completes.
Impact: the firewall reloads, dropping VPN sessions and traffic through the device until it comes back up.
Follow-on: repeated requests can prolong the outage; Cisco and CISA have not described persistence, data theft or the actors behind the attacks.
who_is_exposed: On-premises and virtual Cisco Secure Firewall ASA deployments offering AnyConnect or Secure Client SSL remote access VPN with secondary authentication.
Cisco Secure FTD devices whose remote access VPN policy (managed in FMC or FDM) enables secondary authentication.
Not affected, per Cisco: Cloud-delivered Firewall, cdFMC, Secure Access and Secure FMC Software.
detect: Version check: compare the running ASA or FTD release with Cisco fixed releases, or use the Cisco Software Checker linked from the advisory.

Configuration check: review the running config for WebVPN enabled on an interface and secondary authentication set on any tunnel group, including DefaultWEBVPNGroup; on FTD review the deployed remote access VPN policy in FMC or FDM.
Unexpected reloads: look for unplanned firewall reboots, crash information files and failover events, and correlate them with traffic to the SSL VPN portal from unfamiliar sources.
Cisco has published no indicators of compromise or log signatures for this flaw; treat repeated unexplained reloads of an exposed VPN headend as possible exploitation and open a TAC case.

steps: Identify every ASA and FTD device with SSL VPN enabled and secondary authentication configured on any tunnel group.
Upgrade those devices to a fixed release listed in Cisco advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75; Cisco strongly recommends upgrading over mitigation.
If you cannot upgrade at once, apply the temporary mitigation Cisco describes (below), accepting its trade-offs, and schedule the upgrade.
After upgrading, remove any temporary mitigation that weakened authentication and confirm VPN access works as designed.
Federal agencies: follow CISA BOD 26-04 and its forensic triage guidance for KEV entries.
workarounds: Cisco says there is no workaround, only a temporary mitigation.
If DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication: disable the tunnel group list in WebVPN settings; users must then know their connection profile name.
If DefaultWEBVPNGroup uses secondary authentication: remove secondary authentication from it and from other tunnel groups; this lowers the security of the VPN.
verify: Confirm the device reports a fixed release for its train (ASA or FTD) after reload.
Re-run the Cisco Software Checker for the device and release to confirm the advisory no longer applies.
Watch for further unexplained reloads over the following days.
if_compromised: Treat repeated unexplained reloads of an exposed VPN headend as an attack: capture crash information and syslog before rebooting again and open a Cisco TAC case.
Upgrade or apply the mitigation immediately, and consider restricting the VPN portal to known source ranges while you do.
Because ASA and FTD VPN devices have been targeted by other campaigns, review the device for unexpected configuration changes and report the incident to your national CERT (CISA in the US).

CVE-2026-76418.caveats: Cisco and CISA give only a high-level description and no indicators of compromise; who is exploiting it, since when and at what scale is not public. The two sources name the flaw class differently (logic error versus NULL pointer dereference). No independent technical write-up was found that could be read.

sources.name: Cisco advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75
CISA: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog (29 Oct 2026)
CSA Singapore alert AL-2026-159
The Hacker News: Cisco patches actively exploited ASA flaw

CVE-2026-76466.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: in CISA KEV since 20 Nov 2026 (due 23 Nov). F6 (via SecurityWeek, 19 Nov 2026) saw it used against a Russian organization soon after a public PoC; no group named. Cisco's advisory still reports no known misuse.
CVE-2026-76466.how_exploited: A flaw in the database service that Cisco Expressway uses to keep cluster nodes in sync. Cisco says it comes from persistent cookies and from client certificates not being validated when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering; CISA catalogs it as use of hard-coded credentials (CWE-798). An unauthenticated remote attacker who holds those cookies and can reach the database service on a clustered device can call specific remote procedure call commands on it. That lets them run operating system commands as root, giving full control of the Expressway node and a foothold to reach the other cluster nodes and the internal network behind them.
preconditions: Cisco Expressway-C or Expressway-E (virtual or appliance) running X15.5.3 or earlier, or X14 or earlier.
The devices are configured in a cluster; Cisco says the flaw affects clustered devices.
The attacker can reach the clustering database service over the network; F6 advises blocking TCP ports 4371 and 4372 except from trusted cluster nodes, which indicates these are the exposed ports.
No authentication or user interaction is needed.
attack_path: Initial access: in the case F6 investigated, attackers exploited two internet-facing Expressway X15.5.3 devices through the clustering database service, soon after a proof-of-concept was published.
Execution: the flaw gave them operating system commands as root on those nodes.
Spread inside the cluster: from one compromised node they reached two further cluster nodes on the organization's internal network.

Staging: with root they placed custom Python tools to scan the network, find SMB shares, use SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab; F6 says the scripts were edited during the attack and their comments suggest an AI assistant helped write them.
Objective: theft of credentials and other sensitive data from the internal network.
who_is_exposed: Organizations running Expressway clusters on X15.5.3 or earlier, or on X14 or earlier, on appliances or virtual machines.

Highest risk: Expressway-E (Edge) nodes in the DMZ, which are internet-facing by design for remote access and business-to-business calling, where the cluster ports can be reached from untrusted networks.
Internal Expressway-C (Core) nodes in the same cluster, which can be reached from a compromised Edge node, as F6 observed.
Standalone, non-clustered Expressway devices fall outside the conditions Cisco names.
detect: Version check: list every Expressway-C and Expressway-E, its release and whether it is clustered; any clustered node on X15.5.3 or earlier, or X14 or earlier, is vulnerable.
Erlang system log on each node: F6 says an unexpected node connection entry there is a key sign of successful exploitation; look for connections from anything other than your own cluster peers.
Firewall and flow logs: connections to the cluster ports (TCP 4371 and 4372) from addresses that are not cluster members, especially from the internet.
Devices: unexpected Python scripts or tools staged on the file system.
Internal network: scanning, SMB enumeration, SQL Server, WinRM and GitLab access coming from Expressway addresses.
Indicators (IP addresses, the log entry and the staging location) are published by F6 in its press release on the exploitation; Cisco's advisory gives none.

steps: Upgrade every clustered Expressway node to X15.5.20 or later; nodes on X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release.

Until all nodes are upgraded, restrict the cluster ports (TCP 4371 and 4372) at the firewall so only the cluster's own node addresses can reach them, as F6 recommends; Cisco itself lists no workaround.

Check each node for signs of compromise before and after upgrading, because the flaw was exploited before CISA's listing; US federal agencies must also follow CISA's forensic triage requirements under BOD 26-04.
Review the Expressway cluster design so Edge nodes never expose clustering services to the internet.
fixed_versions: X15.5.3 and earlier: first fixed release X15.5.20
X14 and earlier: migrate to a fixed release
workarounds: Cisco states there are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

F6 (as reported by SecurityWeek) recommends blocking TCP ports 4371 to 4372 at the firewall except from trusted cluster node addresses if patching cannot be done at once; this is a researcher's mitigation, not Cisco's.
verify: Confirm every node in each cluster reports X15.5.20 or a later fixed release.
Test from outside the cluster that the cluster ports cannot be reached from the internet or from untrusted internal networks.
Recheck the Erlang system log after the upgrade for node connections from unknown peers.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected nodes from the internet and the internal network.
Preserve logs (Erlang system log, system and firewall logs) and a disk image before rebuilding.
Rebuild compromised nodes from a clean fixed release rather than only upgrading, since attackers held root.
Rotate credentials and certificates held on the Expressway nodes, and any credentials that may have been reachable from them, including SQL Server, WinRM, SMB and GitLab accounts.
Investigate the internal network for lateral movement from the Expressway addresses, and report the incident to your national CERT (US federal agencies: CISA).

CVE-2026-76466.caveats: Cisco's advisory (21 Oct 2026, unrevised) gives no exploitation details or indicators. The attack account is F6's as reported by SecurityWeek and Security Affairs; F6's page refused automated reading (403). The ports come from F6, not Cisco. Cisco blames persistent cookies and weak client certificate checks, CISA calls it hard-coded credentials; how attackers get the cookies is not explained. One victim reported; scale unknown.

CVE-2026-76519.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: Cisco PSIRT learned of active exploitation in October 2026 and published on 14 Oct 2026; CISA added it to KEV the same day (due 17 Oct). No attacker named by Cisco or a government.
CVE-2026-76519.how_exploited: A relative path traversal flaw (CWE-23) in the Advanced Malware Protection File Reputation handling of Cisco Secure Email Gateway. An unauthenticated remote attacker only has to send an email carrying a crafted attachment through an affected gateway; while the attachment is processed, its content can be written to arbitrary locations on the underlying operating system. Cisco says a successful exploit lets the attacker write arbitrary files and run commands as root, giving full control of the mail gateway.
preconditions: The attacker can get an email delivered through the gateway; no login and no user interaction are needed.
The File Reputation service (part of Cisco AMP) is enabled and assigned to an incoming or outgoing mail policy.
Content Scanner Tools is earlier than 25.3.0.5525 on a physical or virtual gateway running an affected AsyncOS release.
attack_path: Initial access: an email with a crafted attachment is sent to, or relayed through, the gateway.
Execution: attachment scanning writes attacker-controlled files outside the intended folder, leading to commands running as root.
Defence evasion: Cisco warns that an attacker with root access can remove or hide evidence on the appliance.

Follow-on: Cisco advises checking for unexpected uploads to or downloads from external addresses, and warns that SSH keys shared between cluster members may have been taken. The sources read do not describe specific campaigns.
who_is_exposed: Physical and virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances with File Reputation enabled in a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools older than 25.3.0.5525.
Clustered gateways: every member of a cluster with one compromised appliance must be treated as exposed.
Cisco Secure Email Cloud Gateway customers need no action; Cisco says it applied mitigations and contacted affected customers.
Not affected: Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance. Shadowserver tracks nearly 300 internet-exposed gateways (BleepingComputer).
detect: Version and configuration check: confirm Content Scanner Tools version with the CLI status command named in the advisory, and whether 'Enable File Reputation' is ticked in each mail policy's Advanced Malware Protection settings.
Run the System Security log search described in Cisco's advisory on every cluster member: it reports a suspected compromise indicator, an incomplete scan, or no indicator found.
Network and firewall logs: unexpected outbound uploads from the gateway to external addresses, or downloads from unknown addresses.
Logs forwarded off the appliance: changes to files, accounts or services that do not match administrator activity, since local logs may have been altered.

steps: Identify every Secure Email Gateway and check File Reputation and the Content Scanner Tools version.
Run Cisco's System Security log check on each appliance and cluster member before changing anything; preserve forensic data from virtual appliances first, as upgrading destroys it.
Update Content Scanner Tools to 25.3.0.5525 or later (applies without a reboot), or upgrade AsyncOS to a fixed release.
Restrict management access to trusted hosts, separate mail and management interfaces, disable unneeded services such as HTTP and FTP, and forward logs to an external server.
US federal agencies: follow CISA's BOD 26-04 guidance and forensics triage requirements named in the KEV entry.
fixed_versions: AsyncOS 16.0: migrate to a fixed release
AsyncOS 16.5: 16.5.0-780 (Cisco recommends this for releases earlier than 15.5)
verify: Confirm Content Scanner Tools reports 25.3.0.5525 or later on every appliance and cluster member.
Confirm the AsyncOS release is at or above the fixed release for its train.
Rerun Cisco's System Security log check and confirm it reports no compromise indicator.
if_compromised: Physical appliances: contact Cisco TAC and enable remote access for the investigation.
Virtual appliances: preserve forensic data, deploy a new VM on a fixed release and rebuild the configuration by hand without importing old configuration files.
Restore every member of a cluster that contains a compromised appliance, since inter-cluster SSH keys may be exposed.
Rotate all credentials and cryptographic material held on the gateway, and monitor for anomalous behaviour.
Report to your national CERT (US federal agencies to CISA).

CVE-2026-76519.caveats: Only Cisco's advisory is detailed; news coverage repeats it and no independent technical write-up was read. Cisco has not said who is exploiting it or how widely. No fix build is listed for AsyncOS 16.0. A search snippet said the fix was first tracked under another CVE in September; that was not confirmed from a page read. Root access lets attackers hide traces, so a clean log check is not proof of no compromise.

BleepingComputer: Cisco patches actively exploited Secure Email Gateway zero-day

CVE-2026-76964.exploitation_status: No in-the-wild exploitation reported as of 19 Nov 2026 and not in CISA's KEV catalog. Onapsis built a working unauthenticated code execution exploit (ICM2SHELL); Field Effect reports no public scanning as of 11 Nov.
CVE-2026-76964.how_exploited: A memory corruption flaw in the Internet Communication Manager (ICM) of SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP, the kernel component that receives HTTP, HTTPS and WebSocket traffic. SAP says it does not validate certain network input; Pathlock describes a heap out-of-bounds write during WebSocket frame reassembly. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the ICM sends crafted WebSocket traffic that crashes it or corrupts memory in a controlled way. Onapsis showed this gives operating system command execution as the sidadm account that owns the SAP installation, which means full control of the SAP system and its data.
preconditions: SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP kernel 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18 or 9.20 without the correction in SAP Note 3778530 (SAP's CVE record).

The attacker can reach the ICM over the network, directly or through a front-end Web Dispatcher; internet exposure is not required, as internal access via VPN, partners or a compromised workstation suffices.
WebSocket traffic is processed by the ICM; disabling WebSocket is a documented mitigation.
No login and no user interaction are needed (CVSS 10.0). AS Java is not affected.
attack_path: Initial access: an attacker with network reach to the ICM sends crafted WebSocket traffic, with no credentials.
Execution: memory corruption in the ICM process lets the attacker run operating system commands as the SAP installation owner (sidadm), as Onapsis demonstrated.
Impact: full compromise of the SAP system, its business data and, through stored RFC and database credentials, possibly connected systems.
No attacker activity in the wild has been reported.
who_is_exposed: Every SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and S/4HANA system on an affected kernel, on-premises or in private cloud.
Most of all, systems whose ICM HTTP or HTTPS ports are reachable from the internet or partner networks, directly or via a Web Dispatcher.
Organisations also running Web Dispatcher or HANA XS, affected by the sibling flaw CVE-2026-89126 in the same component.
detect: Check the kernel release and patch level of every ABAP instance and Web Dispatcher against SAP Note 3778530 and its FAQ, Note 3778788.
Look for processes started by the ICM process (icman) or by sapwebdisp, which should not spawn shells or tools.
Watch for unexpected ICM crashes, restarts and core dumps in the instance work directories, and unusual WebSocket traffic in ICM logs.
Review user creation and authorization changes made since 10 Nov 2026; SAP and researchers have published no indicators.

steps: Apply SAP Note 3778530 by updating the ABAP kernel to the patch level it names, on every instance.
Update every standalone and embedded Web Dispatcher per SAP Note 3778556 (CVE-2026-89126), and apply Notes 3798345 (Gateway) and 3849308 (SAML2) from the same Patch Day.
Restart the instances so the patched kernel is loaded; an update without a restart leaves the vulnerable kernel in memory.
Start with systems reachable from the internet or partner networks, then internal ones.
Until patched, limit network access to the ICM to traffic coming through a patched Web Dispatcher, or disable WebSocket support.
fixed_versions: SAP kernel 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18 and 9.20: the kernel patch level named in SAP Note 3778530 (note behind SAP login, not read)
workarounds: SAP-documented, per Pathlock: route all ICM access through a qualifying patched Web Dispatcher, effective only if no affected access bypasses it.
Disable WebSocket support in the ICM; this breaks ABAP Push Channels and some Fiori applications.
verify: After restart, confirm in the system status or kernel information that the running kernel patch level matches SAP Note 3778530.
Check that every application server and Web Dispatcher was updated, not only the central instance.
If a workaround is used, test that the ICM can no longer be reached except through the patched Web Dispatcher, or that WebSocket is off.
if_compromised: Isolate the affected SAP host from untrusted networks and preserve ICM traces, work directory logs, core dumps and the security audit log.
Look for files, scheduled jobs or processes created by sidadm and for new or changed SAP users and roles.
Rotate privileged, technical, RFC and database credentials, and check connected systems.
Rebuild from known-good media if operating system access is confirmed, and report to SAP and your national CERT.

CVE-2026-76964.caveats: SAP Note 3778530 and the November Patch Day page need an SAP login and were not read; this rests on SAP's CVE record, CSA Singapore and secondary write-ups. Exact fixed patch levels are not stated here. Field Effect cites Onapsis listing kernels 7.40 to 7.89, while SAP's record lists 7.53 to 9.20. The Onapsis research was not read directly; whether its exploit is public is unclear.

CVE-2026-84869.exploitation_status: Exploited in the wild: in CISA's KEV catalog since 11 Sep 2026. Huntress saw guests spraying file-run requests at MSP servers from 20 Oct and a technician workstation fully compromised on 12 Nov 2026. No actor named.
CVE-2026-84869.how_exploited: A missing authorization flaw in the ScreenConnect client (host client and Access agent), not the server. Inside an active Support or Access session, the other party can transfer a file to the connected client and have it run without the host's authorization or confirmation. Huntress saw attackers join sessions as malicious guests and wait for an MSP technician to connect; the technician's own client then ran the attacker's script, which installed a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to the attacker's relay. That gives the attacker lasting remote access to a workstation holding RMM consoles, saved credentials and customer access.
preconditions: ScreenConnect host client or Access agent older than 26.6.5; patching only the server does not help.
A technician joins a session the attacker is in as a guest, including real customer support sessions or blank-named sessions the attacker created.
The session role allows file transfer, so no prompt stops the file from running.
The attacker needs a foothold in a session (a rogue client on an endpoint or a guest link); Huntress saw a related startup-folder trick work only against the Windows client.
attack_path: Initial access: attackers place rogue ScreenConnect clients on endpoints or open guest sessions on MSP servers and repeatedly request that a script be run.
Execution: when a technician connects, the vulnerable client runs the script from its temp folder within seconds.
Discovery: the script hides itself, reports the new victim to an attacker-controlled bot and runs system reconnaissance.
Persistence: it unpacks a rebranded ScreenConnect client under a Windows Update-style name that connects to the attacker's relay, and alters a Windows logon service.
Next: the attacker can act with everything the technician can reach; earlier waves spread scripts for discovery, tunnelling, security changes and coin mining.
who_is_exposed: MSP and IT support technicians whose workstations run an older ScreenConnect host client, cloud or on-premises.
Organisations whose ScreenConnect Access agents are older than 26.6.5.
Downstream customers of an MSP whose technician workstation is taken over, through the RMM and remote access it holds.
detect: Check the version of every ScreenConnect host client and Access agent; anything before 26.6.5 is vulnerable.
On technician machines, alert when the ScreenConnect client starts command shells, PowerShell or script hosts, especially from a temp folder, or downloads installers.
Look for a second ScreenConnect client, installer files in user or temp folders, new Startup folder entries, and clients connecting to relays you do not run.
In the ScreenConnect session database and audit logs, look for guest-originated file-run or file-send events, repeated blank-named sessions and file paths that climb directories.
Huntress publishes indicators and hunting guidance in its 12 Nov and SCKit posts; use them from there.

steps: Upgrade every technician host client and Access agent to ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later; on-premises servers must also be on 26.6.5 to serve the fixed client.
Cloud customers: servers were updated by ConnectWise, but reinstall or upgrade host clients and Access agents as ConnectWise advises.
Until clients are updated, remove the file-transfer permission from every role and session group that grants it.
Delete blank-named guest sessions that keep requesting files, check again later, and restrict who can join sessions as a guest.
Limit access to the ScreenConnect web interface and installers by IP address or VPN, and do not join unattended sessions you cannot tie to a customer.
Disable the RMM+ extension versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 if installed, linked by Huntress to the related SCKit attacks.
fixed_versions: ConnectWise ScreenConnect 26.6.5 and later (host client, Access agent and on-premises server)
workarounds: ConnectWise: remove the file-transfer permission from each role in the Administration security settings; it reduces exposure but does not replace the update.
verify: Confirm the client version on each technician workstation and endpoint agent reads 26.6.5 or later.
Confirm the file-transfer permission is off for every role until all clients are updated.
Review audit logs after the change for any further guest file-run requests.
if_compromised: Isolate the workstation, and investigate it from a clean device rather than through ScreenConnect.
Preserve logs, the session database and the rogue client files, then remove the rogue client, its folder, the downloaded installer and any persistence.
Restore the altered Windows logon service to its normal start type, or reimage from known-good media.
Rotate every credential reachable from the machine: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault and customer admin accounts; end active web sessions.
Check customer environments the technician could reach, and report to CISA or your national CERT.

CVE-2026-84869.caveats: ConnectWise's own bulletin page refused automated access; its terms come from ConnectWise's CVE record and GitHub disclosure. Huntress's SCKit post does not show SCKit using this flaw; its spread to technicians relied on stolen session cookies and was not seen to succeed. Exploitation start dates differ between reports (late August to October). The RMM+ step is from the related SCKit campaign, not this CVE.
